Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:09:55 GMT

US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorised search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC.

The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation", the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home.

Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponise federal law enforcement".

"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Her communications director Jacklyn Rogers called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."

The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.

A BBC crew saw several agents at the home, some carrying boxes to a van. News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which has said the investigation is about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.

The timing of Monday's raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - has raised concerns from Democrats who have rallied behind Omar.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.

The US House Democratic Party leadership said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump.

"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," it said.

Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar.

Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.

Omar denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email, an archive of which has been seen by the BBC.

She has been targeted by Trump with the president previously suggesting that she "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.

Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession".

The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."

Some Republicans celebrated the search. "Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota Representative Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"

Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.

She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote.

Senior political leaders in Minnesota have also criticised the search. Governor Tim Walz criticised the search on Monday. "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."

Minnesota senator Tina Smith called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections."

Do Lionesses lack ruthlessness in front of goal?

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:54:32 GMT

Alessia Russo (left) started, while Beth Mead (right) came on as a substitute in the first-leg victory over Greece last week

England take a two-goal lead into the second leg of their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off against Greece on Tuesday - but should it have been more?

Sarina Wiegman's side claimed a 3-1 victory in Crete on Friday but left the door open for their opponents - and the manager has demanded more ruthlessness from her team in Leicester (19:30 BST).

The Lionesses had 74% possession in the first leg but only netted three goals from their 26 shots and conceded in the second half, while Greece also hit the bar with a powerful strike.

It is not the first time the Lionesses have struggled to make the most of their chances, so is it an area they need to address?

How do Women's World Cup hopes look for home nations?

Russo named England player of the year

Lionesses on track, Cuthbert returns and Kirby on Brighton's start

Alessia Russo is England's second-highest goalscorer since Euro 2025

England's lack of ruthlessness in front of goal has been an occurring theme since 2023 when they finished runners-up to Spain in the World Cup.

In that tournament, they came through the group stage unconvincingly, beating lower-ranked opposition Haiti and Denmark, both 1-0.

In the knockout stage, they got past Nigeria via a penalty shootout and had to come from behind to beat Colombia 2-1 in the quarter-finals.

In World Cup qualifying this year, England have performed well but have not won with ease, edging past Iceland and Spain and under-firing against Greece.

They are creating chances though, and had 58 touches in the opposition box against Greece and 210 passes in the final third.

"We played differently back then [in 2023]. There's a lot more pressure when you're at the World Cup," said midfielder Keira Walsh.

"In these [qualifying] games, the worrying thing would be if we were not arriving in the final third. That would be a bigger problem.

"It's the final pass, final cross and final shot. That was what was missing [on Friday]. I see the girls do that in training every day. They are fantastic at it.

"It's just putting that in the game tomorrow and hopefully we will."

Walsh said their hesitancy in front of goal was "frustrating" and they know there is work to do in the second leg.

One player who has stepped up to the challenge is Arsenal midfielder Georgia Stanway, who is England's top scorer since Euro 2025 with 10 goals.

She ranks inside the top three for most goals scored by European players in internationals and has a minutes-per-goal ratio of 81.

Wiegman hopes others will follow suit and was clear on where she thinks the team can improve when asked about it on Monday.

"We got in good positions but then it's staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time and deciding what cross, what cutback and whether to go for the far post," added the Dutchwoman.

"That is also about the connections between the players in those situations and taking out the counter-attack [threat]."

England's problem is not a lack of talent but perhaps where best to utilise them.

Chelsea's Lauren James has switched positions from being a winger, to a number 10 and even a centre-forward on occasion.

Injuries to strikers Aggie Beever-Jones and Michelle Agyemang has meant there is little competition for Alessia Russo in the number nine role.

Lauren Hemp has been in fantastic form but is not known for her goalscoring prowess, while Beth Mead is used in midfield as well as attack.

Former England striker Ellen White, who remains the Lionesses all-time top scorer, believes building connections and setting the right tempo is crucial.

"You need to build your own rhythm. You can't just whizz the ball around quickly all the time so you need players in midfield who can dictate it," White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast.

"You then have to have connections with players who are close to you, for example between a number 10 and a number nine.

"Fran Kirby was like a dream for me because she could always put the ball near me and I felt like we had a good connection. You have to build those."

The goals are at least being spread around the team with England having had 11 different goalscorers since Euro 2025.

Defenders Lucy Bronze, Jess Carter and Maya le Tissier have all netted in the past 18 months, while England's number nine has added six to the tally.

But England are still not clinical and have not won any games in which they have trailed since the end of Euro 2025, losing to Brazil and Spain on those occasions.

Regular starter Hemp, who has played 687 minutes, has scored just twice, while the talented James has not found the back of the net in her past 425 minutes.

Part of the problem has been that England have often come up against weaker opposition that sit in a low block and they have found it hard to break them down.

"The movement you have around the box is so important. You need to be unselfish in your movement," ex-England midfielder Kirby told Women's Football Weekly.

"You need runs in behind, even if they won't get the ball. You have to entice teams to come out. You need one person to make a mistake and leave space.

"You also need to pass to someone who has a higher percentage shot position than you. It seemed rushed [against Greece] instead of controlled.

"You have to be intricate in and around the box."

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:28:10 GMT

It was a journey at high speed through the desert - in a pick-up truck with armed fighters in the back. We were travelling with Yemen's pro-government forces, catching glimpses of the Arabian Sea, and forbidding mountain peaks in the distance. Houthi rebels were dislodged from here just days ago, we were told.

When you are battling over expanses of empty desert, progress can be hard to see. But these soldiers, in Shaab-al-Jinn in Lahj governorate, showed us new sandbagged defences - new lines in the sand.

"There was heavy fighting," said Tawfiq Al Haboun, a bearded commander in camouflage uniform.

"They have snipers, artillery and ballistic missile launchers."

Here in the far corners of the Middle East, a war is being waged with global implications.

Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. It's part of wider conflict, stretching from Tehran to Riyadh, where missiles slammed into the international airport this weekend. Yemen's Houthi fighters – already a threat to global shipping – are an increasing threat to Saudi Arabia. And they provide leverage for their backers in Iran, Saudi's regional rival.

Tawfiq Al Haboun pointed to shards of fibre glass and bits of metal at his feet – part of a downed Houthi drone that he said was carrying C4 explosives.

Commander Al Haboun is from the Southern Forces, part of the loose – very loose – alliance of groups fighting for Yemen's government, which is internationally recognised, and backed by Saudi Arabia and its air strikes.

The Houthis swept into the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, ousting the government. A year later a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened, trying to dislodge the Houthis. Despite years of devastating air strikes, that hasn't worked.

The commander tells us about 500 Houthi fighters remain on high ground overlooking a strategic maritime corridor – Bab al-Mandab – connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The narrow waterway, which is crucial for oil exports, was just out of sight on our trip.

The Houthis seized the area after a lightning advance in September. The commander claims pro-government forces have wrested back about 85% (the Houthis have denied losing territory in other areas but not here, as far as our local sources know).

Until they regain complete control, there will be pressure on global oil supplies and on prices.

We heard later that there were heavy clashes the day of our visit. Five military vehicles apparently hit improvised explosive devices planted by the Houthis. It's unclear how many fighters were killed or injured.

As jitters run through international energy markets, hunger menaces weary Yemenis forced to flee this latest spasm of violence.

Around 200,000 have been driven from their homes since the start of this escalation at the beginning of September, according to the International Organization for Migration - all this in the Arab world's poorest country.

As we left the area, we saw a tableau of suffering with families dotted around seeking shelter under scrawny trees. Among one group of women and children we met Aisha, gaunt and elderly and sitting on the ground.

She fled in fear from her home in the Kahboob mountains – an area which has been hit by Houthi drone strikes.

"We have been here for 30 days," she told me.

"I have no animals, no money, no water, no food, not even a blanket... we had to run, with just the clothes on our backs."

At the weekend it was Saudi civilians at the international airport in Riyadh who were doing the running. The Houthi attack - the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade - sent shockwaves around the region and punctured the kingdom's sense of security.

But in operating rooms in Yemen's port city of Aden, geopolitics feels remote. Hospitals are overstretched and doctors are working night and day to treat wounded government fighters coming from the front lines.

We visited one military hospital where 51 casualties arrived in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations.

In a crowded ward, a Houthi fighter lay alongside fighters from the other side. Doctors tell us they make no distinctions.

"I don't care where he comes from, his background or his religion. He is a human being so I should treat him as a human being, "said Dr Bassam Hazar.

Even if the war ends, some will never leave it behind. One man was sitting silently on his bed, a white bandage wrapped around the stump of his left arm, and staples running along his crown.

Others have not lost their fighting spirit, like Ahmed Ali Mahmoud who is smiling and animated, despite multiple fractures.

"I am not waiting to be fully recovered," he tells us.

"I just want to be able to stand. I think it is a religious duty and a national duty [to go back to fight]. The Houthis have destroyed the country. With victory I won't even feel these fractures."

In the next ward lies 12-year-old Ali, a brown-haired boy, who is just one year older than Yemen's civil war. Ali was injured by a drone as he walked down the street and is facing a complicated surgery.

"There is shrapnel near his spine," says Dr Amr Reyadh Assaqaf, standing by his bedside.

"The operation won't be easy, but God willing our staff will be able to handle it."

He tells me Ali is quiet and gentle.

"At first he was depressed," he says, "but we gave him toys to play with and his mood is gradually lifting."

But will war follow him into adulthood?

A truce in 2022 brought a few years of relative calm. But now the Houthis are a stronger enemy, as they have proven at the weekend. They already control most of Yemen's population. If there is a new attempt at mediation – and there is some speculation about this - they may drive a hard bargain.

Back at the hospital, as he prepares for the next wave of casualties, Dr Bassam Hazar hopes for change but doesn't expect it soon.

"Maybe war is good for news," he says, "but it's horrible [for people].

"Sons are losing their fathers, and mothers losing their sons. We need peace."

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

Garvaghy Road residents fail in bid to challenge Drumcree decision

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:24:48 GMT

The Garvaghy Road residents have failed in a bid to challenge the Parades Commission's decision to allow the Drumcree parade to walk down the predominantly nationalist road, the Court of Appeal has ruled.

Judges said their decision was confined to the lawfulness of the decision - it was not deciding whether or not the march should occur.

Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan said the ruling was decided before the secretary of state banned the parade on Friday.

Residents had argued the commission's decision was flawed over how it weighed up the potential for disorder when it approved the parade for the first time since 1998.

In September, the Parades Commission announced that a planned Orange Order parade would be allowed in Portadown.

The commission said the parade should start earlier than the Orange Order wanted and with fewer people, but could go ahead for the first time in 28 years.

On Monday, the Lady Chief Justice found the Parades Commission properly dealt with a police assessment on the potential risk of disorder and gave adequate reasons for its decision.

"This application for leave to appeal has no reasonable prospect of success," she held.

In a statement, the Parades Commission said it noted the decision and it "will study the full judgment carefully once it is received".

Earlier at the High Court, an Orange Order challenge to a decision to ban the Drumcree parade was delayed after Northern Ireland's police chief Jon Boutcher was added to the case.

The Portadown Orangemen want to overturn the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant's intervention on Friday night, which came after he received advice from the chief constable.

Spokesperson for the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition Breandán Mac Cionnaith said the decision was "very academic", considering Sir Chris has "banned the march in question".

He said that discussions on whether to take further legal action will take place with solicitors "later on".

"The ban is in place, that's what we sought, we have prevented the march and we will be back again to prevent further marches," he told reporters outside court.

He added that there are "questions there about the parades commission" and said they will have to "provide a full explanation" on their decision to allow the march.

Mac Cionnaith also acknowledged there was "continued uncertainty" as the Orange Order would "more than likely" plan other marches along the Garvaghy Road.

He said he was hopeful changes to the commission in the new year would "bring a fresh focus and a fresh view" to procedures.

Also speaking outside court, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson said the "lawlessness and the lawbreakers have been defeated", adding that "the law is clear".

"The Portadown District had a legal right to walk the Garvaghy Road.

"The objections to it were unarguable as a matter of law.

"They have lost twice in the high court, twice in the court of appeal - how many times do we need to beat them before they will abide by the law?"

"For those 11 residents' groups dug up from the 1990s to threaten parades, go ahead, go ahead, open them all up," Bryson added.

"Because see after the court of appeal decision today, we're going to be walking all of those traditional routes again."

Bryson said the ruling was "humiliating" for the chief constable and the NI Secretary, who he said the Orangemen would be challenging next week over the decision to ban the parade.

The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time.

Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

Last month the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead on 27 September with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.

That morning, up to 1,000 people - including nationalist politicians - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.

Since then there have been repeated attempts by the Orange Order to walk the route, but they have been stopped by police.

Residents maintained a constant presence on the Garvaghy Road, but that ended on Friday when the NI Secretary Sir Chris Bryant banned the parade following advice from the PSNI chief constable.

Renshaw delivers again as Australia close on win

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:02:01 GMT

Renshaw had South Africa captain Temba Bavuma caught at short leg in the final hour

First Test, Durban (day four of five)

Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56

South Africa 284 & 102-4: Bedingham 46, Markram 45*; Hazlewood 2-20

South Africa need 319 runs to win

Scorecard

Australia are primed to earn a statement victory and end South Africa's unbeaten run under captain Temba Bavuma after Matt Renshaw's remarkable Test continued on day four of their series opener in Durban.

Renshaw, in his second game back after a three-year absence, followed his 190 in the first innings with 89 to allow Australia to declare on 314-6. The 30-year-old then dismissed Bavuma with his part-time off-spin late in the day for his first Test wicket.

Captain Pat Cummins followed with a perfect set-up of Tristan Stubbs - pushing him back with shorter balls before nicking him off with a full delivery - to leave South Africa 102-4 at the close.

Set a world record 421 to win, they need to bat out the final day for a draw with six wickets remaining.

South Africa have won 11 and drawn one of their Tests under Bavuma's captaincy, including their run to the 2025 World Test Championship final where they beat Australia at Lord's.

This is the first Test in a South African summer that includes two more against the Australians, two against Bangladesh and three against England over Christmas.

Even bad light, which cut short the first three days, did not come to South Africa's aid on the fourth evening.

The Proteas' hopes rest largely on the shoulders of opener Aiden Markram who battled to 45 not out from 115 balls.

The right-hander scored a sensational 136 against Australia in the fourth innings of their Test Championship final win and only one active player - Sri Lanka's Kusal Mendis - can better his average of 45.56 in the fourth innings of Tests.

Dragging South Africa out of this position will require immense skill, however. Only twice has a team survived 140 overs to save a Test in the past 13 years.

While Markram shared a stand of 66 in 19.4 overs with David Bedingham the pitch appeared becalmed, but by the close even Renshaw was finding extravagant turn.

One thing in Markram's favour is he has now faced 313 balls from Australia's premier spinner Nathan Lyon in Tests and is yet to be dismissed.

Australia may also be without the fielding excellence of Steve Smith. The former captain spent time off the field on day four having been hit on the helmet by a Anrich Nortje bouncer in making 27.

After Ryan Rickelton top-edged a loose pull shot to Josh Hazlewood in the fourth over, Markram showed similar to restraint to that shown by Renshaw in his first-innings hundred.

Renshaw again held Australia's innings together, but was more adventurous in his strokeplay to set up his side's declaration.

Whether bad light returns on the final day may determine if the tourists were right to bat on until tea.

Wildlife park fatal tiger attack - what we know so far

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:21:11 GMT

Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster remains closed after a man died in the tiger enclosure on Saturday.

Here's what we know so far about the attack.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was busy with visitors when the alarm was raised on Saturday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the park at about 13:30 BST to reports a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway.

Visitors were moved away from the area as the tiger attacked the man, who died a short time later.

The park confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

The park was closed on Saturday and has not yet reopened.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park spans 150 acres with 15 unique habitats featuring wide paths and raised viewing areas.

It focuses on large animal conservation, and counts species including lions, meerkats, lemurs, African penguins and sea lions among its residents.

The tigers are housed in the park's Land of the Tigers, which has a 300m-long raised walkway so visitors can watch the animals from above.

The park's website says people can witness the "majestic cats freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or playing in their very own waterfall pool".

The man has not been named, but eyewitnesses described seeing a man in his 20s on the walkway at the tiger enclosure, wearing headphones and "pacing around" minutes before the incident took place.

South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.

Speaking to the BBC, Ella Ford, 24, from Wirral, said she saw the same man had climbed up onto the barriers and was spoken to by a woman before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".

Ford said she then saw the man shouting for help and the tiger grabbed hold of him.

She estimates about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.

People nearby were confused, she said, and one man was "trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything".

Altai is a rare Amur tiger, also known as a Siberian tiger, the largest big cat in the world.

According to the park, the average weight for males is 160-190kg (25-30 stone), while females are smaller, at 110-130kg (17-20 stone).

Altai, now five years old, moved to Yorkshire Wildlife Park from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025.

The tiger was moved to Doncaster as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers, to join the park's resident tigress Tschuna.

Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time."

A spokesperson for the park thanked everyone who showed concern after the incident.

In a statement on Sunday, they said: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies remain with the family and loved ones of the man who tragically lost his life.

"The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support.

"Many, many people have contacted us about Altai, the tiger.

"We can reassure everyone that he is safe and well and will not be euthanised as a result of this incident."

Dr David Sands, a human-companion animal practitioner at the Animal Behavioural Clinic in Chorley, Lancashire, said tigers were predators that would naturally attack.

"The animal is just being the animal that a million years of evolution has produced," he said.

"It is the top apex predator of its group of animals.

"I don't think any blame could be put on the animal itself."

He added: "Tigers are territorial. This is a male tiger and the incredible weight and power, there's only one outcome because the tiger is in captivity - the enclosure is its territory and a male who can be scented becomes either competition or prey.

"We're so used to seeing them on the small screen in wildlife documentaries.

"This is a very big animal that's got the power to bite and break through bones."

City of Doncaster Council confirmed a health and safety investigation had been launched into the death of the man in the enclosure.

Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.

"As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," he said.

"We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident."

Health and safety inquiry after fatal tiger attack

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:16:08 GMT

A health and safety investigation has been launched into the death of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was closed over the weekend following reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway on Saturday afternoon.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.

"I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," a City of Doncaster Council spokesperson said.

Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.

"We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident," he said.

"At this time, we won't be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time."

The wildlife park remains closed for third day as investigations continue.

A park spokesperson said: "Due to the events over the weekend, the park will remain closed today. Thank you for your understanding."

South Yorkshire Police said the man died at the scene and his family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park said the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

Cars could be seen coming and going from the park earlier, but there were no visitors.

In a message to ticket holders on Monday morning, Yorkshire Wildlife Park said anyone with a booking would be contacted within the next five days to reschedule.

Angela Seivewright, 47, from Bawtry, was laying flowers outside the park gates in tribute to the deceased man. She said she had an annual pass and had visited many times with her two children.

"My daughter was unfortunately sent the video and she's a teenager," she said.

"I found it very distressing, but I think what I've found more distressing is the reaction of the public that I received when I said I hope the human is OK.

"I was surprised at the amount of anger and hatred the people seemed to have towards the gentleman."

On Saturday evening, police said they were aware of videos circulating online and encouraged people not to share the footage.

Dr Campbell Murn, a previous member of the government's zoo expert committee and lecturer at the University of Reading, said while it was a tragic incident, determined people could get inside zoo enclosures.

"I view it in the same way a determined thief will get into somebody's house or somebody's car and despite the best security systems and enclosures sometimes these things happen," he said.

"One of the fundamental approaches of a modern zoo is to give people a wildlife experience and keep them safe so they can learn and they can enjoy being near the animals, but keeping a safety distance that is relevant but not making it too heavy handed."

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Murn said public safety was an "enormous consideration" for zoo standards in the UK.

A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an "urgent review" into "how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next".

Born Free's co-founder Will Travers said: "Putting dangerous wild animals on public display in zoos and safari parks creates a false relationship with humans.

"Visitors are encouraged to get up close and personal - that is a deeply unnatural situation and not without risk."

Jo Judge, chief executive of the British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums, said zoos were subject to a "huge number" of risk assessments, along with full inspections every six years and periodic inspections every three.

"There are so many processes and procedures in place to ensure the safety of everybody who is visiting zoos and aquariums and these are incredibly rare incidents," she said.

"Zoos are actually one of the safest places you can visit."

She added the body had received many messages of support for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park.

"There's no concern from the rest of the community, because we know how well regulated we are, how well licensed we are, all of the procedures and policies that have to be put in place to make sure zoos and aquariums are safe for staff, for the animals and for the public."

The tiger has been at Yorkshire Wildlife Park since it was moved from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025 as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers.

Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said Altai was born at the site in 2021.

She said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time."

Retired animal behaviourist Dr David Sands said anyone entering an enclosure would be seen as a threat.

"The animal is just being the animal that one million years of evolution has produced," he said.

"It's the top apex predator of its group of animals and I don't think any blame can be put on to the animal itself.

"Could you make the enclosure higher, bigger, more inner protections - well, where do you stop?"

Pope pulls out of controversial Afghanistan T20 league

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:13:54 GMT

Ollie Pope has played 64 Tests for England

England batter Ollie Pope has pulled out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League.

Pope had been due to be the only centrally contracted England player in the running for the inaugural edition of the APL, which is set to take place in the United Arab Emirates later this year.

On Monday, when England's latest batch of contracts were confirmed, director of cricket Rob Key said he would not play in the APL but it is "legally hard" to prevent England players from taking part.

In order for any English player to take part in the league they would require a No Objection Certificate from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB).

With batter Pope being a contracted player, Key would have been involved in deciding the Surrey man's availability for the APL.

However, it is understood Pope has taken the decision to withdraw from the draft taking place later this month independently of Key's view on the competition.

"Legally it is hard to stop players going over and playing in these competitions," Key told the Test Match Special podcast. "It becomes a moral judgement and players have to be prepared to take the right moral stance.

"Personally, and it is easy for me to say, I would not go and play. But it is down to the player to make that decision."

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal

The ECB has refused to schedule bilateral cricket with Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in the country in 2021.

Last year, ECB chair Richard Thompson described the Taliban's oppression of women and girls as "gender apartheid".

England have, however, continued to play against Afghanistan at global events, including World Cups in both limited-overs formats and the Champions Trophy.

"I don't agree with the way women have been treated in Afghanistan," said Key. "The way things happen out there is not something I agree with so it is not something I would go and do."

Pope has been handed a new 12-month England contract despite not playing international cricket since the third Ashes Test in Australia last December.

He was recalled to the Test squad for the series against Pakistan in the home summer and has stood in as captain on six occasions, including against India at The Oval in 2025.

When asked if he had made his feelings clear to Pope, Key replied: "I had that conversation and Ollie will have to make his decision."

Before England's last meeting with Afghanistan, at the 2025 Champions Trophy, Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi led calls for the fixture to be boycotted.

In September, she told BBC Sport: "Why are we here again? Women and girls in Afghanistan are denied the same rights as those in our country, and the women's team lives in exile," she said.

"Does that not concern the players, especially those with daughters, sisters or mothers?

"I hope the International Cricket Council (ICC) refuses to sanction this event. Continuing to allow Afghanistan full member status makes a mockery of its own membership criteria."

Former England batter Dawid Malan is entered into the APL draft, alongside the likes of Moeen Ali, James Vince and James Rew – Somerset's Rew made his Test debut in June.

"As players we take our guidance from the ICC and the boards," Malan told the TMS podcast.

"As a player it is tough because you have what is morally right and what is by the law. I have a daughter and I want her to play sport and get into sport and enjoy it. I fully understand the argument, but at the end of the day I am a cricketer and need to be able to pay my rent and be able to earn a living while I can.

"England don't play bilateral series against Afghanistan, but they do play them in World Cups – what's the difference? As players, you sometimes want a board decision to be made that says 'we don't think this is right, we are making a stance against it', then the players will buy into it.

"I don't think anyone agrees with what is happening in Afghanistan, but once something gets approved you sit there as players and say: 'It's a job, and I have to play and do what I need to do', then you're stuck in a position of what is morally right and what is morally not."

On Friday, Dean Ahmad, an agent who represents ex-England all-rounder Moeen, wrote on X: "Morality in sport matters, but so does consistency.

"The Taliban's treatment of women is indefensible. Yet why are cricketers singled out while governments and corporations maintain ties with states accused of serious human rights abuses. Selective outrage isn't morality."

Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine?

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:54:19 GMT

US President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for the global reduction in diesel exports and the spike in prices around the world, saying President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world".

"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".

But others have pointed the finger of blame at the US-Israel war with Iran for cutting exports of the refined fuel from the Gulf region.

After Trump announced a controversial deal to import diesel from Russia - promising "lower prices for Americans" - BBC Verify has looked at what has been affecting supplies of the fuel in recent months and years.

The figures suggest that while both the Ukraine and Iran conflicts have significantly reduced global diesel exports - the fall in supplies from the Gulf states due to the war with Iran has been greater.

While the rising cost of diesel directly hits drivers, there's a wider concern because of its use in the lorries, vans and ships that form the backbone of global supply chains. Any increase in transport costs could be fed through to consumers in the form of higher prices.

Average US retail diesel prices on 5 October were $6.20 (£4.69) per gallon, just shy of the record of $6.50 per gallon seen on 21 September, according to the latest figures from the US Energy Information Administration.

Before the war with Iran a gallon of diesel in the US cost around $3.50.

Similarly, average UK diesel prices are currently touching record highs, with data from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero showing that on 5 October a litre cost 199p.

In 2025, around 6.8 million barrels of diesel per day were being exported to the global market, according to figures from the shipping data company Kpler. Exports account for around a quarter of total global diesel consumption. The rest comes from countries' domestic production.

In September 2026, global exports had fallen to 5.8 million barrels per day - a decline of around one million barrels per day.

Some countries, notably the US, have increased their diesel exports over the past year, but overall net global exports have declined.

And analysts say it's that drop which has been responsible for pushing up the retail price of diesel.

In 2025 Russia was exporting around 810,000 barrels of diesel per day but by September 2026 that had fallen to around 140,000 barrels per day - a decline of around 670,000 barrels per day.

Jonathan Leader Maynard, from King's College London, says "many analysts" would see the decline in Russia's exports of oil products, including diesel, as being "primarily due to Ukraine's drone attacks" rather than international sanctions.

As well as being a major exporter of crude oil, the Middle East is also a significant global hub for the production of diesel.

In 2025 the Gulf states - Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman - were exporting around 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day.

In September 2026 that had fallen to around 670,000 barrels per day.

This sharp decline has been driven by the impact of the US-Iran war on the flow of exports of refined diesel from the Gulf states through the Strait of Hormuz.

Traffic flows in the waterway have been badly disrupted by Iranian strikes on tankers and the US blockade of Iran's ports.

While estimates from ship-tracking firms suggest the flow of crude oil through the waterway returned close to pre-war levels last month - due, in part, to the US navy helping to protect shipping - the flow of refined diesel from the Middle East has remained far below pre-war levels.

The figures suggest the conflict with Iran has had a greater impact on the global drop in diesel export volumes than the Ukraine war.

Exports from Russia are down around 670,000 barrels a day compared with a fall of around 810,000 from the Middle East

Though analysts stress both are significant.

"The US-Iran conflict delivered a major shock to global energy markets in 2026, but the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict is now amplifying this pressure by taking Russian refineries offline," Paul de Leeuw, director of the Energy Transition Institute at Robert Gordon University, told BBC Verify.

His comments were echoed by Rory Johnson, an oil analyst at Commodity Context, who said Ukraine's attacks are "bringing the pain of the war to the Russian homeland and largely knocking the world's second-largest diesel exporter out of the market".

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:22:24 GMT

Piero Hincapie (right) and Martin Zubimendi joined Arsenal last summer

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says it is "far from ideal" that Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi were injured in a post-match training session after the Gunners' 2-1 Premier League win against Leeds.

A training session was held after Saturday's match at Emirates Stadium for players who either did not feature in or did not play the full 90 minutes against Leeds.

Ecuador defender Hincapie was carried off by goalkeeper Illan Meslier during the session, and Arteta later confirmed Spain midfielder Zubimendi was also hurt.

Hincapie, 24, came on after 82 minutes as Arsenal saw out victory against Leeds, while Zubimendi, 27, was an unused substitute.

"We had a training session planned after the match for everyone that didn't get enough minutes, and in two unfortunate actions we lost two players," Arteta said in a news conference before Tuesday's Champions League match against Lille.

"They'll have further scans to see where they are and we'll have that time frame for how long they are going to be out for."

When asked by the media what could have been done to prevent the injuries, Arteta joked the pair should not have trained.

"Never train and they don't get injured. The consequence of that is when you ask them to play they have no rhythm and no impact in the game," the Spaniard added.

"It's never happened in seven years I've been here. It could happen in the training session the next day.

"It's happened now and hopefully it doesn't happen again, but what can you do?

"If I had a crystal ball I would just say 'guys, get in the jacuzzi and I will see you tomorrow'."

Hincapie has made three Premier League appearances off the bench this season but started Arsenal's Champions League win over Napoli last month.

Zubimendi has also largely featured as a substitute, making five Premier League appearances from the bench.

Arsenal had planned for the players who did not play a full game or had not had minutes in the 2-1 win to train at the Emirates Stadium so that all of the squad could have a recovery day on Sunday and then train on Monday.

Arteta regularly arranges for the players who have not played a full match to take part in a small-sided game on the pitch, and this is how Hincapie and Zubimendi picked up the injuries.

The manager does this so that all of the players have a similar output when they are navigating their busy fixture schedule.

Arteta, who says it was done to get "everybody in the best rhythm", said Hincapie's ankle injury was more serious than Zubimendi's.

Substitute goalkeeper Meslier was seen carrying Hincapie off the pitch on his back, even though there were staff members present.

And this is something that Arteta does not seem to be happy about, saying: "that's something else, not to discuss here".

Tom Cruise film Digger forecast to become one of Hollywood's biggest flops

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:11:27 GMT

Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance at the box office.

Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend in cinemas.

It brings Digger's total box office takings so far to around $35m (£26m) globally. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".

The film's box office takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.

That would put Digger in the same bracket as other films which lost upwards of $100m, including 1995's Cutthroat Island, 2002's The Adventures of Pluto Nash, 2005's Sahara and 2012's John Carter.

Other films estimated to have lost nine-figure sums include Mars Needs Moms (2011), Amsterdam (2022), The 13th Warrior (1999), The Marvels (2023) and Speed Racer (2008).

Digger's performance stands in sharp contrast to the success of major franchises starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of Top Gun and Mission: Impossible.

Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.

The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.

However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).

Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.

The film is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.

Digger received generally poor reviews from critics, prompting Warner Bros to launch a new marketing campaign urging audiences to "decide for yourself".

Meanwhile, the new sequel to the Oscar-winning hit The Social Network also struggled at the box office on its opening weekend.

The Social Reckoning took $5.5m (£4.1m) in the US, significantly lower than the $22m (£16m) its predecessor took on its opening weekend in 2010, not adjusted for inflation.

Globally, Aaron Sorkin's latest film, starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong and Jeremy Allen White, took around $9m (£6.8m).

The film tells the true story of a Facebook engineer, Frances Haugan, who leaked internal documents to a reporter after becoming concerned about some of the company's practices.

The Social Reckoning was beaten in the US box office chart by horror movie Other Mommy, psychological thriller Verity, video game adaptation Resident Evil and Brad Pitt's wilderness thriller Heart of the Beast.

Normandy veteran Henry Rice dies aged 100

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:34:49 GMT

World War Two veteran Henry Rice, who survived a near-miss when a torpedo was fired at the boat he was on, has died at the age of 100.

Rice, from Cranleigh in Surrey, was a signalman aboard HMS Eastway as part of the Normandy landings, arriving at Juno Beach five days after D-Day.

He received the Legion d'honneur from the French government and had called for schools to teach children more about the Normandy landings because the "world is dangerous at the moment".

A spokesperson from the Spirit of Normandy Trust, a charity for veterans, said: "Henry was a great character, with a cheeky smile that endeared him to everyone he met."

Rice previously told the BBC that revisiting Normandy for a remembrance service in June this year meant "everything" to him.

"I've had a super lifetime," he said.

When thinking about veterans who had died, he added: "I find it too easy to wipe a tear away, so I don't let myself think too deeply. But when I'm on my own, then I do."

Troops from the UK, the US, Canada, and France attacked German forces on the coast of northern France on 6 June 1944, known as D-Day.

Rice delivered vehicles, men and equipment to reinforce the effort.

It was the largest military naval, air and land operation ever attempted and marked the start of the campaign to liberate Nazi-occupied north-west Europe.

Rice died just two weeks after Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay died at the age of 101.

Hay had survived being captured just weeks after D-Day and spent years educating children about World War Two.

The Royal Navy said Rice went on to Malta where he was land-based for 12 weeks before travelling through the Suez Canal into the Red Sea.

He spent some time based in the Gulf before going on to Sri Lanka, Burma and Singapore.

The Royal Navy said one of Rice's close encounters was a torpedo being fired towards the boat he was on, only for the missile to go beneath the hull.

In March this year, his family hosted a special celebration for his 100th birthday.

He told the BBC that, generally, veterans like himself only shared wartime experiences quietly amongst themselves.

"At home or with friends, you just say 'yeah, I was a matelot mate'," he chuckled.

The Spirit of Normandy Trust said he was committed to remembering those who were sent to war and never returned.

He attended remembrance events in the UK, including the Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey and the Cenotaph Parade.

At the planting of ceramic poppies at the Tower of London, he handed Queen Camilla the last poppy to be placed to mark VE Day 80, according to the Spirit of Normandy.

Earlier this year, Rice met fellow D-Day veteran Ronald Hendrey, from Clacton-on-Sea in Essex for the first time to share memories of the Normandy invasion - one of his last acts of remembrance.

"He will be greatly missed by all and we offer his family our most sincere condolences," a Spirit of Normandy spokesperson said.

Schoolboy knife attacker texted 'sorry' to mum

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:12:41 GMT

The mother of a teenage boy who stabbed a girl in a masked attack at a school said she received a message from her son saying "sorry" shortly after the attack, a trial has heard.

Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March following reports a 15-year-old had been stabbed in the back.

The defendant, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, denies attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.

After learning about the unfolding events on social media, his mother told the jury at King's Lynn Crown Court she "was in complete shock" when she realised her son was involved.

The mother told the trial that her son was "very quiet, very funny, very smart" and had a "dry sense of humour".

The court has previously heard how the defendant had written notes saying he hated women while the schoolgirl victim described to police how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed".

During Monday's proceedings, the mother described the night before the attack as "completely normal", and said her son left for school at his usual time the following morning.

She said she first became aware something was happening when she was "doom-scrolling".

She messaged her son asking if he was OK, but said she did not "get an immediate response".

"When you realise there has been an incident at the school and you don't hear from children, it's worrying," she said.

She had the ability to see her son's location using a phone app, and messages on social media had said there had been a knife attack and that someone had left the school grounds.

"When I saw he wasn't at school and someone had run away, I was concerned [my son] was involved," she told the court.

She said she received a message from him saying "I'm sorry", and when she called her son and asked what had happened, he replied "nothing good" and that he had "hurt someone".

She told the court her son did not sound like himself, spoke in "very short sentences" and "sounded very upset".

Alongside her husband, she went to try to find her son and was passed by two police cars "with blues and twos on".

She called 999, gave the police her son's location, and was advised to head home.

"I was in complete shock," she told the court.

Prosecuting counsel Christopher Paxton, KC, asked the mother if there were any concerns about how her son was using his phone and if she was checking his phone.

She answered "no" to both questions.

A teacher who chased the boy following the attack described how the then 15-year-old had "legged it".

He told the court that a person who witnessed the stabbing came to him and said "she's been stabbed".

When he went to the corridor, the teacher said "the only person I saw was dressed completely in black".

He said he was "very shocked" and shouted to the boy to stop.

He told jurors he ran after the boy for about 25 seconds and continued to shout "stop" and saw that a black glove had been dropped.

The trial continues.

What happens to sports kit that never gets worn?

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:18:31 GMT

This video can not be played

What happens to unworn sports kit?

For an elite athlete, pulling on Olympic kit can be the reward for years of sacrifice. But some of that clothing never makes it out of the packaging.

Inside a warehouse on England's south coast, boxes are stacked with pristine Team GB clothing from Paris 2024 and Milan Cortina 2026. Tracksuit bottoms, jackets, hoodies and T-shirts sit untouched. Among them are garments created for Olympic opening ceremonies. All of it is unworn.

Commercial constraints can make excess stock difficult to shift at scale.

Now a new partnership means hundreds of items of surplus Team GB clothing and unsold merchandise will be resold through a specialist platform, with proceeds supporting the British Olympic Association's (BOA) charity arm, the Team GB Foundation.

The initial launch will include 700 items from Paris 2024.

It is one way of giving sportswear a second life. But why does that surplus exist, and why can perfectly usable clothing be so difficult to pass on?

The BOA is far from the only organisation dealing with excess kit – elite sport in general struggles with kit wastage.

5thread, a consultancy specialising in sustainability, estimates that up to 100,000 items of sports kit end up in UK landfill every year.

"It is a huge issue and it's also a complex issue," says Joanna Czutkowna, director of 5thread and a doctoral researcher in sports apparel and the circular economy.

"A lot of this kit is bought before they know which athletes are going to complete in the sport or the event. So there's a lot of excess stock generated at the point of order.

"Also, the types of contracts that you get for this have something called value in kind, so it's not a transactional contract. There's almost an incentive to get free product."

Czutkowna is describing practices across elite sport, rather than Team GB's arrangements.

Performance requirements also complicate efforts to reduce waste. Athletes need clothing designed to help them compete, so reducing quantities or changing materials is not always straightforward.

The total surplus is difficult to measure. Kit can remain in warehouses or athletes' garages without entering a waste stream where it can be counted.

The issue extends across sport, from clubs to countries.

European football governing body Uefa estimates that up to 60% of professional team apparel, external is disposed of at the end of the season, although this figure has not been independently verified.

The obstacles are not to do with the condition of the clothing.

"Contracts can prohibit reuse because they don't want it on the market or there might be a particular innovation that they want to hold back," Czutkowna says.

Adam Stevens, co-founder of Kitround, the specialist resale platform working with Team GB among others, says sponsorship and supply agreements remain financially important to sport, but there are ways to respect them while allowing clothing to be used again.

"There are an awful lot of people, whatever sport they do, whatever teams they support, who simply can't afford to buy new," he says.

British kitesurfer Lily Young training off the coast of Weymouth

For British kitesurfer Lily Young, who is targeting a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the pressure to find a competitive edge can itself create surplus.

Athletes preparing for major championships want to leave nothing to chance.

"That does mean that we also end up with a lot of waste - a lot of things where you're like, 'this is basically brand new, but it's not quite good enough to maybe win'."

Changes in sponsors can also leave athletes with clothing they can no longer wear.

Young and fellow athletes have passed T-shirts to younger squad members and youth teams. Wetsuits and other equipment can also be passed on where they remain suitable.

But equipment that no longer meets an elite athlete's needs could help someone else start, and more organisations such as Sail GP and the Royal Yachting Association are using specialist platforms to sell second-hand elite kit to the public at much lower prices.

"We know that one of the main barriers to entry is cost," Young says.

For Czutkowna, organisations need to think harder about how long their products can remain useful - and who could benefit from them.

"A lot of this comes back to common sense," she says. "It's kind of a waste not, want not."

Jen Rouse, managing director of the Team GB Foundation, says ordering is becoming more precise and the amount left over is reducing.

Team GB is also considering producing some clothing without dates or event-specific names, so it could be used across more than one Olympic cycle. It is also exploring opportunities for athletes to return clothing they no longer need.

She rejects the suggestion that excess clothing has previously simply accumulated unused.

"It's not necessarily been sitting gathering dust in storage. It's always found a way out," she says.

The partnership with Kitround creates another route, with sales supporting the Team GB Foundation.

The aim is a circular economy for kit: keeping clothing and equipment in use through reuse, repair and resale.

For Stevens, the principle behind finding kit another home is simple.

"A kit was made to be worn. It was made to be out there on the field, on the water, in the pool, and it should be back out there.

"That's really what underpins everything - making sure this kit doesn't go to landfill and that it can have a second life."

Halloween 'bigger than Christmas', say businesses

BBC News Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:14:42 GMT

Halloween has become so popular that some attractions now make more money from the spooky season than Christmas, operators say.

From pumpkin festivals and haunted mazes to zombie experiences, businesses say demand for Halloween events has soared as the celebration grows from a single night into a month-long attraction.

At Avon Valley Adventure Park near Bath, Halloween activities now generate around a third of the site's annual income. Founder Doug Douglas said: "Halloween is really important for us, it has surpassed Christmas."

"We make half of our turnover in October, and one third comes from the week of Halloween alone," said David Gaze, owner at Chaplins fancy dress shop in Bristol.

Retailers, farm attractions and scare parks say people are spending more on costumes, decorations and immersive experiences, helping to make October one of their busiest times of the year.

Chaplins has been a staple in the city centre for 35 years, back when people wore fancy dress on New Year's Eve.

"People don't do that so much anymore, now it's mostly for Halloween," Gaze said.

Last year, it saw its busiest October to date, with customers individually spending an average of £40 on fancy costumes and accessories.

"People are spending more and the week of Halloween is our busiest every year, we get queues outside the front door."

"It's usually what people are seeing on TV that sells well. Some years ago it was boiler suits from Squid Game, everyone wanted that," he added.

Halloween's growing popularity is also benefiting supermarkets and retailers selling sweets, decorations and party supplies.

In a survey carried out in March by market researcher IGD, 36% of shoppers said they planned to celebrate Halloween this year, up from 27% in 2025.

Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the British Retail Consortium, said at this time of year "retailers will be competing hard" as they see "greater demand for sweets and chocolate, as well as decorations and costumes".

"Halloween has become an increasingly popular occasion for people to enjoy," he said.

And some like to start celebrations as early as possible, like Catarina Vieira, who lives in Swindon and started decorating her house last week.

"I spend between £150 to £200 every year on Halloween," she said, adding that is mostly on decorations and thrill events.

Vieira said feeling scared about monsters is a "fun escape" from the stresses of her everyday life as an A&E doctor.

"I think having a holiday where you are scared about something that is 'real', instead of the usual daily mental pressures, touches me in a way."

"It helps me escape reality for a bit, being scared about something that is tangibly scary, like monsters or bats," she added.

But it is not just retail. Many farmers have found ways to diversify their land, by turning it into lucrative family attractions on Halloween.

In October, pumpkin patches where you can pick your own pumpkin are high in demand, with popularity being largely driven by social media.

Farms often charge an entry fee which can vary significantly, from around £2 to £15 per person, for children and adults alike.

With the biggest whoppers selling for upwards of £15 a piece, a fun family day out pushing wheelbarrows full of pumpkins can become costly, yet some attractions sell out quickly.

Heather Parry, managing agent at National Farm Attractions Network (NFAN), said Halloween has become one of the biggest seasons of the year for some farmers.

"Ten years ago, a pumpkin patch was a field and a wheelbarrow. Now it's a wonderful experience for the whole family," she said.

The network has around 200 members and "almost all" embrace the spooky season with a mix of "maize mazes, after-dark trails, scare attractions and pumpkin festivals".

"Diversification is key for many farms to thrive," she added, saying it has helped them mitigate existing challenges.

Parry said: "Farmers are coping with climate change, change in government support and requirements, high input costs, the changes to inheritance tax relief on farms along with many other things."

"Halloween gives farms a short, high-footfall season," she added.

Doug Douglas, founder of Avon Valley Adventure Park, said their Halloween events grow every year and now generate a third of their yearly income.

"We turn over £2m from our activities in October," said Douglas.

He added: "Halloween is really important for us, it has surpassed Christmas."

The park sits on a 90-acre farm in Keynsham, near Bath, and was once a fruit farm after his dad bought the land more than 30 years ago.

Now Douglas runs family activities during school holidays and seasonal events, including for Halloween and Christmas.

FEAR Scream Park is their award-winning attraction offering "immersive scare experiences" over 13 nights in October, with scare mazes and live actors.

This month, they are expecting around 30,000 visitors but Douglas said the event is not "massively profitable" due to costs.

"It costs us about £750,000 to put on the event," he said. "On staff wages alone, we employ about 200 staff, including around 120 actors."

In addition, they run a popular pumpkin event which attracts around 120,000 people each year.

Douglas said: "Everyone thinks they're easy [to put on], but we've got fire shows, stilt walkers, actors, we put in a big bar and we turn it into a real festival field."

At HMP Gloucester, it is zombies that visitors must try and escape from as they walk past old prison cells, facing all sorts of scary encounters.

The post-apocalyptic zombie experience 'Salvation-Z' is run by Gloucester Prison Events at the defunct prison and employs around 30 actors from the local area, according to actor manager Clive Barzillia.

"We get lots and lots of people apply for the acting roles. They have to audition and if they're shy we have to shake it out of them," he said.

He said actors are taught welfare training and paramedics are also on site.

"Ultimately it's a safe environment", he said.

"Actors are trained to look out for people that might be vulnerable or sensitive, and they can adapt their acting."

He added: "People get right into the spirit of it," talking about the visitors.

"We've noticed they want to come in fancy dress now, they want to become characters themselves."

Number of known species of giant waterlilies almost doubles

New Scientist October 08, 2026

Giant waterlilies are not exactly inconspicuous plants. But in the past few years, we have discovered no fewer than three new species, taking the total to five. The latest species to be described was identified with the help of social media, satellite photos and a mad jungle dash in the dark.

“I think it’s incredible that we find something so new, which is so large, in this world where we think everything is already known,” says Maarten Christenhusz at the Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, who has helped describe two of the new species.

Why rediscovering extinct species can actually be a bad thing

Giant waterlilies are famed for their massive leaves, which grow up to 3 metres wide. For many decades, just two species were known: Victoria amazonica and Victoria cruziana. Then in 2016, Carlos Magdalena at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew, London, noticed that giant waterlilies grown from seeds from Bolivia were a bit different, with even larger leaves. In 2022, Magdalena and his colleagues published a paper showing that this was a new species, Victoria boliviana.

Advertisement

Magdalena hasn’t stopped there. In 2021, Jeremiah Harris, who runs a carnivorous plant business in the US, posted pictures online that he took while swimming near the Inírida river in Colombia next to what he assumed was V. amazonica.

Magdalena was struck by the photos because scientists had thought there were no giant waterlilies in this region. “This river is geographically completely separated from the Amazon, and has been for millions of years, and that is why this is such an interesting find,” says Christenhusz.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their team examined satellite photos and found telltale green dots confirming there really were giant waterlilies growing there. They then organised an expedition to the region. The team found two plants but neither was flowering – and analysing the flowers is a crucial step in establishing whether a waterlily really is a new species.

At 11pm on the last night of the expedition, with the plane due to leave at 9am, the researchers seemed to have failed. Then one of the guides, Gustavo Melo from the Indigenous Tucano community, said he knew where some more giant waterlilies were growing. The team set off by boat in the dark, and found five plants in a small lake just before sunrise, including some that were flowering.

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues have now published a paper describing the new species, which they have named Victoria colombiana. It differs from V. amazonica in the orientation of the spines beneath the leaves, and in the shape of its flowers and fruits. The spines are a defence against manatees and plant-eating fish, Christenhusz says, so they vary between species depending on which herbivores are most prevalent.

Botanists have finally proved what Charles Darwin was unable to nail down – that a genus of plants known to catch insects also digests them, suggesting the extent of plant carnivory has been underestimated

As far as the team is aware, V. colombiana is found in only one small area. A single event, such as a pollution spill, could wipe out the entire species, says Christenhusz. But the team is planning to try to collect seeds to help ensure the species survives.

Meanwhile, Magdalena also realised that the giant waterlilies growing in the Pantanal region of South America, hundreds of kilometres to the south-east of Colombia, must have been isolated from other populations for a very long time. Sure enough, genetic studies revealed that they are another distinct species, despite looking very similar to V. cruziana. Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues will publish a paper soon to describe this fifth species, which they have decided to name Victoria mattogrossensis.

Phytotaxa DOI: 10.11646/phytotaxa.778.2.1
