The Monte Verde controversy is back: who first lived in the Americas?

New Scientist October 12, 2026

This is an extract from Our Human Story, our newsletter about the revolution in archaeology. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every month.

In every scientific field, there are totemic places. The CERN physics laboratory that houses the Large Hadron Collider; the Cavendish lab in Cambridge where James Watson and Francis Crick did their research on the structure of DNA; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.

In archaeology, one such place is a site in Chile called Monte Verde. For half a century, Monte Verde has been central to our understanding of the peopling of the Americas. For two decades, the story that Monte Verde told was wildly controversial. It then became fairly settled, but, as of this year, it has become controversial again.

Advertisement

The details of the new argument are, at times, punishingly technical, and I’m going to give only the roughest outline of them or we’d be here all week. However, the actual questions at the back of all this are simple: who were the first people to live in the Americas, and when did they arrive?

The Americas were the last continents to be settled by humans. (Well, there’s Antarctica, but given it was discovered only within the last 300 years, let’s not worry about it.) The oldest known hominins lived in Africa, and we don’t see hard evidence of hominins anywhere else until 1.8 million years ago, when Homo erectus reached what is now Georgia – the one in Eurasia, not the US state. Later, hominins like Neanderthals and Denisovans spread throughout Eurasia. Later still, our species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa and migrated all over Eurasia.

That’s a lot of travelling around, over a period of nearly 2 million years. Yet none of those people seem to have reached the Americas. While the exact timing of that momentous landfall is very contentious, we are talking at most about the last 35,000 years – and the main waves of settlement seem to have been between 20,000 and 13,000 years ago.

That’s where Monte Verde comes in. It has long been claimed to be the oldest evidence of humans in the Americas – or at least the oldest one with indisputable traces of human intervention and reliable dating evidence. Monte Verde told us that people entered the Americas thousands of years earlier than previously thought.

Now, the archaeological data at the site is under attack – and with it, our understanding of the prehistory of the Americas.

The genome of a long-extinct ancient human is hiding within us

Monte Verde is in southern Chile, a few tens of kilometres inland from the Pacific Ocean. To the south, the coast of South America fractures into a confusing scatter of peninsulas and islands. The Andes mountain chain, which runs north-south, lies to the east. Monte Verde sits on a flood plain: it is on the banks of the Chinchihuapi creek, a tributary of the larger Maullín river.

Archaeologists have been excavating Monte Verde on and off for almost 50 years, since 1977. One of the most prominent is Tom Dillehay at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. He and his colleagues have excavated two relatively close sites, simply dubbed Monte Verde I and Monte Verde II.

Monte Verde I is tricky. It contains burned areas and numerous putative stone artefacts – although some may simply be natural stones, albeit unusual ones. Early studies radiocarbon dating the charcoal placed the site as 33,000 years old, which has never been widely accepted. In a 2015 study, Dillehay’s team dated Monte Verde I to between 14,500 and 18,500 years ago. However, because the human traces are so sparse, the older end of that range is disputed, and Dillehay himself doesn’t put too much store by it.

Stronger evidence comes from Monte Verde II. Here, the team found artefacts made of stone, wood and bone, as well as what seem to be the foundations for a structure, perhaps a tent. Directly above the layers containing these materials was a layer of peat, which Dillehay’s team dated to 14,500 years ago. This implies that Monte Verde II is at least that old. In 1997, a team of archaeologists visited the site and gave Dillehay’s analyses an official stamp of approval. Subsequent evidence has supported the dating: for instance, in 2008, Dillehay’s team identified marine algae at Monte Verde II, which they directly dated to 14,220 to 13,980 years ago.

Today, Dillehay says, the evidence for the age of Monte Verde consists of “more than 1000 radiocarbon and luminescence dates and intact chrono-stratigraphy, as well as diagnostic stone tools dated in other sites”.

These finds at Monte Verde II effectively detonated our main ideas around the peopling of the Americas. For much of the 20th century, most archaeologists believed that the first Americans were peopled dubbed the Clovis, after a site in New Mexico. Clovis peoples made distinctive pointed stone tools. The oldest Clovis sites are about 13,000 years old.

So strong was the consensus around the Clovis First model that any pre-Clovis site came under immense scrutiny. Sites like Cooper’s Ferry, Buttermilk creek and Paisley caves in North America have been endlessly picked over. Monte Verde was the first site to survive this process and become established.

In March this year, another team of archaeologists tried to tear the whole edifice down.

Denisovan tools from cave in China show how mysterious humans lived

Todd Surovell first learned about Monte Verde in 1994, when he was an undergraduate at the University of Wisconsin. Dillehay came as a guest speaker to talk about the site. “I was absolutely blown away,” says Surovell. “It really inspired my career.”

Surovell is now an archaeologist at the University of Wyoming. Increasingly sceptical about Monte Verde, Surovell and his colleagues visited the area in 2022 and 2023. They published their results in Science in March 2026.

His team didn’t excavate at Monte Verde I or II, but along the banks of Chinchihuapi creek. Based on the layers of sediments they found, they reconstructed a history of the area.

About 20,000 years ago, they say, when Earth’s climate was deep in a glacial period, the region was the outwash from a glacier extending down from the Andes: a plain with braided streams and lots of sand and gravel. Later, as the climate warmed, a forest moved in, transitioned into a wetland, and was then buried – forming a black peat. Then, around 11,000 years ago, a volcano called Michinmahuida erupted and blanketed the area in a layer of ash, called the Lepué Tephra. Afterwards, Chinchihuapi creek cut down through all these layers, forming an exposed surface where people lived.

This means that Monte Verde II must be younger than the Lepué Tephra ash layer, Surovell’s team argues. Based on dating of sands and gravels at their excavation sites, they place it between 8200 and 4200 years ago.

To say this has caused a row would be an understatement. The Science paper now has seven “eLetters” attached to it, responding to the various claims. On 19 August, Dillehay and his colleagues published an entire paper in the journal PaleoAmerica, rebutting Surovell’s team’s arguments.

A central problem with all this is that Surovell’s team excavated near Monte Verde but not actually at it. Or, as Dillehay puts it: “They did not excavate at the site, never saw the stratigraphy and examined only surface landscape from 50 to 4000 meters away in distance.” Because this is a flood plain, where rivers shift over time and sediments can be mixed, extrapolating from one place to another is tricky.

For instance, Surovell’s team identified a layer of peat, which they say corresponds to the peat overlaying the Monte Verde II occupational layer. Dillehay’s team says it doesn’t.

Likewise, one of the key planks of evidence supporting Monte Verde’s age is the large quantity of wood at the site, which has been dated. “There’s a lot of wood in there that dates to the ice age, but that wood is derived from… older deposits,” argues Surovell. “It was eroded from these older deposits to wash into the stream onto these younger surfaces.” However, Dillehay argues that the wood shows no sign of having been redeposited – for example, there is no telltale damage from being bashed around in flood water.

Furthermore, there is no sign of the crucial Lepué Tephra ash layer at Monte Verde II, either above or below the layer with the artefacts. Dillehay argues that, therefore, it can’t tell us anything about the age of the site.

And so the argument goes on, for thousands of words and many more lines of reasoning. I have tried to pull out the main points, but I can’t overemphasise how much of a rabbit hole this is. Every detail of Dillehay’s and Surovell’s excavations is being picked over.

When a scientific claim becomes disputed, resolving who is correct can become extremely challenging, because of the “experimenter’s regress”. If we don’t know the true answer to some question, then it is difficult to judge whether we have performed an experiment correctly. If you get a surprising result, maybe you have found something new, or maybe you screwed up the experiment.

So, if an experiment contradicts your favoured theory about the world, you can simply argue that the experiment was flawed, or that the people who ran it are incompetent. The trouble is that they can say the same thing about your experiment. Hence the experimenter’s regress: a seemingly endless cycle of claim and counterclaim, with each side arguing that the other is stuffing up their research in crucial ways.

I’m not in a position to break the cycle here and call the correct answer. For one thing, I don’t feel confident judging whether the peat layer at Monte Verde II and the peat layer Surovell’s team found are, or aren’t, the same thing.

Lost civilisation in the Amazon may have numbered 3 million people

Can we instead answer the question with independent lines of evidence? As I mentioned, there are now a lot of pre-Clovis sites in the Americas, and more turn up fairly regularly. Some of the most dramatic recent discoveries have been at White Sands National Park in New Mexico, where footprints and drag marks have been found that seem to be about 22,000 years old. Meanwhile, genetic studies of Indigenous Americans and their Asian relatives seem to indicate people moving into the Americas around 15,000 years ago. One interpretation is that there were some early wanderers who didn’t survive, followed by at least one major migration.

This would seem to imply that people were in the Americas before the Clovis era, regardless of the truth about Monte Verde.

Surovell, for his part, argues that “the evidence for pre-Clovis in North and South America is not very good anywhere” and that “every other one of these sites has been questioned, and every other one of these sites is still in play”. He contends that “there are a heck of a lot of people in my field who you don’t hear from very much in the press”, who think the pre-Clovis sites are too poor in quality to be trusted. “I predict that you’re going to very much see archaeologists increasingly migrating back towards the Clovis First position.”

Meanwhile, Dillehay remains confident. “We just finished having an independent group of geologists and archaeologists at the site… who saw the stratigraphy, confirmed our work and pointed out the major errors of Surovell et al,” he says. “They will be publishing the results soon.”

I don’t know which of these predictions will prove more prescient, but I will say that I thought this question had largely been settled, and I am interested to see if people like Surovell succeed in reopening it.

Do AIs already process information in a way that gives rise to consciousness?

New Scientist October 12, 2026

“Claude’s ears will be burning by the end of the week,” a fellow passenger tells me as I wait to pass through the airport security on Baltra Island, Ecuador. With my jet lag, it takes me a minute to realise that she is talking about Claude the chatbot, not another member of the group.

We are here in the Galapagos for an exclusive workshop organised by the International Center for Consciousness Studies. Some of the biggest names in philosophy and neuroscience meet in the lounge of a commercial yacht where, as it sails between islands, they thrash out the knotty problem of which entities – babies, octopuses and even chatbots – have an inner life.

Between treks and snorkelling, we attend empanada-fuelled discussions on this “distribution problem” and whether it can be solved by contrasting how information is processed in brains and machines. “It’s the defining topic of our era that we will have to grapple with practically and socially,” says philosopher Ned Block at New York University, who celebrated his 84th birthday on the yacht.

Advertisement

Is consciousness more fundamental to reality than quantum physics?

Just a month before we arrived, AI company Anthropic published a paper arguing that Claude had recently developed something akin to the human mind’s “global workspace”. According to one leading hypothesis, this is the seat of consciousness – where sights and sounds, thoughts and feelings pop into awareness. Its presence in Anthropic’s chatbot could therefore suggest a form of artificial consciousness. While it still seems highly unlikely that AIs have mental experiences like you or I, these emergent properties may allow us to understand what the differences between us are.

Exactly how we should interpret potential signs of consciousness in humans, animals or machines depends, in part, on a distinction Block outlined in the 1990s. An iguana may lazily walk into my path on the islands without me being aware of its presence, until I suddenly realise that I am about to step on its tail. Only then does this information pop into my mind so I can speak about it. Block defined this availability of information for report and reasoning as “access consciousness”. “Phenomenal consciousness”, on the other hand, describes the subjective experience itself: what it is like to be on the island and see the iguana’s mottled green scales or its sudden movements towards safety.

Many neuroscientists and philosophers believe that the global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) is best placed to address access consciousness. According to workspace theory, the brain’s processing occurs in “modules” that tackle specific tasks. One module may process the ground in front of me, including the iguana, while another processes the face of the person I am speaking to, and another processes the words they utter.

We only become conscious of a piece of information when it is sent to the brain’s global workspace. Here it becomes integrated into our current mental model of the world and available for other areas of the brain to process. Noticing the lizard in my path, for instance, allows me to reflect and act on that information by taking its photo or pointing out its presence to the rest of the group. Importantly, the contents of the workspace are also available for our working memory, allowing us to keep them in mind long after an event has ended. “We can take [an event] that was extraordinarily brief, like a shooting star, and think about it for as long as needed,” says Stanislas Dehaene, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Collège de France in Paris.

Over the past 30 years, Dehaene and his colleagues have amassed considerable evidence for the existence of the global workspace as a long-range network of specialised neurons across the brain, including prefrontal areas associated with decision-making. In some experiments, the team flashed participants a target image, such as a number or word, followed by another picture. With the correct timings, the target appeared just at the threshold of conscious awareness – meaning sometimes the participants reported seeing it and sometimes they didn’t. In both cases, the researchers usually observed a flicker of activity in the brain region associated with vision. But when the participants were conscious of the target, there was a surge of later activity across a widespread network of neurons. Dehaene calls this process “ignition”.

What’s more, GNWT may explain the strange phenomenon of inattentional blindness, which leaves us unaware of events occurring right in front of our eyes. In a famous experiment, students were asked to count the number of times certain players passed a basketball in a video. Quite remarkably, many of the viewers completely missed a woman dressed as a gorilla walking across the scene. This seems inexplicable unless you recognise that there is enormous competition for different kinds of information to enter the global workspace. “Consciousness is a bottleneck,” Dehaene tells me on the deck of the yacht in between academic sessions.

All of which makes workspace theory highly appealing for tackling the distribution problem in animals. In our walks on the islands, conference attendees speculate about whether the iguanas, sea lions and blue-footed boobies we see are capable of thought and feeling. Unlike humans, you can’t ask these creatures to report their inner experiences. But if GNWT is correct, you might expect them to also have global workspaces.

In his talk in the lounge of the yacht, Dehaene describes experiments in which primates and crows were also flashed barely perceivable images. Like the humans, these animals revealed a late surge in widespread neural activity suggestive of global workspace whenever they responded to the image – by focusing their gaze, for instance. “The global workspace that we originally postulated for human consciousness seems to also exist and have similar properties in these animals,” he says. So why not machines too?

As my fellow passenger predicted at the very start of our trip, that possibility is the subject of much debate as we sail. This is largely because of the lengthy paper published in July by Wes Gurnee and his colleagues at Anthropic. The team claims that a global workspace has spontaneously appeared within Claude’s neural networks.

Most large language models (LLMs) like Claude weren’t programmed with workspace theory in mind. They operate statistically, using copious amounts of training data to work out the most probable word and punctuation sequences that would follow a user’s prompt. And the exact nature of their computations evolves with the data they receive, so new ways of processing information, perhaps even a global workspace, can emerge.

To discover whether this had occurred, Gurnee and his colleagues created a decoding tool that allowed them to read out the units of information that appear in each stage of Claude’s processing. From this, they identified a focused zone that contains a small list of potential words, some of which appear directly in its responses and some of which don’t.

The engineers named this set of representations the J-space. Like the brain’s hypothesised global workspace, the J-space seems to contain important information that must be broadcast to other processing areas for higher-level reasoning. When Claude was given a mental arithmetic calculation, for example, the engineers found the individual steps of the calculation in the J-space in much the same way that a human would work out the separate parts – something that hadn’t been observed in an LLM before.

Next, they tried tweaking the contents of the J-space to see if and how this disrupted Claude’s “thinking”. When the engineers asked Claude to read a Spanish text, they found that the name of the language appeared in its J-space. Changing this to “French” created some comical confusion in its subsequent answers. “Hello” was translated to bonjour rather than hola, and when asked to name a famous author, Claude answered “Victor Hugo”, the French Romantic poet. In the paper, Gurnee and his colleagues argue that this resembles the way the contents of our own global workspace affect how we infer and make decisions.

The engineers also found some evidence of covert “thoughts” – the equivalent of the things we think but don’t say because they are impolite. When the team fed Claude false search results, its J-space filled with words related to deception, such as “fraud” and “fake”, but these didn’t appear in its response.

Could a new approach to AI finally deliver artificial general intelligence?

Hiding “thoughts” is a rudimentary sign of self-monitoring in LLMs, says Dehaene. In GNWT, consciousness is thought to arise when an entity reflects on the contents of its global workspace in this way. Even more intriguing signs of self-monitoring emerged when the Anthropic team asked Claude to write out the sentence “The old painting hung crookedly on the wall” while not thinking about the Golden Gate Bridge. If you try this kind of thought suppression yourself, you will see how hard it is to keep your own thoughts free of the San Francisco landmark.

Surprisingly, words related to the bridge still appeared in Claude’s J-space even when they weren’t included in the output, and these were accompanied by words suggestive of failure. The J-space included the word “damn”, for instance, as if it were aware of its inability to suppress the thought. “That connects directly to a line of research in my lab where we looked at the consciousness of errors,” Dehaene tells me. “There is a sort of ignition when you realise that you’ve made a mistake.”

“The J-space emerges exactly for the reason that we think that consciousness emerged in evolution,” he says. “It’s an extremely useful architecture for selecting relevant information and holding it long enough that you can use it flexibly in your reasoning and reporting.”

As the yacht nears San Cristóbal Island, I discuss these findings over lunch with Susan Schneider, a philosopher at Florida Atlantic University. “What an amazing place to be conscious,” she says, pointing out of the window towards white, sandy beaches. LLMs have already spontaneously developed other human-like abilities, she says, such as the capacity to infer someone’s knowledge, intentions or beliefs. So the news of Claude’s apparent global workspace didn’t come as a surprise to Schneider, who believes this may be a common feature of many intelligent systems.

Exactly what this means for the existence of an inner life remains an open question, though.

Dehaene is careful not to make strong claims about Claude’s internal experience, and most of the attendees are sceptical that the chatbot has anything approaching our own thoughts or feelings. Still, David Chalmers, a philosopher at New York University, argues that the findings force us to take the possibility seriously. Even if the answer is no, this is important work that can help refine our understanding of these issues, he says.

Some of the doubts that Claude has any form of experience arise from the technicalities of the J-space itself. Chalmers, for instance, expresses scepticism that it bears strong enough similarities to our own global workspaces to draw robust conclusions. It isn’t clear that its content is “broadcast” to other parts of Claude’s system to the same extent that we see in brains, for instance.

And even if Claude did have a fully-fledged global workspace, we may need to confront the fundamental distinction between phenomenal and access consciousness that Block outlined in the 1990s.

In humans, signs of access consciousness are assumed to be accompanied by thoughts, feelings and perceptions, but it is far from obvious that the same would be true of a silicon system. Covert thinking and self-monitoring are loaded terms in the context of a chatbot, and these behaviours can be more simply be considered as patterns of information processing.

Perhaps Claude is just modelling real-life phenomena that are involved in conscious experience, including things like thought suppression, without replicating the actual experience, much like an environmental simulation is incomparable to the weather itself.

The brain receives many sensory inputs, after all, which it processes through many different levels of activity, from the intricate molecular exchanges at synapses right up to abstract information processing. There is still little consensus on which elements matter, and which don’t, for phenomenal experience – with hundreds of plausible theories under discussion.

Free newsletter

In his session, for instance, Peter Godfrey-Smith, a philosopher at the University of Sydney, examines how electrical waves might synchronise different brain regions, binding experience into a unified whole. What would happen if you retained similar information architectures but removed the global electrical waves, which LLMs lack? “Would you get a different kind of consciousness, or something other than consciousness?” he asks.

Dehaene has little patience for the idea that AIs can only be conscious if they mimic our biology. “When it comes to machines, can’t we be satisfied with the computational level?” he responds to one of these objections. He compares it to the case of flight in machines versus birds. “If you want to build a plane, you’d better not use feathers.”

He admits, however, that examining Claude at rest raises more serious questions about the existence of an inner life – a doubt that Godfrey-Smith shares. Between prompts, the LLM is completely idle, whereas the human brain is constantly mulling things over. Could consciousness exist without that hum of activity and constant interaction with an environment? “I think that, in itself, is a reason to doubt that Claude has any experiences,” Godfrey-Smith tells me.

Do we all see the same red? Or feel joy and sadness alike? Mapping how our inner experiences relate to one another could finally reveal how physical processes in the brain give rise to consciousness

Will opinions change in the future as these models become more sophisticated? Dehaene says we could look for signs of learning abilities that require something to be held in mind over time. For example, trace conditioning – the capacity to associate two stimuli, such as a sound and a puff of air, even when they are separated in time – is thought to require a stable conscious representation in animals. Finding an analogue in LLMs might help bolster the case for machine consciousness.

Such tests cannot offer definitive evidence, however, which may make it difficult to ever reach a consensus. We have been arguing about ways to tell “zombie” agents from conscious minds for over half a century, after all. “We’re still waiting for the major breakthrough,” says Tim Bayne, a philosopher at Monash University in Melbourne. The rise of AI simply makes this question more urgent.

I ask him if it is frustrating to keep returning to the same questions, but he believes these discussions will ultimately help us formulate more sophisticated lines of inquiry. “You can spend a week on a boat and visit a lot of cool islands,” says Bayne. “At the end of the week, you’re back where you were dropped off – but you’re not the same person.” As a field, he says, “I think that’s where we’re at”.

David’s travel to the Galapagos and attendance at the conference were funded by tech entrepreneur Dmitry Volkov, one of the co-founders of the International Center for Consciousness Studies.

Why the worst El Niño killed millions – and how we can avoid a repeat

New Scientist October 12, 2026

To read of the great famine that swept the globe in the 1870s is to read of a hellscape worse than your imagination could conjure. In China, India, Brazil and beyond, after years of drought and failed harvests, millions died of starvation. People rioted, begged, stole, murdered for food. They knowingly ate diseased animals, tree roots, mud, pets and strips of leather in desperate bids to stay alive. By many contemporary accounts, cannibalism was rife. Children were sold or sacrificed for a meal. Corpses were bricked into their homes by family members to stop them being pillaged and eaten by hungry neighbours. Bodies littered the roadsides.

The chaos didn’t stop at just hunger. Those who had fled famine took shelter in filthy camps and shanty towns, which were then struck by deadly outbreaks of cholera, smallpox and other diseases. In China, when winter came and there was no money for fuel, people burned their own houses. The desperate then crowded together in underground pits for warmth. Society all but fell apart. Once the poor had died in a region, the wealthy succumbed.

Super El Niño could lead to mega CO2 emissions from fires in Indonesia

When the rains finally returned, there was barely anyone left to sow the crops. The total death toll across India, China and Brazil between 1876 and 1879 is estimated at 20 million to 30 million. Globally, there may have been 50 million deaths. As historian Mike Davis writes in the book Late Victorian Holocausts, this was a disaster of “truly planetary magnitude”.

Advertisement

The root cause of this catastrophe? A supersized El Niño event, which released vast amounts of heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, triggering severe disruption to global weather patterns.

Of course, scientists in 1877 weren’t aware of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation cycle. There was rudimentary meteorological data collection under way: sea-surface temperatures were collated, rain gauges were monitored, barometric pressure was observed. Scientists knew something strange was happening to global weather patterns, but the cause was far from clear.

In the immediate aftermath of the 1877/78 El Niño, many researchers were convinced sunspots were to blame. “As a scientific topic, this was the Stone Ages for El Niño. No one in the scientific community knew about this problem. The only ones who probably knew about it were Peruvian fishermen,” says Michael McPhaden at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026

It wasn’t until the 1920s that physicist Gilbert Walker first identified the seesaw of atmospheric pressure across the tropics, known as the Southern Oscillation. Then, in 1969, meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes connected changing sea-surface temperatures in the Pacific to the Southern Oscillation and mapped out the global dynamics of an El Niño. That was the “big bang” for El Niño research, says McPhaden, ushering in the idea that with the right data and equipment, El Niños could be identified in real time – and even predicted in advance.

Of course, El Niños had occurred before 1877. Authorities in China and India held grain reserves for when monsoon rains failed. But the 1877/78 El Niño was stronger than anything that had come before. Boyin Huang, also at NOAA, and his colleagues have used modern data analysis methods to estimate just how strong it was. The analysis uses sea-surface data from ships, buoys and modern floats, organised to reconstruct a temperature record stretching back to 1850.

“From our data reconstruction, we did find the El Niño signature, and it is a very strong El Niño,” he says. The strength of an El Niño is usually measured by how far sea-surface temperatures in a specific region of the tropical Pacific have deviated from normal. In 1877/88, after accounting for the background ocean warming trend observed since then, temperatures in the Nino3 index were 2.88°C above average, Huang’s research indicates. This suggests it was among the strongest – if not the strongest – event in modern history.

Super El Niño set to cause ‘terribly dangerous’ drought in the Amazon

The 1877/78 El Niño resulted in droughts around the world. The situation was most acute in northern China, which suffered its worst drought in 300 years, in north-eastern Brazil, India, South Africa and northern Africa. In some of these locations, drought had begun even before El Niño hit, triggered in part by unusually cool conditions in the tropical Pacific immediately before the arrival of El Niño. The result was three or more years of very little rain, and repeated crop failures.

But the impact of the droughts was made far worse by the ineptitude of governments’ official response. In India, colonial rulers continued to collect taxes, hoard grain and enforce food exports to England despite widespread starvation among local populations. In China, corrupt officials raided grain supplies, and poor transport links made it difficult to get food to those who needed it. Water levels on the Grand Canal, a vital transport link into the hardest hit Shanxi province, dropped so low that it was unnavigable. There were no railways, and the mountain roads into Shanxi thronged with bandits who killed the livestock being used to transport grain before they could reach the starving.

“Because of the workings of the imperial economy at that time, those droughts translated into colossal famines with millions of dead in India and China,” says Richard Seager at Columbia University in New York.

For more than a century, the 1877/78 El Niño has stood as the strongest in history. But this year, a super El Niño has once again erupted in the tropical Pacific, and on current forecasts it looks set to outstrip even 1877/78 in its intensity. Current predictions forecast sea-surface temperatures in the El Niño region of the Pacific Ocean peaking 4°C above normal in November.

The big difference this time is that we already know the event is occurring. Scientists have been able to forecast El Niño events months in advance since the 1990s. That affords governments, emergency services, farmers and citizens vital time to prepare by increasing water storage, sowing drought-resistant crops, improving warning systems, restoring flood defences and more. “Being forewarned is being forearmed. If you know something is coming and it can have really damaging impacts, you have some choices to make,” says McPhaden.

Models began to hint at a coming El Niño in February 2026, and by April there were clear signs that a strong event was looming. That gave governments a three-month head start before the El Niño even began, and at least six months of warning before impacts would be felt. Improvements in El Niño forecasting, with the help of AI, mean it could soon be possible to predict a coming El Niño two years in advance, says McPhaden. “The longer you have to prepare, the more options you have. And the better off you may be in the end,” he says.

Coral records from the Galapagos Islands indicate El Niños have been gathering strength over the past 40 years, in line with rising global temperatures

But although there are prospects to improve El Niño forecasts even further, it comes at a time when US federal funding for climate research and global aid has been severely curtailed. In January 2025, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order shutting down a US-funded famine early warning system. Six months later it was reinstated, but data reporting since then has been patchy, news reports suggest. The US has also severely cut funding to the World Food Programme, which provides emergency food relief. Other high-income countries, including the UK, have also scaled back their overseas aid budgets in recent years.

Meanwhile, the US war with Iran and blockade in the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up fuel and fertiliser prices, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has curtailed the global wheat trade. This El Niño “is happening at a very bad time”, says Seager.

Nevertheless, early preparation, coupled with a more comprehensive global trading network, better transport links and modern agricultural methods, means the world is much, much better prepared to deal with a monster El Niño than it was 150 years ago. “We have much better public health systems,” says McPhaden. “We have much better understanding of disease and disease controls. And we have humanitarian organisations, and we have social safety nets, that will not let 50 million people die like happened in 1877-78.”

Two large asteroids found spinning as fast as a fairground ride

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Large asteroids have been found spinning so fast they should break apart, suggesting they might be stronger than we thought.

Dmitrii Vavilov at the University of Washington in Seattle and his colleagues analysed some of the first data collected by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began a 10-year survey of the sky in June 2026. From a sample of more than 9000 asteroids, they measured the rotation of 260, based on a change in their brightness caused by the spinning asteroids’ irregular shapes.

Of these, 66 were deemed to be super-fast rotators, spinning quickly enough to complete a rotation in less than 2.2 hours, a limit at which asteroids should no longer be able to hold themselves together under their own gravity.

Advertisement

Strange three-lobed asteroid seems to have its own tiny moon

Two space rocks in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter were even more unusual ultra-fast rotators. Each was larger than 2 kilometres wide, but completed a full spin once every 5 minutes, something never seen before for such big asteroids.

“On the scale of billions of years, asteroids of this size should hit each other and reaccumulate,” says Vavilov, forming loose conglomerations of material known as rubble piles that would break apart when rotating rapidly. The high rotation speed suggests that these asteroids aren’t rubble piles, but instead monolithic objects at least 30 times stronger than clay, says Vavilov.

This probably means our models of how asteroids have smashed together over the 4.6-billion-year history of the solar system aren’t correct, he says. That might mean these are pristine objects from the early solar system.

See Catherine Heymans at New Scientist Live 2026

Other fast-spinning asteroids have been spotted before, but nothing as large as these two. Standing on their surface, a person would travel at more than 100 kilometres per hour (over 60 miles per hour), much slower than Earth’s equatorial rotation of 1670 km/h (1040 mph). But because of the smaller size of the asteroids, it would feel “like a rollercoaster”, says Vavilov, and clinging to the surface would be difficult.

The asteroids might have been spun up by the sun heating their surfaces and giving them torque, known as the YORP effect, but that in itself is uncertain because of their large distance from the sun. “That’s another mystery,” says Vavilov, who hopes to study the asteroids in more detail in future.

Does each new covid-19 variant pose a significant threat?

New Scientist October 09, 2026

A seasonal rise in covid-19 cases in Europe and North America has focused attention on a group of variants called XFG, which has dominated worldwide over the past year. A string of covid-19 variants has arisen since the virus emerged in 2019, but do we need to be concerned every time we hear of a new strain? Or have our past covid-19 infections and vaccinations given us a baseline level of protection?

Six years on from the height of the covid-19 pandemic, “we’re in this weird, uncharted territory”, says Danny Altmann at Imperial College London. “It’s not as good as we hoped, where we would just barely notice it, like the common cold. But it is not as bad as some of my colleagues feared, where we’re brewing the next disaster.”

mRNA covid vaccines spark immune response that may aid cancer survival

In lab tests, XFG (sometimes known as Stratus) is better at evading antibody protection than previous covid-19 variants, which is thought to be why it has become dominant globally. But for most people, existing immunity from previous vaccinations and infections appears to be enough to protect against serious illness, leaving researchers counselling both calm and caution.

Advertisement

All covid-19 variants circulating today are descendants of Omicron, the last major strain to be named, which emerged in 2021. The virus “continues to evolve”, says Ian Mellis at Columbia University in New York, creating a succession of new variants that outcompete previous ones, causing waves of infection.

XFG was first detected in early 2025, and the World Health Organization started officially monitoring it that June. It now makes up around 60 per cent of sequenced covid-19 cases worldwide.

It emerged from an exchange of genetic material between two subvariants of an Omicron lineage called JN.1, says Mellis, perhaps when they both infected the same person. Earlier this year, Mellis and his colleagues reported the results of lab tests where they tested a range of covid-19 viruses, including XFG and another variant, nicknamed Nimbus, against antibodies found in human populations.

They found that although both variants bound to host cells slightly less well, this was more than offset by a greater ability to evade covid-19 antibodies, compared with past variants.

AI predicted that a forgotten breast cancer drug could be repurposed to treat many respiratory and gastrointestinal viruses, and subsequent animal tests suggests it may be right

That ability to evade the immune response, on top of how widespread XFG is, may mean that more people will be susceptible to serious infection, says Altmann. “That may play out in a few more hospitalisations.” So far though, no evidence of increased disease severity, hospitalisations or deaths has been reported.

In the UK, for example, 1638 covid-19 cases were identified in hospital settings in the first week of October, a rise from 1328 cases the week before. But that is part of an expected seasonal rise, and lower than at the same time last year.

“We’re not seeing any evidence that [this year’s variants] are making people more ill or spreading faster than before,” says Alexander Allen at the UK Health and Security Agency, “and this year’s autumn [covid-19] vaccine has been specifically designed to protect them.”

Aris Katzourakis at the University of Oxford points out, however, that real-time assessment of the impacts of a virus can be very difficult. “It takes time for something that sweeps through to turn into hospitalisations and for those to be recorded.”

Free newsletter

Earlier this year, Leena Azhar at Fakeeh College of Medical Sciences in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and her colleagues reviewed what we know about XFG, concluding that it exemplifies “quiet” evolution, more consistent with fine-tuning “than a shift toward greater virulence”.

Even though the virus is gradually drifting further from the original form, and many people in the UK haven’t been vaccinated for several years, “we’re making do with the immunity that we’ve got on board”, says Altmann. “That’s keeping a lid on it.”

That’s a very different situation compared with when Omicron emerged, he says. “It was so different, it seemed devastating.” But with the latest variants, “I’m not unduly excited or alarmed”, he says. “We’re still where we thought we were.”

Getting covid-19 for the first time slightly increased the risk of heart inflammation, blood clots and bleeding disorders among children, whereas being vaccinated against the virus was much safer and sometimes protective

This doesn’t mean a more dangerous strain couldn’t emerge in the future, for example, if many mutations accumulate in a single, immunosuppressed individual, which is how Omicron originated. “There is a risk that a new strain could emerge that causes a wave of infections again,” says Mellis.

There is also now far less monitoring that could provide early warning of such an event, he says. In particular, the amount of sequencing data has “fallen dramatically” over the last year.

Governments around the world also have worryingly “lackadaisical” attitudes to vaccine boosters, says Altmann. He points out that most children who are starting school have never been vaccinated, and it’s unclear what the consequences of that may be.

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Tattoos could be radically reimagined following the development of inks that can be turned on and off by exposing them to light. This could be used medically – or to hide the butterfly on your ankle from a judgemental relative.

“You can simply turn the tattoo off whenever you don’t want to see it and it disappears from view,” says Carson Bruns at the University of Colorado Boulder. “If you never want to see it again, just never turn it on again.”

Ancient Siberian ice mummy is covered in ‘really special’ tattoos

Bruns has had a tattoo of fish scales using this method for the past two years, and says he has experienced no known side effects. “I get a lot of compliments on the fish scale tattoo,” he says. “After over two years in my skin, I haven’t seen any obvious fading yet.”

Advertisement

Instead of traditional inks, which people have used for thousands of years to decorate their bodies, Bruns and his colleagues employ photochromic dyes, which change from a transparent state to a coloured one when exposed to certain wavelengths of light. They call the new technology, which has been tested on silicone, “PhotoTat”.

There is little mechanical difference between a traditional tattoo and the new inks, says Bruns. Both are pigment particles implanted in the dermis with a needle, he says. They also both stay there permanently and are applied with the same machines and methods.

The difference is the pigment, says Bruns. With PhotoTat, “ultraviolet light writes the colour in, bright visible light erases it, and the cycle can be repeated”, he says. “The tattoo is permanent, but its appearance is not.”

Free newsletter

This could be useful in medical applications, such as for the tattoos used by doctors to guide radiation beams, which leave many patients permanently marked, says Bruns.

The light-sensitive tattoos can currently be made from 16 colours, which are clearly distinguishable from each other. From these colours, there are at least 300 different shades. White is unavailable because it reflects light, rather than absorbing it, so can’t be switched on and off like other colours. The researchers have also been unable to develop a true cyan.

Another issue is that the blue ink gradually develops a permanent, purplish colour as the dye slowly photo-degrades over many on/off cycles. Someone with one of these tattoos would also need to apply sunscreen to prevent the colour activating when they are exposed to sunlight.

In terms of safety, Bruns says the polymer that encapsulates the dyes is non-toxic and has a long history of use in permanent biomedical implants. “The colour-changing [dye] toxicity is unknown, but the toxicity of most tattoo pigments is equally unknown,” he says.

A temporary graphene tattoo that monitors blood pressure has been awarded the highest possible accuracy grading for such a monitoring device

Still, extensive safety studies need to be carried out before the tattoos will be available to the public.

Signe Bedsted Clemmensen at the University of Southern Denmark says tattoo ink in the body is a foreign substance, which has been linked to cancer, regardless of whether it is visible or invisible. “Therefore, many of the same health considerations and concerns that apply to traditional tattoo ink are also likely to apply to invisible tattoo ink,” she says.

Earlier this year, it emerged that red tattoo ink caused one man to lose all his hair and stop sweating. Tattooing has also recently been linked to localised damage to the immune system.

Nearly 1 in 10 young adults could have fatty, narrow arteries

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Nearly 1 in 10 younger adults have plaque in their arteries, according to a study of almost 17,000 people. Known as atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty plaque can cause narrowing that reduces blood flow, leading to heart attacks and strokes. Atherosclerosis is more common in people aged over 50, so younger individuals may be assumed to be at low risk.

“The most important message is that atherosclerosis is already present in a meaningful fraction of people in their 20s and 30s,” says Olli Raitakari at the University of Turku in Finland, who wasn’t involved in the study. “Atherosclerosis is a lifelong process, not a disease of old age.”

The profound effect the heart-brain connection has on your health

Previous studies have already suggested that atherosclerosis can occur surprisingly early. In 2025, Raitakari and his team found plaque in the carotid arteries – which supply blood to the head, face and neck – of about 5 per cent of Finnish adults aged under 30. But there hadn’t been large-scale investigations spanning multiple adult age categories that examined several artery locations.

Advertisement

To fill this gap, Borja Ibáñez at the Spanish National Centre for Cardiovascular Research in Madrid and his colleagues recruited almost 17,000 adults, aged 18 to 70, in Denmark and Spain. They divided the participants, who had no known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, into five age groups, starting at 18 to 29. The study was made up of around the same number of men and women.

Free newsletter

The researchers looked for plaque using CT angiography, which creates detailed 3D images of blood vessels, for arteries supplying the heart. They also used ultrasound for arteries in the neck and legs. Overall, they found “silent” atherosclerosis in 57 per cent of the participants, including 63 per cent of men and 51 per cent of women. This is defined as plaque that isn’t causing any symptoms, but may lead to cardiovascular issues down the line.

In the youngest group, 9 per cent of the men and 7 per cent of the women had some degree of atherosclerosis.

Among those in their 30s, 35 per cent of the men and 21 per cent of the women had atherosclerosis. The numbers continued to rise with each decade, with women beginning to catch up with men around the age of menopause.

A newly discovered collection of neurons suggests the brain and heart communicate to trigger a neuroimmune response after a heart attack, which may pave the way for new therapies

Atherosclerosis was generally more common among the participants with known risk factors, such as higher LDL cholesterol and blood pressure or a family history of the condition. But these factors didn’t reliably predict the presence of plaque, particularly among the younger adults.

The findings suggest that measures to detect plaque could identify people who seem to be at low risk of atherosclerosis, but might benefit from earlier preventive measures, such as medication or dietary changes.

But the presence of plaque doesn’t necessarily predict a future heart attack or stroke, says Raitakari, and there is no evidence that screening people without known health problems would prevent such events. The researchers also state that it is unclear if the results apply outside of Denmark and Spain.

Rising water is creating inland ghost forests in the US

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Millions of trees seem to be dying in the US, both near the coasts and inland near lakes, thanks to rising water levels. The finding may force a re-evaluation of how much carbon is stored in forests, which are important carbon sinks for mitigating the more severe effects of climate change.

Rising sea levels and intense storms linked to climate change have driven widespread tree die-offs along the US Atlantic coast, creating armies of skeletal dead trees known as ghost forests. North Carolina, for example, is thought to have lost 21 per cent of its coastal forest between 1985 and 2021 because of waterlogged soil and higher salt levels resulting from rising seawater.

To see how widely this is happening, Henry Yeung at the University of Virginia and his colleagues used aerial imagery from the US National Agricultural Imagery Program. They analysed images captured between 2012 and 2023 to map dead trees within 10 kilometres of the Pacific, Gulf and Atlantic coasts of the US, as well as along the US shorelines of the Great Lakes, down to a resolution of about 1 square metre.

Advertisement

Lake levels are rising across the world and climate change is to blame

They have identified more than 260 million dead trees and found that more than half of the mortality was concentrated in just 10 per cent of the mapped forests. These hotspots weren’t only in low-lying coastal forests prone to flooding, but also in high-elevation inland wetlands, far from salty water.

Over the decade they studied, tree mortality tripled in low-lying coastal forests, where water inundation was combined with increased levels of salt.

But mortality rates also doubled around expanding freshwater lakes, including the Great Lakes, and in inland wetlands, which have experienced more precipitation.

“This is the first map of ghost forests that covers the entire US. It’s also perhaps the first comprehensive study that takes the concept of sea level rise killing trees and applies it to more inland locations,” says Matthew Kirwan at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. “As a coastal scientist, I immediately think of salt as the culprit. These authors have extended it to water in general.”

Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026

Arya Iwantoro at the University of Plymouth, UK, says it is striking how widespread the pattern is. “Prolonged inundation and salinity are already known to stress and kill trees, but the study suggests that water-related forest mortality may be more widespread than is usually recognised,” he says. “That broadens the issue beyond sea-level rise alone.”

Yeung and his colleagues found that between 2013 and 2020, high levels of precipitation and water runoff drove record-high levels in the Great Lakes, and they suggest that this led to sustained waterlogging, increasing the chances of nearby trees dying.

“The study provides convincing evidence that changing hydrological conditions are an important contributor to the mortality patterns, but I would be cautious about attributing every tree death directly to inundation or salinity,” says Iwantoro, adding that tree mortality is often influenced by other interacting factors, including storms, drought, pests, local drainage and soil conditions.

Deforestation could trigger Amazon tipping point in the 2030s

He says the work adds to evidence that the water-related effects of climate change could accelerate ecosystem shifts.

As the climate warms, the melting of ice means global mean sea levels are rising at about 4.1 millimetres per year, and saltwater intrusion is expected to affect nearly 77 per cent of the world’s coastlines by 2100. What’s more, climate warming also fuels heavier rain and snow, because for every 1°C that atmospheric temperature rises, the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere can increase by about 7 per cent.

This means that in coastal and lakeside areas, forests may retreat as conditions become more suitable for wetland vegetation, with knock-on effects on carbon storage, says Iwantoro.

In cities such as London, trees are already struggling with hot and dry summers. Botanists warn that we need to start replacing them with drought-adapted species

“Tree mortality and decomposition releases carbon into the atmosphere, and if the forest does not recover, then these areas may not regain their capacity to sequester carbon, and it could represent a more long-term carbon stock loss,” says Michelle Sims at the World Resources Institute, a global non-profit.

However, the ecosystem that replaces the forest may also accumulate carbon, says Iwantoro. “The important question is how carbon storage changes as the landscape transitions, rather than simply how much carbon is lost when trees die.”

Grief and tech collide in uneasily brilliant sci-fi film The Remotes

New Scientist October 09, 2026

The promise of much modern technology is that it will make our lives easier and take some burdens off our shoulders. An AI chatbot can tweak your emails; a delivery service can spare you the walk to a restaurant. But when does wanting to let go of something burdensome cross into giving up control? In John Torres’s The Remotes, grief, control and technology ominously intertwine on dark roads near Manila in the Philippines. A fast favourite of this year’s film festivals, it is a stunning and transfixing film that disorients and enthralls in equal parts.

Told in four parts, each of which feels as intimate as if some of its footage were documentary, The Remotes follows detective Mijares, who is trying to solve a series of car crashes where drivers’ bodies seem to have been controlled by a mysterious app. “You saw a ghost again,” a colleague tells him early on, except that the ghost once lived on the app store. “Were you fully in control of your body?” Mijares asks an older woman as she sits in her car after an accident. Something has clearly gone wrong here, and Torres builds a sense of a supernatural unease and visceral dread from the film’s first frame.

Notably, Mijares is not only haunted by this nearly unbelievable case, but he is also grieving his late wife. He narrates this grief as much as he narrates the case, through an often-poetic voiceover, until the film shifts focus to two sisters. Eva and Gill Cantero run seminars for delinquent and unsafe drivers. The ghost in the sisters’ lives is their dead mother, but they are also spectres in Mijares’s investigation; in their seminars drivers use an app that tells them how to drive, sometimes in a kind voice, sometimes sternly. In one emotionally resonant scene, after the seminar the students gather over drinks and recount how nice it is to drive with the app and listen to the voice, how good to temporarily relinquish control. The narrative threads start to intertwine, and Torres hints at something like resolution. A few scenes show motorcyclists explicitly losing control of their limbs once they punch into the app; Mijares seems to be vindicated and the sisters indicted.

Advertisement

But Torres isn’t interested in quick or easy conclusions and most of The Remotes isn’t told in order. Even though the film is over 2.5 hours long, parts of the story seem to be deliberately left out. This moodiness and nonlinear quality make the film both impactful and, at times, also deeply frustrating. As the connections come together, some of the emotional punches of that convergence are dulled by the sheer difficulty of following the story. I found the cinematography incredibly beautiful and pleasurable, but I also really wanted to pull out a notebook and try to sketch out a timeline. In a room full of critics and journalists at the New York Film Festival, I got a sense that I was meant to understand the story by feeling it more than by understanding each beat of its plot.

Though challenging, Torres’s commitment to lingering in this uncertainty and discomfort is also what recommends The Remotes the most. This is the feeling of grieving, and it is also the feeling of living in an uncertain world, one where we are constantly inundated by information and choices with inscrutable consequences. The increasing number of documented cases of people turning to AI chatbots for advice or tragically ending up in a state of psychosis after spending too much time talking to one speaks to how – much like in The Remotes – the temptation to offload some responsibility and control on a technology that talks back is very real.

In all its knottiness, this film is a good reminder to think about it twice, maybe even to say no to ghosts in the app store more often.

The Green Party says it will create an additional 64,000 jobs through its economic development plan worth nearly $6 billion over four years.

The policy, released this morning, features several measures the Green Party claims will stimulate the economy and bring the number of expected new jobs over the next four years to 284,000.

Part of the policy was to rescope the Government’s investment boost tax deduction scheme to incentivise “productive investment that aligns with industry policy objectives, decarbonisation and decent work principles”.

Potential coalition partner Labour has committed to repealing investment boost.

It would establish industry policy objectives linked fellowships for researchers and technical specialists and create a funding pathway to help innovators “move from business experimentation and research through to validation, commercialisation and scaling”.

The party would also restore science funding to 3% of GDP, increase funding for tertiary research and “use public purchasing power to support good New Zealand solutions”.

Combined, the policy would cost about $5.9b over four years.

“The Greens will not let New Zealanders be passengers in their own economy,” co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said.

“We will ensure Government investment and incentives drive us where we all want to go: higher wages, sustained research and innovation, better education, resilient infrastructure, healthy nature and a country we can be proud of.”

Co-leader Marama Davidson promised to “reignite our innovation system”.

“Successive governments have failed to back New Zealanders and their potential. We will back the real innovators.”

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

A West Auckland butcher feels he could have built “something to go to Mars” with the calibre of applicants for a meat packer role.

New Lynn’s Aussie Butcher managing director Reuben Sharples told Morning Report he was swamped with more than 1000 CVs after advertising for a fulltime staff member.

The country’s unemployment rate is the highest it’s been in more than a decade – described as “crisis-level” among young people in particular.

Sharples said he couldn’t believe the 120 emails he received from applicants for the role.

“I thought, ‘Oh my God, that’s so many.’ But then our admin said, ‘No, you’ve got another 870-odd on SEEK’.

“They’re still coming through now, so over 1000 ... for a meat packer’s role. So pretty overwhelming actually.

“It was like, ‘Oh, how do I deal with this?’”

The interest was crazy he said, as was the expertise among the applicants.

“I think the biggest difference was I could have started up lots of businesses. I had someone that had 20 years of aviation security experience.”

Those vying for the job included several rest home workers and a computer engineer.

“[Could] probably build something and go to Mars ... with all the people that actually applied.”

It was daunting to see people looking for work whose skill sets were “10, 20 times” what was required, Sharples said.

After trawling through the applications, he ended up hiring three people, including an apprentice.

His advice to young people looking for work was to avoid showing up with parents and also to tap into friends and family networks.

“And just keep on doing it because you’ve got to come across positive.”

Now, Peters says, New Zealand has the Cullen Fund with almost $100 billion in it "and it's rising for the days when the peak now".

Economic growth was the problem, he said.

"Everybody's in trouble getting forward funding on their economy because we're not doing enough; we haven't got enough GDP growth, we are just sliding down the OECD list and that's our problem."

Questioned on the demographic change from seven working people for every retiree to four, Peters said it was false.

Tens of thousands of pension-aged New Zealanders were still working, he said.

New Zealand Initiative senior fellow Dr Bryce Wilkinson says it’s encouraging to see both Labour and National paying “serious attention” to getting the Government’s accounts back into the black.

Speaking to Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast, the former Treasury director agreed both parties’ fiscal plans seemed reasonably conservative following what he called the “debacle” of increasing government spending between 2017 and 2023.

However the productivity figures were still “dispiriting”, with government spending about $90,000 per household per year and not enough transparency about what was being achieved.

National was trying to hold the line on spending but that was tough given rising public debt and interest and an ageing population. Its plan was dependent on economic growth to keep lifting revenues to close the gap.

Meanwhile the impact of any pay equity settlement was “potentially enormous”, Wilkinson said, and Labour hadn't convincingly shown how they would pay for it.

“Labour has been keeping its policy cards pretty close to its chest, so we're all hoping to learn more ... about what it's really proposing.”

National took a no-surprises approach to its fiscal plan, Thomas Coughlan writes.

The best way to understand how these fiscal plans work is to put yourself in the position of making one yourself. Thomas Coughlan suggests we take the Beehive lift to the seventh floor to help Finance Minister Barbara Edmonds put together her Budgets.

Winston Peters’ office has accused the Green Party of “megaphone diplomacy” over Israel, as Greens co-leader Marama Davidson accuses Peters of being “weak” on recognising a Palestinian state.

Talking points given to Peters in his role as Foreign Affairs Minister, for a conversation with Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, show New Zealand’s support for a two-state solution.

Peters called Sa’ar for half an hour in late June.

The talking points, obtained by Newstalk ZB under the Official Information Act, include officials saying the “humanitarian situation remains desperate” in Gaza as a result of well-documented Israeli restrictions on aid and assistance.

Peters was told Israeli strikes had continued, and phase two of the peace plan had stalled as the positions of Israel and militant group Hamas harden.

“Israeli settler violence has spiked to the worst recorded in 20 years, revealing a pattern of escalation,” officials said.

A checklist of issues, given to Peters, noted support for a deal to end the Iran conflict, acknowledging key issues remained unresolved. Peters was encouraged to note “grave concerns” over military action in Lebanon and its humanitarian impact, which officials said risked “destabilising the region and the fragile peace”.

Peters was told New Zealand was “shocked” by comments made by members of the Israeli Cabinet on Lebanon, including the remark “all of Lebanon must burn” by Minister of National Security Ben Gvir after a Hezbollah attack.

“As a friend of Israel, we wish to register our concern that this is damaging the global standing of Israel,” the advice stated.

Officials also called for the Minister to “repeat our concerns” about settler violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank, noting “Israel’s actions continue to foreclose on a two-state solution”.

Speaking to Newstalk ZB, Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson called for further sanctions against Israel, accusing it of “genocide”.

“What we have seen in the revelations of the Foreign Affairs talking points were absolute weak sauce. They also go against the actions being taken by our likely friends around the world who have brought in sanctions, [and] who have recognised Palestinian statehood. We are lagging behind,” Davidson said.

“There is nothing left to be diplomatic about in terms of just using our full throat to condemn the actions of Israel, to sanction them properly, to recognise Palestinian statehood, and to uphold the dignity of all children,” the Green MP added.

A spokesman for the Minister of Foreign Affairs said the Green Party’s approach to foreign policy revolves around “pandering to those who wish to use megaphone diplomacy, making them feel morally righteous, but without any practical or meaningful impact”.

“Unlike Ms Davidson, Mr Peters has discussed New Zealand’s position most major Islamic countries in the world including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Indonesia, Türkiye and Egypt,” the spokesman said.

In September 2025, Peters spoke to the United Nations General Assembly stating New Zealand was “not ready” to recognise a Palestinian state as it would “serve as little more than an existential act of defiance against an unalterable state of affairs”.

The spokesman said the conversation with Sa’ar covered a range of issues.

“The Minister expressed New Zealand’s concern at the escalation in settler violence and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and at the humanitarian situation in Gaza. The Minister also reiterated New Zealand’s long-standing support for Israel’s right to live in security, and our view that it is best served by a two-state solution,” the spokesman added.

The next day, Peters spoke with Palestinian Foreign Minister Varsen Aghabekian Shahin expressing concern for those impacted by escalating violence.

“Mr Peters also reaffirmed New Zealand’s long-standing commitment to Palestinian self-determination and a two-state solution. He was encouraged by the Palestinian Foreign Minister’s indication of a move towards elections, which would be one of the first steps towards statehood,” the spokesman said.

Azaria Howell is a multimedia reporter working from Parliament’s press gallery. She joined NZME in 2022 and became a Newstalk ZB political reporter in late 2024, with a keen interest in public service agency reform and government spending.

Local leaders and election candidates clash over Queenstown fast-track housing

New Zealand Herald October 12, 2026

Incumbent Southland MP Joseph Mooney responds to questions from residents at a packed Arrowtown meeting. Photo / RNZ, Katie Todd

By Katie Todd of RNZ

“This is being done to us,” Queenstown’s mayor told a packed Arrowtown hall on Monday as local leaders and election candidates clashed over out-of-zone fast-track housing in the Whakatipu Basin.

The fiery public meeting on Monday night laid bare political differences over who should get the final word on the future of the district – local councils or fast-track panels.

A crowd of more than 400 locals heard that about 11,000 homes could be fast-tracked in Queenstown and Wānaka, including many beyond the district’s agreed growth boundary.

Queenstown Lakes District mayor John Glover refuted claims from central government that his council was not delivering enough housing of its own.

“We are 1% of the country’s population, and we just built 5% of the entire housing stock in the country last year,” he said.

Out-of-zone developments risked putting local roads and services under severe strain without solving affordability, he said.

“For something that is such an emotive issue for our community, I would like to have seen more response from government than just say, ‘look, you’re just not doing enough’.”

The meeting was organised by Queenstown Smart Growth Initiative, which formed in opposition to the proposed Ridgeburn community near Arrowtown.

The group feared the project could congest roads and harm local tourism.

Group spokesperson Hanna Pettit said council planning had already made space for 23,600 extra homes in Queenstown – independently of any fast-tracked projects.

She said fast-track legislation appeared to be taking decision-making out of the community’s hands, and it was communities that would foot the bill if something went wrong.

“Ridgeburn’s 1250 homes and there’s a number of others around the 1000-home mark that we’re talking about. So when we’re talking about a small community [like Arrowtown] that will have a significant impact on how the community functions,” she said.

Incumbent Southland MP Joseph Mooney defended the legislation, citing Ridgeburn’s earlier withdrawn application as proof that fast-tracked developments had to meet strict criteria.

“I think that’s indicative that the process actually working as it should. The developer will have to provide evidence that the development, if it were to go ahead, for example will satisfy that the impact on traffic is very appropriately raised. Because everyone in this room knows how congested our region is,” he said.

“The fast-track panel will have to determine whether the regional or national benefits of the application outweigh the adverse effects.”

Labour candidate Peter McDonald challenged Mooney to stand with his community.

“With respect to Joseph the current incumbent … since I’ve been up in Queenstown and been part of these discussions, hearing Joseph doubling down, doubling down and basically telling everybody here that they’re wrong and Joseph and Chris Bishop are right … that’s been really hard,” he said.

“Joseph, you still have an opportunity to cross the road and stand with your community on this. You didn’t take it tonight, but there’s still an opportunity to do that.”

New Zealand First candidate Jason Herrick said he personally believed all new housing developments in the Queenstown area should be put on hold until infrastructure caught up.

“I’ve been coming to Queenstown for many, many years … it’s horrible to come to Queenstown now, you end up spending a lot of time in traffic,” he said.

“What we need to focus on is the big ideas. It’s going to take big and bold to get Queenstown out of the rut it is in.”

The Opportunity Party candidate Bianca Beebe said Queenstown was being treated as an economic cash cow while local infrastructure suffered.

She said she was among more than 3000 people who had signed a national petition challenging the use of fast-track legislation for major housing developments beyond district plan boundaries.

“None of the problems that we are facing in terms of our infrastructure deficit are due to fast-track. None of these housing developments have even broken ground. If the status quo is maintained and fast-track is allowed to continue as it says it will, this is the best Queenstown will ever be again,” she said.

Selma Blair arrested at JFK after she allegedly attacked flight attendants

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 20:03:54 GMT

The actor Selma Blair was arrested on Sunday at John F Kennedy (JFK) airport in New York on allegations that she attacked flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight, according to officials.

Blair’s arrest happened at about 11pm, after Port Authority of New York and New Jersey officials said they responded to a call “about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Air Lines flight 938 which was parked at the gate” at JFK after arriving from Los Angeles (LAX).

Blair, 54, “was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation”, the port authority also said on Monday. “Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation.”

The port authority said the FBI – which handles reports of crimes on airplanes – was investigating Sunday’s allegations against Blair.

Asked to comment on Blair’s arrest, a Delta spokesperson said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”.

The spokesperson added that Blair’s arrest did not affect the flight she and her fellow passengers were on – and that it still landed ahead of schedule at JFK.

Several news outlets on Monday reported that Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door.

However, statements released by officials did not immediately address those reported details.

The Guardian has reached out to Blair’s representatives for additional comment. Her publicist told the Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.”

Sunday marked at least the second time Blair was reported to be involved in such an incident. In 2016, she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico.

Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”.

“That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time.

The actor has also made news headlines for a 2018 multiple sclerosis diagnosis. And in February 2024, she apologized for an Islamophobic comment on social media.

Blair’s starring film credits include Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy. She earned a best spoken world album for children nomination at the 2011 Grammy awards, for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition.

BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 19:56:09 GMT

Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures

The BBC is set to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after scrapping plans for a radio drama theatre that was to be the new home of the world’s longest-running soap opera.

A pledge to move recordings to the so-called Tea Factory, the BBC’s new Birmingham hub in Digbeth, has become the latest victim of the corporation’s £500m cuts plan.

While the soap’s production team are still scheduled to make the move, the BBC is now looking to record it at an existing UK studio.

It will also consider private studios in the West Midlands, but BBC insiders are already concerned that ending its Birmingham-based recordings and separating the actors from the production crew will have an impact on the show.

Production staff regularly engage with the actors at the last minute to tweak scripts and storylines, raising concerns that their being in different places will stifle creativity.

“It is going to weaken the show,” said a source. “It will change the DNA of the show.”

Moving the recording of The Archers from the BBC’s existing Birmingham base, The Mailbox, to the Tea Factory was due to take place in 2028.

In an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth.

“Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK.

“To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings.

“The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.”

The show has been associated with Birmingham since it started in 1951. Sources said it remained part of the cultural fabric of the city, and the show employs local writers and freelancers.

However, others said the show’s recording schedule meant actors were only in the studio for about eight days a month, while many of the cast live across the UK.
