Ilhan Omar says she will not be silenced after federal agents raid her home

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:20:42 GMT

Trump and key allies have accused Omar of immigration fraud, and have called to expel her from the country

Federal agents searched Representative Ilhan Omar’s home on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation, according to the Department of Justice and reports in the Associated Press and Fox News.

In a social media post later on Monday, Omar criticized the raid as an attempt by the Trump administration “to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement” and said she would “not be silenced”.

A video posted by Fox showed what appeared to be law enforcement in HSI jackets at what Fox News said was Omar’s Washington DC residence.

“Today in the Washington DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” a DoJ spokesperson said.

It was unclear what the nature of the warrant was. Omar’s office did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House and Department of Homeland Security referred comment to DoJ. Citing two unnamed sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News reported that the search was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork, which her late father filled out when she was a child.

Donald Trump and key allies have accused Omar of fraud related to her family’s immigration history, fantasizing openly about denaturalizing her and expelling her from the country.

The congresswoman has consistently denied the accusations, though Trump has repeatedly made them national news with gratuitous attacks against Omar, who along with Representative Rashida Tlaib became the United States’s first Muslim congresswoman in 2019.

But even amid a presidency known for political and legal retribution against his critics, the search of Omar’s DC home just three weeks before a crucial midterm election day will surely lead to new accusations that Trump was using the government for his own political ends.

Administration officials, and the president himself, have long hinted at a federal investigation into Omar. “Let’s see what happens,” Trump said at a rally on Saturday after attacking Omar by name, adding that Vice-President JD Vance “and our people are looking at it very strongly”.

It was just the latest in months of talk about investigating Omar. Trump in December accused her of having “married her brother” and said she “should be thrown the hell out of our country”, a reference to a years-old but unsubstantiated claim that Omar sought to help her ex-husband – who they allege is really her brother – obtain immigration papers via a sham marriage.

Days later, his “border czar” Tom Homan said: “We’re pulling the records now,” referring to Omar, and said a fraud investigator in Homeland Security Investigations, the ICE division that historically has been tasked with investigative work, would look into the matter.

In March , Vance told rightwing media personality Benny Johnson: “We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud” and that he had recently spoken to top Trump aide Stephen Miller about “what the remedies are”. Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin told Johnson last month that there was an ongoing investigation and “something’s going to happen”.

“We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States,” Mullin said. “We know he lives now in London. We feel that there may be more to this, the whole family migration, and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with. But all of us, we’re investigating.”

Soon after, Homan said he could not “comment on an ongoing criminal investigation.

“We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations continue to do their investigation,” he added.

Omar’s social media post after the raid on Monday said: “I’m OK. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

The congresswoman also said Trump had spent years targeting her “with baseless lies and smear campaigns”.

“This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Omar has for years denied unsubstantiated rumors from Trump and others about herself and her family, including the accusation that her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother, and that the marriage was part of an effort to earn him immigration status. Marriage fraud is a felony, though it has a five-year statute of limitations. Omar and Elmi formally divorced in 2017 after separating in a religious divorce years earlier.

The New York Post last month also quoted an unnamed “top immigration official” who said “the Trump administration could initiate a denaturalization process” against Omar if there is sufficient evidence that she or her father lied on immigration applications. The story noted accusations that Omar was older than her recorded age of 17 when she was naturalized, which could be relevant because she received citizenship via her parents. The report also raised questions about Omar’s father, who reportedly claimed to be an educator, though his obituary later described a military career.

As the most prominent Somali-American in the United States, Omar has faced years of racist attacks from the president and his supporters.

At his rally Saturday, Trump said of Somalia: “All they have is crime and squalor” and suggested that “our” US constitution did not belong to Omar. Two days earlier, he had written that Minnesota “is being taken over by Somali Immigrants”, even though the vast majority of Somali-Americans in the state are US citizens.

“The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing,” Trump wrote, urging supporters in the state to “fight back!”

Somali-Americans, especially, have borne relentless insult from the White House in Trump’s second term. In December, the president referred to them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”.

“Let them go back to where they came from and fix it,” he added.

Grounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the open

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:12:01 GMT

Long-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignore

It took 147 days for Rayo Vallecano to walk out for a competitive game on the Avenida de Albufera and 24 minutes and 56 seconds for them to walk off again. Half of those had been spent watching thousands of paper planes touch down on the turf, play suspended while a message was delivered, over and over, until it was impossible to avoid. Forced from their home, the team from the barrio had been away for five months. On the bright Saturday afternoon that they came back, there were just 13 minutes of football, a fans’ protest instead forcing the abandonment of their match with Athletic Club, the latest episode in a never-ending story.

The last time there had been a league game here was a victory over Villarreal in May. A lot has happened since: little Rayo, Rayo Vallecano, had played a European final, 11,000 fans heading to Leipzig where, as the banner perfectly put it, they knew no greater victory than being with you in defeat. Iñigo Pérez, the manager who took them there, had departed. And Óscar Trejo, the man who gave up the armband over treatment of staff – the best thing he could do as captain was to stop being captain – had retired and been immortalised the way the barrio does best: in graffiti four storeys high. Then, in late July, the Madrid government suspended the agreement that allows them to use the ground in return for €81,784 (£69,094) a year.

The cup, the coach and the captain were not coming back. As a new season began, nor were any of them. Rayo’s president, Raúl Martín Presa, said he was furious with the council, locking the gates to keep their technicians out and accusing them of condemning the club to segunda. But when the report described the ground as unsafe and unhealthy, Rayo’s fans knew they were right: they had been saying so for years, relieved to be finally heard. The ground’s upkeep was the tenants’ responsibility but – like so much else – it had been abandoned, left to ruin. They were furious with the president they believe condemns them to a fate far worse that relegation, a man they could not despise more and who despises them back, of whom they ask just one thing, as often as they can: for him to leave.

They are not alone. Last season players had complained about conditions, forced to train at Getafe and play at Leganés; as the new season began they would have to do so again. After a long summer and three home games played 20km south, where 4,280, 4,529, and 3,742 came to see Alavés, Racing and Espanyol, respectively – collectively fewer than in a single afternoon in Vallecas – they were finally back. Leganés had been left three-quarters empty, boycotted by supporters, but in football terms it had been good to them, which sums Rayo up: all wrong but somehow all right. Last season’s victory over Atlético there was followed up by two wins and a draw this season. Yet this is home. Besides, down at Rayo, in the heart of the self-styled independent republic of Vallekas, the football is the least of it, striker Sergio Camello says; it’s about what they stand for. And this weekend they were going to make another stand.

They could not have chosen a better opponent: Athletic’s fans are allies, supporters packed into the bars around the ground and the plaza in front of the Mercado de Numancia alongside Rayo’s fans, singing in the sunshine. The protest had been planned from the start; what they probably did not plan for was the way it ended. On surfaces all around the stadium, green stickers proclaimed “SOS Rayo Vallecano”. Presa’s image appeared on walls and scarves with familiar Mickey Mouse ears. From bags they handed out little plastic balls in many colours. And from boxes they handed out flyers.

Printed on grey A4, the sheets declared: “Today is a day to protest.” After “years of putting up with this”, they had reached a “point of no return”. And so, in the 13th minute, everyone was invited to chant “Presa, go now!” Then to turn the paper into a plane and fly it on to the field. On the back of the sheet were handy, Ikea-style instructions for those who did not know how to fold a paper plane.

An Athletic corner arrived with perfect timing, setting it all up. The whistles started bang on the 13th minute and so did the planes, swooping in from all three stands. The referee, José María Sánchez Martínez, stopped the game and shrugged, which he did a lot. Small, multicoloured plastic balls came down too, bouncing and rolling across the pitch, while a banner unfurled in the main stand declared the ball in Presa’s court (which is precisely their problem). An announcement was made, a first warning, two more strikes and they were out. For now, they would play on but not until the pitch was clear.

Ballboys dashed across, applauded all the way, to do what ballboys do: pick up the balls. Planes were pushed off the pitch. Players kicked about among themselves. And, after a pause of eight minutes and 43 seconds, Sánchez Martínez, satisfied now, sent them back over to take the corner, Pathé Ciss congratulating a ballboy on a job well done as he returned to his position. The corner came in, Yuri Berchiche volleyed just wide, shot flashing past the post, and then the planes came down again. Two touches, strike two. This time, the referee took them off. The stadium clock had rolled on but now it was reset as they headed down the tunnel to chants of “Presa, go now!”

They had been out there 24 minutes and 56 seconds but it might as well have been half-time. In the shadows of the narrow corridor under the stand, conversations unfolded. In the sunshine, so did the tinfoil, supporters happily eating the sandwiches meant for the break. Half an hour after kick-off, there was an announcement: they would begin again in 20 minutes. And if more objects are thrown, the match would be abandoned. From the tunnel, Isi Palazón and Óscar Valentín came out to speak to fans behind the goal. This was bad: if it happens again, the game is over. This was good, a plan forming: if it happens again, the game is over. A clear protocol, postponement easily forced, a statement made more visible, more powerful than ever before.

Thirty-eight minutes and 16 seconds after kick-off, the players reappeared, Athletic first. Sánchez Martínez bounced the ball, said it is flat, swapped it over, and gave it to Emil Audero, whose goal-kick would be the new kick-off, 43 minutes since the first time. From behind him, someone started a countdown: five, four, three … As the ball flew into the air, so did more paper planes. Sánchez Martínez shrugged, looked at the end, a hint of defiance. Leaning against his post at the other end, Unai Simón watched it all happen.

Sánchez Martínez called over the captains, then the coaches. A circle formed on the pitch: the referee, his assistant, two captains, two managers, a delegate, La Liga’s match director, the security adviser and a police officer. The Rayo coach, Beñat San José, translated for Edin Terzic, whispering in his ear. Terzic nodded. Álvaro García argued, but there was nothing he could do. The referee’s hands were tied, the police wanted to go, and at nine minutes to three, 49 minutes and 18 seconds after the game started, he signalled towards the tunnel. They had played 13 minutes.

after newsletter promotion

Rayo’s players departed, Ivan Balliu first, to applause. The referee stood, hands on his hips, a disapproving parent who had sent the kids to their room. Athletic’s players went to their fans in the far corner, then back towards Rayo’s supporters, who chanted: “Athletic! Athletic!” Iñaki Williams and Simón were the last off. They stopped for photos with the ballboys. Williams gave someone his shirt, Simón handed over his gloves. As they reached the tunnel, Williams signed someone’s shirt. As they disappeared, the stadium launched into the Vida Pirata, usually a victory song.

They may not have won, may never win, but many wonder what they had left to lose. They were not planning to get it postponed, an opportunity opening instead, but they might next time. Presa says he will never leave, even if they fall to the third tier, but what if they do it again and again? At what point does someone step in? The club attack the “ultras” – that old get-out clause – and call the rest of the ground “victims”, but that is not how the rest of the ground sees it, flying their paper planes and happily heading off into the afternoon. Even Athletic’s supporters, their big day out brought to an early end, were on side. They joined Rayo fans in the bars while down in the offices, there were negotiations over when to replay the game, probably behind closed doors: Athletic wanted to return the following morning but that was rejected and so at 4.23pm on Saturday their bus pulled out for Barajas, applauded up Payaso Fofo street and right on to Avenida Albufera, still none the wiser.

Málaga 1-1 Espanyol, Rayo 0-0 Athletic (abandoned), Alavés 1-2 Atlético Madrid, Barcelona 3-0 Getafe, Real Madrid 1-0 Villarreal, Elche 0-0 Celta, Real Sociedad 3-2 Deportivo, Betis 5-2 Osasuna, Racing Santander 2-2 Valencia

Monday: Levante v Sevilla (8pm BST)

Rayo’s supporters’ association called this “the inevitable consequence of exhaustion, frustration and anger” after “15 years of abandonment of the facilities, chaotic management, a loss of identity and a continuous contempt for employees and fans, as well as the club and its values”. They called Presa “dictatorial”; the protest, by contrast, “peaceful and democratic, necessary”.

“An unsustainable situation has reached its limit,” the captain Valentín posts. “This has got worse and worse bit by bit for too long without anyone doing anything to stop it getting this far. We have to listen to and understand the fans’ discontent. We need to find a way to bring everyone together for the common good and the good of Rayo Vallecano above all. That’s the only way we will ever live great moments together again.”

Zelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:10:22 GMT

Ukrainian leader says he was surprised by Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement, posted as Russian drones hit Kyiv

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.

Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.”

On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones.

Russia then launched a “targeted attack” on a Kharkiv power station hours later, as much of Kyiv was plunged into darkness. “It’s clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said.

Russia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said. “It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added.

Zelenskyy also suggested that Ukraine’s recent counter-strikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex had reduced the number of bots posting messages in Europe and the US. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said.

The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday, when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post.

Earlier a furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries.

“We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.”

Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision to lift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

“This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.”

Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war.

Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries.

The US president has blamed the high price of diesel on Ukraine’s attacks, rather than the global shock to energy markets from the US war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz.

According to the Financial Times, the US ⁠has threatened ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons, paid for by its European allies. The White House has also said it could turn off intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halts its ‌long-range strikes on ​Russian oil refineries.

The Kyiv Independent newspaper said Ukraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper.

Ben Hodges, the former head of US forces in Europe, described the energy ceasefire “deal” as a fantasy and “a classic ‘Trumpian’ announcement of something not based on any facts.”

“No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”.

He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”

Champions Day – and Balding v O’Brien – can give Flat season a fitting finale

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:02:43 GMT

The Ascot head-to-head battle for the trainers’ title adds spice to a fascinating day of racing on Saturday

With five Group Ones, a £250,000 juvenile race and a decent racing surface (if the weather forecast is correct), the schedule for Champions Day at Ascot on Saturday looks like the fitting finale to the British Flat season that its architects envisaged 15 years ago. Add in the bonus of a live contest for the UK Flat trainers’ championship and this is a card that promises twists and turns from the first race to the last.

Less than a month ago, Andrew Balding was a double-figure price to win the title for the first time, while Aidan O’Brien was effectively “no offers” to win for the third year running, and ninth time in all. He starts the week as a 6-4 shot with Paddy Power, while O’Brien is 1-2 – and it is a measure of the extent to which the two trainers have dominated the campaign that even before Champions Day, both have already surpassed John Gosden’s record prize-money total of £8.52m in 2017.

Unless the wheels suddenly fall off completely, Balding and O’Brien are highly likely to be the first trainers to reach £9m in prize money in a calendar year in Britain – and yet one of them will still finish second. As William Haggas, currently third in the table, pointed out during a Champions Day press call on Monday: “We’ve had a pretty good year and we’re £1m in front of Karl [Burke], but £3m behind Aidan and Andrew.”

There can be little doubt who the majority of fans at Ascot on Saturday will be rooting for. Balding inherited one of the most historic and well-appointed yards in the country when he took over the licence at Park House Stables from his father, Ian, in 2003, and has built on that legacy year-on-year to the point where it is a 250-horse string.

Yet he still feels very much like the underdog up against the might of O’Brien’s operation and will be only the fifth trainer to win a first title outright this century – O’Brien, in 2001, was the first – if he can maintain his lead until the end of the year.

Balding will be significantly outnumbered in terms of runners this weekend, too. He has just four remaining entries that are likely to go to post after the five-day stage on Monday, while O’Brien has 15 possible runners with a grand total of 20 entries, and so plenty of options when it comes to playing his hand.

There is no final decision as yet, for instance, on whether Gstaad, the Irish 2,000 Guineas winner, will head for the £1.1m Queen Elizabeth II Stakes over a mile, or step up two furlongs for the Champion Stakes, the day’s £1.3m feature event. Wherever that one goes, Constitution River, the brilliant winner of the Eclipse Stakes in July, is likely to head in the opposite direction, and both will set off as leading fancies.

Neither, though, is a sure-fire favourite for their chosen assignment. Charlie Appleby’s fast-improving Talk Of New York, a supplementary entry on Monday, heads the market for the QEII, while Calandagan, last year’s winner, and John Gosden’s Ombudsman, the Prince of Wales’s Stakes winner at Royal Ascot, are vying for favouritism in the Champion.

The two title rivals have a Group One favourite apiece elsewhere on the card, as Kalpana, Balding’s King George winner earlier in the campaign, will bid to win the Fillies’ & Mares’ Stakes for the third year running, while Scandinavia, who was O’Brien’s 100th Royal Ascot winner in the Gold Cup in June, is around 2-1 for the Long Distance Cup.

Even so, O’Brien – and the punters too, for that matter – will be taking very little for granted on Saturday. Last year’s meeting left the backers baffled and impoverished by winners at 200-1 and 100-1 in the Sprint and QEII respectively. O’Brien, meanwhile, has not saddled a Group One winner on Champions Day since Magical won the Champion Stakes in October 2019.

That is a grand total of 25 Champions Day Group Ones without a winner from Ballydoyle, which is a surprising statistic, to say the least.

Scandinavia, meanwhile, was beaten at long odds-on on his most recent start at Longchamp on Arc weekend, and there has been a nagging sense in recent weeks that O’Brien’s string is a little short of its usual dominant form. That impression is backed up by Timeform’s current “Run To Form” rating for O’Brien of 61.7% which, while thoroughly respectable, is still some way short of the 70%+ level of several recent seasons.

Of course, O’Brien could easily reel off a Group One treble on Saturday and put the championship race to bed. Balding, though, has been in irresistible form since high summer, and may never have a better chance to bring the title back to Kingsclere for the first time since 1971. The timing, the weather and the ground often conspire against Champions Day as a showpiece event, but this year’s card could well redress the balance.

Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:42:37 GMT

Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences

Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?

Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.

The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.

The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.

The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”

He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.”

An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.

Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.

The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen.

Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.

The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.

Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.

On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.

He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”.

A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.

The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.

The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.

The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.

Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.

Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

Reform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every day

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:59:15 GMT

On the Today programme, his comments were disconnected, cliche-riddled and unremittingly stupid. But to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense is exactly the point

Had Reform merely announced its intention to suspend the asylum system for an entire parliamentary term, I’d have just ignored it. Even to dignify its policy platform with a response is to enter its alternate universe, in which it’s preparing for government. I prefer, if only fractionally, this universe we’re in, where the party hangs by a thread on the results of a parliamentary inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from a disinterested well-wisher.

Had Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, gone on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme merely promising a British version of ICE, I still would have ignored it, not due to complacency, more due to a bone-penetrating despair that anyone, even he, would look at the US’s shadow militia, performing staged acts of unfettered violence and inhumanity, and think: “That looks cool – I bet I could get some political capital out of that.”

However, as Yusuf laid out his arguments, they were so dumb, so random, disconnected, hammy and cliche-riddled, just so unremittingly stupid, that it turned out to be impossible not to react. I cannot let his nonsense slide. It would be an insult to words.

An elderly woman, he said, waited 23 hours for an ambulance and the coroner found this contributed to her death. A Welsh 15-year-old’s educational attainment is below the OECD average. Many young people have to live with their parents into their 30s and 40s because they can’t afford rent. How does any of this relate to asylum seekers? Are they displacing elderly people in ambulance-demand? It seems unlikely, although if they are an immediate fix would be to stop masked gangs surrounding their living quarters and scaring the hell out of them. Those are ethno-nationalist thugs, of course, and nothing to do with Reform.

High private rents, meanwhile, are not driven by asylum seekers, who have no right to work even if they arrive through a formal route, and as for Welsh 15-year-olds … well, we have some data here. They’re underperforming compared with English 15-year-olds, who are above the OECD average, indeed, above every other European nation, except Estonia and Ireland. If migrants destroy educational standards, how is Ireland managing to thrive? Why, with its very low number of asylum seekers, is Slovenia full of 15-year-olds who (no offence) suck at reading?

None of it makes sense because none of it was meant to. It’s bilge punctuated by soothing mantras (“Charity begins at home”, Yusuf repeated), aimed at the half-asleep mind dreaming of a whites-only yesteryear. It had that in common with a Trump rally, but lacked his pizzazz. Reform can’t even do neo-fascist mimicry right.

A word entered my social-media lexicon recently, which I wish I’d never had cause to look up, because I wish it wasn’t so useful: “agnotology” is the deliberate creation of ignorance, confusion and doubt. You can do it with misinformation and fake news, or you can do it with half-truths pouring out of bot factories, then leave an entire body politic tearing chunks out of itself as it seeks to establish whether the discursive environment has been deliberately polluted, or whether people are just mean and wrong nowadays. But you can also do it by simply talking nonsense, which we’ve seen writ large in party conference season and its aftermath.

“Let’s build an impenetrable and state-of-the-art defence dome for £10bn, and call it the Britannia Shield, even though that’s already the name of a Oxfordshire roofing company,” says the party that spent vastly more than that trying and failing to build the HS2 train line. “Let’s stop all refugees coming from everywhere, until the conditions for every single Briton at every conceivable stage of life have been improved,” from the party whose only discernible allegiance is to its billionaire donors.

The policies don’t even matter. Florid, premeditated stupidity is an end in itself, to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense, chase down every citizen who woke up in a good mood, with a scintilla of confidence about the future, and kill their mojo. The only defence is to hold your line. Insist on the difference between truth and untruth; guard your precious mojo with everything you’ve got.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments!

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:55:40 GMT

Tate Modern, LondonThe Lebanese artist has turned trumpets, drums, cones and voices into an ingenious, interconnected sonic beast with funny, sad and mystical results. Prepare to feel the earth move!

On the floor of the Turbine Hall, there are wide water basins and huge flattish rough-hewn rocks you might see on moorland or in a desert. You can sit or stand or climb on them. But if you look up, you won’t be able to stop looking up – because it’s raining musical instruments. Immense elongated brass trumpets and giant glowing drums seem to float in the air, suspended from the girders of the former power station’s roof.

If Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui had just left it at that, it would be an impressive, intriguing installation, but this is Tate Modern, honey, and Atoui hasn’t been asked to occupy its grandest space with mere physical objects. Instead, his sculptural creations and found stuff resonate and echo with an ever-changing, invisible art of noises. An earth-shaking bass note throbs from a hanging trumpet – or is it from that translucent cone rising out of the ground like an ethereal minaret? Then a drumbeat booms through the space and a woman’s plangent, achingly lovely voice sings notes of infinite nostalgia and melancholy.

It’s entrancing. The music has you hooked. It is music, I think, though abstract, non-melodic, a rising and falling of sounds that lead you around and through the installation’s forest of solid things. But then – is music ever not sculptural? Listening to the scything percussive notes of Stravinsky certainly is; and the desire to crystallise sound waves into something visible has haunted everyone from the inventors of opera to designers of psychedelic lightshows.

Yet Tarek Atoui still manages to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. He teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear, how the stones and water basins, pipes and strings have produced this sonic outpouring. The entire installation is an interconnected musical machine.

It’s funny too. There’s a warm, generous if absurdist humour to it all. In the past, a crazy mechanical contraption like this would be called “Heath Robinsonish”, after the early 20th-century British cartoonist who came up with such things. A better comparison is Leonardo da Vinci, who invented wild musical instruments among his other real and impossible machines: organs worked by water, a string instrument shaped like a fantastic beast.

Atoui, like Leonardo, seems to be looking for a lost harmony in the world, a secret note that pleased the Lord. Sadness hovers in the sounds that fill this vast grey space, as the bass notes pound harder, building up to an apocalyptic blast. What is being mourned and where is he taking us? You start to feel you are in a city of sounds and sights. The crowd of towering, floating pinnacles, the mysterious voice and crescendo of percussion, suggest an ancient, tumultuous labyrinth of a city. I thought of Lahore and Marrakesh, of a street-singer heard once in an Istanbul market. Yet this city is purer, less tangible. Its towers fly in the air.

Ultimately, you can’t reduce this magical, elusive work of art to a fixed meaning. You have to surrender to it. The sound gathers you up in its ecstasy like a spiralling mystical dance. There is a strong similarity with Sufi drummers and dervishes who use music and motion to inculcate a liberating, trancelike calm. I certainly didn’t want to leave. The vibrations and complex visual composition keep your brain busy but you are also soothed and at peace.

It also suggests the urban life all around this site, the exotic sounds of Bankside: the music of the city, gathered into Atoui’s collage of random noise. But reality slips and fades as you are shown a world beyond the physical. All these objects, from the cones to the stones to the electric guitar played live at the press view, are but as air. They fascinate the eye but the sound eventually dissolves the material world. The solid stuff Atoui begins with becomes as unreal as a reflection in a courtyard pool.

Atoui has grabbed the opportunity to work in this vast space with both hands, creating something rich, ingenious, funny, sad, mystical. This is a Turbine Hall installation to lose yourself in for hours, dreaming and wondering. It’s the sonic answer to a sun indoors – and Atoui is a modern magus.

Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall installation is at Tate Modern, London, from 13 October until 11 April 2027

Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:53:31 GMT

Just 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?

Name: Wikipedia.

Age: 25.

Appearance: Patronising and deeply biased.

Is this because you haven’t got your own page? Well, yes. But these aren’t my words. They’re the words of Sandi Toksvig.

But it has 65m articles across more than 300 languages! It’s the largest knowledge resource ever assembled! That may be, but it isn’t very good at women.

According to Toksvig? Yes – and she’s very serious about it. As we speak, she is travelling the world trying to raise money to build something better.

She is? Yes. Along with the University of Cambridge, she hopes that her Mappa Mundi project will be an “interactive digital atlas where we can find a home for the vast amount of knowledge that is currently sidelined or deleted”.

And a lot of the sidelined or deleted knowledge is about women? It is. She cites the case of Donna Strickland, a Canadian physicist who repeatedly had her draft biographies rejected by Wikipedia, until she won a Nobel prize for her work.

Awkward. But it goes broader. By the Wikimedia Foundation’s own estimate, only 19% of Wikipedia biographies concern women. Toksvig puts this down to the site being edited by “mostly white, middle-aged, European men who have both the time and the technology”, she told Cheltenham literature festival this weekend.

I didn’t know that. Its content is weighted heavily towards wealthy countries. In 2013, for instance, the Oxford Internet Institute discovered that Wikipedia contained more coverage of Germany than of Africa and South America combined.

Isn’t Wikipedia too leftwing anyway? Oh God, are you Elon Musk? This is a claim he has repeated for the last couple of years, to the extent of calling it “Wokepedia”.

And what did he do about it? He started his own version – an AI-powered alternative called Grokipedia.

And is it better? A paper published in November 2025 discovered that Grokipedia articles are 13 times more likely to contain a source blacklisted by the English Wikipedia community.

What’s a blacklisted source? The paper pointed out that, at the time of its publication, Grokipedia included 42 citations for the banned neo-Nazi website Stormfront.

Yeesh. Bring on Mappa Mundi! Indeed, Toksvig’s version has better intentions. If nothing else, hopefully it will update Wikipedia’s list of people who died on the toilet to include more women.

Do say: “Wikipedia is systemically biased.”

Don’t say: “At last, something Elon Musk and Sandi Toksvig can agree on.”

Six questions facing England as they target next year’s Women’s World Cup

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:33:15 GMT

Starting positions at centre-back and No 10 are up for grabs, while Sarina Wiegman’s future continues to be in the air

England have two jobs to do on Tuesday. The first, avoiding an almighty upset and progressing past Greece on aggregate in their Women’s World Cup playoff to reach a final tie, should be a formality for one of the world’s best-resourced teams. The second, honing their style to play like contenders for next summer’s World Cup in Brazil, is a far trickier but crucial challenge.

Friday’s relatively uninspiring 3-1 first-leg victory in Crete left room for improvement and England had plenty to work on as they trained at St George’s Park on Monday under gloomy-looking clouds. More broadly, over the next eight months, there are six questions facing the European champions.

England had 58 touches in Greece’s box and turned that into three goals, whereas Greece had two touches in England’s box but managed to score and hit the crossbar. Sarina Wiegman said she was not happy her team had conceded. Their defending in June’s 4-0 defeat by Spain also left much to be desired, and it feels as if England are not yet certain about who should partner the captain, Leah Williamson, at centre-back. Wiegman mentioned on Monday that stopping counterattacks was something they must fix – they also struggled defending quick breaks in April 2025 when losing in Belgium. That year, they found a way to win the Euros but they must tighten up defensively if they want to win a first world title in the Maracanã in July.

England were wasteful in the final third in Greece and not for the first time in recent months. In the World Cup qualifying group England were 1-0 and 2-0 winners over Iceland in games where they should have scored more. A ruthless Spain, the world’s No 1 side, secured 6-1 and 3-0 wins over Iceland. On Monday Wiegman was asked what one element of Friday’s performance she would most like to improve and replied: “The execution in the final third. We got in good positions but then it’s [about] staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time, and deciding what cross or cutback you’re going to choose.”

For the past year, it has repeatedly felt as if Wiegman does not know who should start as the No 10, with Jess Park, Lucia Kendall and Laura Blindkilde Brown given chances along with Lauren James. Dropping – and recalling – Ella Toone, plus the late addition of Grace Clinton to this squad, adds mystery. Erica Meg Parkinson’s debut on Friday adds another youngster into the mix, and Beth Mead can also play as a 10. Asked on Friday whether the No 10 position had the most question marks surrounding it, Wiegman said: “There’s a lot of competition on that position, where we have a lot of options, which also means, tactically, we can do different things. You can call it a ‘question mark’ – I call it many options.”

England’s left-wing starting position feels nailed on for Lauren Hemp, who has been in tremendous form for Manchester City. The right side, however, looks uncertain, not least because Chloe Kelly has been left out. James, England’s most technically gifted player, would be the first choice for many, but she can also play centrally, and the uncapped Freya Godfrey has impressed for London City Lionesses. On Friday, Blindkilde Brown started on the right before being replaced at half-time by Mead. Whoever starts, there are only a handful of matches before next summer to build fluidity.

Winning is not enough for Manchester City to move on from this crisis

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:24:02 GMT

It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too

Sign up for our free newsletter here

The language of football is a fine and highly nuanced dialect. The majority of people involved in the game speak it with a high degree of sophistication. Minor deviations from the familiar, almost imperceptible to outsiders, can set off alarm bells: what’s really going on there? Why isn’t he happy? What’s she hinting at? But it’s an argot developed to talk about football, and when applied to other subjects, it can sound extremely jarring.

Erling Haaland is one of the brighter, more engaging players. There’s an appealing quirkiness to him that suggests he has a higher-than-usual level of self-awareness. He doesn’t mind stepping outside the norms, being a bit different. But consider his assessment of Manchester City’s 3-0 win at Liverpool on Sunday.

“It was tough,” he said. “It was hard but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone. [It’s] important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about, and the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That’s the only thing we can do.”

Strip away the context and he could be talking about an injury crisis, or perhaps the resignation of a manager or a suspension to a key player. The tropes are familiar: it was hard but we stuck together and so we prevailed. “You want to win games, it’s as simple as that,” he went on. “Perform well, play good football and win games. This was a mental battle, [it’s] never easy coming back from internationals.”

But of course this wasn’t really about coming back from internationals; that’s not what made this difficult for City. This was about the verdict of the independent panel looking into the charges brought against City, the fact that the club have been found guilty of the greatest act of sustained cheating in the history of English football. Nobody knows what’s coming next.

The gravity of the situation still seems to have not dawned on many in football. City, as is their right, continue to maintain their innocence and have appealed. The propaganda battle goes on. But this is no longer about whether the financial regulations were fair. If City had objected to the regulations they had every opportunity to raise objections and vote against them. They did not. They agreed to the regulations, and while everybody else played to them, they did not.

The excuse that they only spent what others did but that they operated under stricter controls because of a lack of historic success is not merely irrelevant but entirely bogus: in the nine years under investigation, City’s net spending on transfers, before taking into account wages, was over £1.2bn ($1.6bn), around 50% more than any other Premier League side. And for all their talk of being proud disruptors, of rebels taking on the “red cartel”, that spending transformed City into the most dominant side English football has ever known, with six league titles in seven years. They are, precisely, an argument for why spending controls are necessary.

None of that, of course, is Haaland’s fault. He is a footballer offered a very competitive salary to play alongside very good players for a very good manager for a club for which his father played. This is another of football’s absurdities: it’s always the manager and players who end up becoming the faces of the institution, being quizzed about things that have very little to do with them as the executives and directors responsible lurk away from public scrutiny.

“My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear,” Enzo Maresca said. “Guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy.”

Which on the one hand is absurd: nobody knows whether the three points City claimed at Anfield will still be theirs by Christmas. Nobody knows what division they will be playing in next season. Nobody knows how bad the sanction could be. And this is not some unfortunate event that has befallen City; this is the direct consequence of the actions of their directors. But on the other, what else can players and managers do? How else can they respond to this situation other than by being professional and trying to win games, even if none of it ultimately means anything?

What this is emphatically not, though, is just another football crisis from which City can move on by winning football matches. This is a crisis unlike anything English football has ever known, and it is one with which football’s language is struggling to cope.

As a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:12:58 GMT

Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld

In pandemic preparedness work, scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning. The World Health Organization (WHO), for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritise emerging disease threats and collect the evidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation.

As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that the death of a single lab worker in Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwide every month. But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened – and ongoing concern about biological weapons research.

The 28-year-old lab worker died after developing severe pneumonia. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, established in 1934, which studies plague and other dangerous pathogens including anthrax and cholera, and is rumoured to be involved in biological weapons research. Prof Ashish Jha, who was the US White House Covid-19 response coordinator, and who co-chaired an Ebola commission with me, wrote on social media: “US intelligence assess that Russia’s scientists continue developing biological weapons capabilities. Those programmes operate in secret. Nobody outside inspects them and nobody inside has much incentive to admit when something goes wrong.”

On top of that, initial local media coverage suggested that she had died from pneumonic plague after a lab accident, possibly a broken test tube. Pneumonic plague is caused by a bacterium (Yersinia pestis), and can spread through respiratory contact and is always fatal if untreated. If antibiotics are given in the first 24 hours after symptoms, or even before onset of symptoms post-exposure, it is largely treatable. If she knew she had been exposed, why was treatment not given in time? (Pneumonic plague is a different disease to the more common bubonic plague, which transmits through flea bites.)

Despite Russian health authorities denying that it was a case of plague and insisting it was pneumonia of unknown origin, they quickly placed about 200 contacts of the lab worker under quarantine. The authorities reported that no high-threat pathogens were detected and monitoring had ended. The WHO released a statement noting a potential second linked case, but Russia denied this. The cause of death remains unconfirmed.

The WHO has pushed the Russian government for more information – including confirmation of the diagnosis and details of the investigations, the reason why it put so many people in quarantine and more information on the second case – but it has not yet received this information.

On the one hand, if this infection was spreading further, additional cases would have emerged by now. The lab worker died on 2 October, and the testing of contacts and release of those in quarantine indicates that any spread has been contained so far. However, given that the incubation period can be one to three days, continued monitoring is important.

There are three hypothetical scenarios if we assume the illness was pneumonic plague. The first is that the lab worker was accidentally exposed to the bacterium while doing research, and either didn’t know, or didn’t tell anyone out of fear – and therefore didn’t ask for treatment immediately. So when she became sick, her window of treatment had been missed.

Second, the lab worker was exposed to an antibiotic-resistant strain. This may sound like a conspiracy theory, but senior academics have raised concerns given the history of the Soviet biological weapons programme and the potential for pathogens to be engineered for hostile purposes.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Third, Dan Singer (the former White House director for countering biological threats) has suggested that this lab worker might have been given an outdated vaccine, which is only available in Russia as it is not approved by the WHO or most other countries. This is a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning a weakened version of the bacteria is given, but it doesn’t always provide protection and sometimes can cause disease.

In short, we don’t know what happened because there is insufficient information from the Russian authorities. To understand what happened, investigators would need access to laboratory and clinical evidence, including genomic sequencing, pathogen identification and details of the worker’s research. Without this, we are left with speculation when only scientific certainty will do.

As a member of the WHO, Russia has an international legal obligation to share information with the agency. The WHO’s health regulations specifically cover “unusual and unexpected” events, as well as those with serious public health impact and with significant risk of international spread, or that risk affecting trade or travel. But unfortunately, as with most international law, there’s no real enforcement mechanism. There is a reliance on broad cooperation across countries, with the understanding that sharing information on disease spread is in all nations’ best interests.

The US government has also put pressure on Russia for answers, with Donald Trump saying he would speak to Putin about the situation. The US state department also formally requested further information under the international health regulations – the irony being that the US withdrew from the WHO in January 2026, but is now invoking the international framework it left behind.

As a scientist watching this unfold, I’m reminded that while we can have research and expert conferences into better diagnostics, faster genomic sequencing, more effective vaccines and accessible treatments, none of these advances can compensate for a failure to share the information needed to identify a pathogen in the first place. Preparedness is a political challenge as well as a scientific one. And without transparency, it will be a case of one step forward, two steps back.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

‘When it went double platinum, Andy Burnham gave us the award’: how Courteeners made Not Nineteen Forever

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:11:47 GMT

‘In nightclubs, I’d be the dude scribbling lyrics in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off’

I had the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever before the band existed. They were in a little red book of poems and scribbles that got me a place on the creative writing course at the University of Salford. Most of what became the songs for our first album, St Jude, were in that book. As well as uni, I was working in a shop and spending five nights a week at the Night & Day bar in Manchester, but in a nightclub I’d be the dude scribbling in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off.

Not Nineteen Forever was probably inspired by a specific incident, although I can’t remember it exactly. The first line, “She had to peel me off the pavement”, could have happened on many a night out then. “Front-crawled the crowd down the stairs” is because the staircase at the 42nd Street club was so tight you’d have to literally front-crawl over people. The chorus: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together”, sounds like the sort of thing somebody might have said to me, but it could easily have been me giving myself a telling off after waking up with a fuzzy head.

I got the chords when I was trying to work out Someday by the Strokes but got the finger positions muddled up. I’d taken a bag of washing to my parents’ house and was working on it in my old bedroom when my dad poked his head in and said: “It sounds all right, that.” Not Nineteen Forever was one of the last songs I wrote before I convinced my three best mates to form the band. I told them: “If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar on my own in Manchester pubs for ever.”

You never think a song’s going to resonate 20 years later, but it’s become easily Courteeners’ most popular song. Ironically, it initially charted at No 19, but years later when it went double platinum Andy Burnham – who comes to our gigs – presented us with the award in the Britons Protection pub. The song’s taken on a poignant dimension now. At gigs I see our original fans together with their kids – who are 17, 18, 19 – and they’re all singing: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together.”

Courteeners had just been signed by a major label who asked me if I could go to Manchester to meet them as they had expressed interest in working with me. I saw them play in one of the university halls and it was mind-blowing. They already had a devoted following who were singing along with the lyrics the way Smiths audiences used to. I’d produced the Smiths, so it was right up my avenue.

In the mid-2000s there’d been a resurgence of indie guitar bands: Arctic Monkeys, Kaiser Chiefs and Kasabian. In a way Courteeners were the last hurrah of that kind of hugely popular guitar group. The next thing I knew we were all in Olympic studios in London recording the album. I was excited to work with them. Not Nineteen Forever was a ready-made anthem and stood out, but so did Cavorting or What Took You So Long?

With a band like Courteeners, you want to capture their performance. Like the best bands, they were like a little gang: us against the world. So we recorded live, only using click tracks to set the tempos. Their arrangements were short and concise and didn’t need much editing. Liam and Conan [Daniel Moores]’s guitar parts were intrinsic to the sound – I lent Conan a nice old vintage Telecaster – and I found the emotion in Liam’s voice really attractive.

When they’d started out in a garage, Liam had to shout to be heard over the guitar, but in the studio I vaguely remember telling him he didn’t need to. When I saw the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever written down it hit me how good they were. “Older woman and an ever so slightly younger man” always makes me laugh. He was 19. The “older woman” was probably 21 or something.

When the album came out I was perplexed by the lukewarm reaction from elements of the press – probably because it was another four lads with guitars – but it’s a really strong collection that I think still stands up today. The reissue of St Jude went to No 1 15 years after it first came out. I’d never had that happen before in my career: I was quite emotional.

God Bless the Band – the best of Courteeners is out now Ignition Music. A UK tour begins on 6 November at First Direct Bank Arena, Leeds.

Student lay in wait for housemate before stabbing him 30 times, Bristol court hears

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:04:19 GMT

Zack Coughlan is accused of murdering Jamie Collins, with whom he studied at the University of the West of England

A university student lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times, a murder trial has been told.

Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home near the University of West England in Bristol, where both were studying robotics.

Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April after returning from campus on his bike, Bristol crown court heard.

Coughlan then allegedly cycled away on the bike, dumped it at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing into a pond.

He returned to the house they shared in Filton, south Gloucestershire, at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends, the court was told.

Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, said: “A few hours later he decided it was time to call the police and pretend that he had just found his friend’s body in the garden.

“At about 2am, eight hours later, the defendant called 999. He said that his friend had been stabbed. They told him to do CPR until paramedics arrived and he told them that he was.”

He told police he had noticed the back gate was open, went outside and found Collins’s body.

The court heard the attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house, which Coughlan showed officers, who initially treated him as a witness.

Coughlan had injuries to his hands but he said he had hurt himself when he fell while climbing trees.

Vaitilingam said that as the evidence against Coughlan mounted, he went from being a witness to a suspect. He now accepted he had killed Collins but denied murder. He said he “lost his self-control” when he carried out the attack, the barrister said.

The jury was told that Coughlan and Collins were final-year students and lived together in a house owned by the defendant.

Vaitilingam said there had been disagreements between the pair about rent and whether Coughlan was charging too much, but they appeared to have been resolved.

“There was nothing that any friends were aware of that seemed to be a significant problem,” he said. “They hung out together, both in person and online, they did gaming together, they went out together; entirely normal student life.”

The trial continues.

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:00:56 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Our testers reflect on a year of discoveries, from family game nights to fewer chores

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It’s our birthday! So to celebrate turning two, we asked our contributors to reflect on their year of testing pretty much everything – from beauty products to video doorbells. It turns out they’ve had some unexpected wins along the way.

Some managed to tick an extra thing off their to-do list. “After six months of testing IPL devices, epilators and then IPL devices again, I had no need to book in for my usual pre-beach wax this summer,” says Lise Smith. Caramel Quin’s children, in turn, are grateful to have one fewer chore to do. “My teenagers got their clothes ironed while I was testing irons. I’ve pressed thousands of items of school uniform over the years, but it’s iron your own clothes these days … except when mum’s testing!”

Others learned an important lesson about value. “Testing so many products has cemented my belief that price isn’t always an indicator of quality,” says Sarah Matthews. Sabine Wiesel, meanwhile, was impressed by a Beauty of Joseon eye serum that came in at just a fraction of the price of some competitors in her test of the best eye creams and left her with a “brighter and rejuvenated-looking eye area”.

For Matt Collins and Sian Lewis, testing outdoor equipment has enhanced their camping experiences in unanticipated ways. Matt discovered a walking trail while trying out gear for camping with kids. “At lovely Holden Farm in Hampshire, I discovered the South Downs Way. Glorious. This ancient route had my son and me wandering beneath veteran oaks and along spring meadows at sunrise.” And Sian upped her cooking skills while testing the best camping stoves: “I’m usually an instant-noodles kind of person, but I’m now a dab hand at cooking on a dinky gas flame and have recently whipped up cornbread and egg muffin breakfast sarnies in the middle of the wild.”

Meanwhile, Jane Hoskyn’s once-white towel got a new lease of life after she purposely stained it to test eco-friendly laundry detergents. “It ended up a right old mess, so I had to dye it. It’s now a gorgeous deep forest green. Much prettier and more eye-catching than it was even before the stain test – it shows less dirt, too.”

Video doorbells unexpectedly helped Andy Shaw sleep more soundly. “If I wake up wondering whether one of my adult offspring has made it home from the pub, I only need to check the doorbell notifications on my phone. They’re so used to the surveillance that they wave at the camera when they come in.”

And finally, one of the biggest upsides seems to be an excuse to get loved ones together. “I spent a lot of time hosting ice-cream tasting sessions with my friends while trying to find the best ice-cream makers. More quality time with friends and free ice-cream for them – I’d say that’s a win-win,” says Danielle Amato. And for Zoë Phillimore, trying out toys and games for our guide to the best gifts for six-year-olds has led to a new family tradition. “My husband, kids and I gather around the kitchen table and play board games together on a Saturday night. Hardly groundbreaking, but it’s easily my favourite time of the week.”

Revealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:42:27 GMT

Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say

A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal.

Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there.

The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate.

As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper.

As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties.

Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative.

The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling.

In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton and Reform UK or Farage.

He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team.

Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations.

Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.”

Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”.

Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”.

The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer.

Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor.

The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures.

Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry had cleared the officials of breaking the law. The matter remains under police investigation.

Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman.

Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”.

He is considered to be part of Farage’s inner circle and was close enough to the Reform UK leader to have been present on a trip to party donor Christopher Harborne’s Thai wellness retreat at Christmas in 2022 to mark the crypto billionaire’s 60th birthday.

Other guests photographed at the meeting include Farage’s unpaid aide and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

In May 2023, Van Scheltinga and Bruni-Lowe were photographed having drinks at a Mayfair restaurant with Farage, Cottrell and Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader.

Rodrigues said: “The existence of personal or social meetings involving individuals associated with the company does not establish a corporate relationship between Redfield & Wilton Strategies and Reform UK.”

While much of Redfield & Wilton’s published polling related to voter intentions in the UK and the US, sources said Bruni-Lowe had its staff develop a “dossier” on local authority performance between autumn 2024 and spring 2025.

One source said he suggested the firm’s work could be sold to political parties, and that Bruni-Lowe appeared “obsessed” with the dossier. Research by employees included freedom of information requests to councils to find expenditure on translation services.

Rodrigues said the FOI project was a “commercial research project” and translation services were just one of “several dozen categories” examined by the company in a project led by Van Scheltinga. He added that none of the research was supplied to Reform or Farage.

The company’s other work, sources said, included polling in Montenegro, Hungary, Hong Kong and the Bahamas, as well as research about attitudes in the UK to gold and cryptocurrencies.

Employees were not always told exactly how their work would be used. According to one former employee, they were told their work on a foreign election would be for the Telegraph, but the polling never appeared in the newspaper. Another said they believed their work on cryptocurrencies was for a client.
