If you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email henry. dyer@theguardian. com.

Finally, our guide at theguardian. com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

One unusual piece of work by the company was an October 2021 submission to an inquiry into central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) carried out by the House of Lords economic affairs committee. The company cited polling it said “was self-funded internally by Redfield & Wilton Strategies Ltd for the purpose of this submission”.

The submission said the scepticism of the British public over the UK government’s capacity for innovation meant “it is strategically important that alternatives to a CBDC from the private sector, including those that are already in use, are also given the opportunity to be developed further”.

According to a person who worked at the company at the time of the submission, “all of the crypto stuff came down from Chris [Bruni-Lowe]”.

One online profile for Rodrigues, a solicitor based in London, refers to him holding a directorship of an “innovative market research firm”. However, according to former employees, he had a limited role in the day-to-day running of Redfield & Wilton. One source said that at a rare in-person meeting Rodrigues was “paraded around on a laptop on a Zoom call”.

Van Scheltinga was frequently quoted giving analysis of the company’s polling and wrote columns for the Times and Telegraph.

Van Scheltinga was the listed contact for the company with the British Polling Council, the trade body for pollsters, but one industry source said he never attended BPC meetings. This led to demands from the BPC for a representative of the group to appear before them: that was ultimately Rodrigues, the nominal director, who maintained “total silence”, according to the industry source.

Bruni-Lowe declined to comment. Van Scheltinga did not respond to requests for comment.

Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:41:21 GMT

‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames

Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily.

Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, ​said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.”

The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red.

The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor, Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground car park, a council daycare facility and community centre.

A determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s.

Rather than demolish the building, the city undertook a six-year, 13m-franc (about €3m, or £2.5m today) renovation project, restoring the market’s historic wood and ironwork frame and glass roof. Les Enfants Rouges reopened as a food court in 2000.

While still hosting some traditional stalls including a greengrocer, butcher, cheesemonger and fishmonger, the 1,000 sq m market was mostly given over to more than a dozen stands offering French, Lebanese, Moroccan, Japanese and other street food at the counter or at casual chairs and tables.

The current Time Out tourist guide describes Les Enfants Rouges as “the coolest market in Paris”, while the authoritative US website Food&Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year after other food courts in London, Bangkok, Lyon and Mexico City.

Lt Col Pierre de Bouvier of the Paris fire service said much of the metal structure of the market had fallen in, and most of the stalls had gone up in flames. More than 150 firefighters and 50 fire trucks battled the blaze after being alerted at 4.15am, he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.

Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:41:17 GMT

Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh

On Saturday, a missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit Riyadh’s international airport, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. On Sunday, another attack ‌killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

CCTV footage showed people cowering at the moment of impact of Saturday’s attack.

Footage filmed in the aftermath of showed damage inside one of the terminal buildings at the airport, which is located about 22 miles north of the Saudi Arabian capital.

The attacks by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, were the biggest escalation yet in their campaign ⁠against Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in recent weeks.

Though the violence might appear at first sight to be restricted to the Arabian peninsula, it could have global consequences, pushing up fuel prices and so international inflation.

The Houthis’ timing is partly opportunistic but also rooted in the dynamics of the conflicts across the Gulf.

The Houthis initially stayed on the sidelines of the conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran earlier this year. But last month, the Islamist militia movement seized control of key territory and gained virtual control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, which dominates the Red Sea, a critical shipping route for oil and gas exports from the region.

The Yemeni government forces and local allies began a major counteroffensive last week to drive back the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab and also hit other Houthi positions.

Saudi Arabia is in the Houthis’ crosshairs because it supports Yemen’s UN-backed government and its forces. Their attacks on high-profile targets in the kingdom such as oil infrastructure and the capital’s airport – key symbols of its international integration and economic future – makes painfully obvious the costs of Riyadh’s strategic choices.

Such attacks also benefit Iran, which has long supported the Houthis as part of its “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Islamist hardline movements that allows Tehran to project power and influence round the region.

The new threat from the Houthis to the Red Sea and to Saudi Arabia highlights again the massive leverage Tehran and its allies can exert on global oil and gas supplies, countering recent US pressure in bold move on the conflict’s chessboard.

The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia have been the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.

They also marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. Businesses in Riyadh’s financial hub have told employees to work remotely, authorities in Riyadh have asked schools to switch to online classes this week, and top energy executives were ⁠dropped from the schedule of a high-profile conference this week in the capital.

Though Saudi Arabia has intervened indirectly in conflicts around the Middle East and beyond for decades, violence has rarely struck the kingdom itself. In recent months, the country has found itself on a frontline, something its rulers have long sought to avoid.

Saudi Arabia has invested enormous sums in its military – the kingdom is the world’s eighth biggest spender on weapons – but Houthi attacks are very hard to stop.

“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at Ottawa University.

Other analysts point out that even the vaunted Israeli air defence systems failed to stop a ballistic missile narrowly missing Ben Gurion international airport last year.

Reprisals against the Houthis and efforts to pre-emptively destroy the movement’s offensive capabilities are not easy either. The US bombardment in 2025 showed how hard it is to destroy the militia’s capabilities, which have been much enhanced over recent years, in part through Iranian advice and investment.

The Houthis say their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – suggesting they are responding to ongoing Saudi strikes on the territory they control in Yemen – but show no sign of stopping their attacks.

“Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” official statements carried by the Houthi-run al-Masirah television channel said.

It seems unlikely Saudi Arabia will halt its counterstrikes, and equally unlikely the kingdom will be able to find a way to block all incoming Houthi missiles, though it may improve its intelligence gathering and early warning to allow better defence of specific high-value targets.

Nor is there any imminent prospect of an end to the hostilities between Iran and the US that are a major factor in the surge of the recent violence in Yemen. And though the Houthis are more a coalition of different factions than a coherent single movement, for the moment they appear unified behind hardline and ideologically committed leaders.

Farea al-Muslimi, a specialist on Yemen and the Gulf at Chatham House in London, said the Houthis had been consistently underestimated over the years.

“They have really upped their game and believe they can get something now which will reposition them within the region. They are very confident at the moment and feeling empowered …. But though they think they can control this [escalation], that may well be an illusion,” he said.

Is it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearance

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:37:49 GMT

Researchers will head to remote Pacific atoll, but sceptics say satellite images unlikely to be of her aircraft

A team of US researchers is approaching a remote Pacific atoll where they suspect the famed aviator Amelia Earhart crash-landed in 1937, in the latest attempt to crack one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century.

The 17-person expedition was inspired by satellite images taken over several years showing a submerged object in the uninhabited island’s sandy lagoon – evidence dismissed by other longtime Earhart sleuths who say it is probably a fallen tree.

These researchers – led by archaeologists who raised funding from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University – hope it will instead be revealed as the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. Separate aerial footage of the area suggested the submerged object has a metallic glint, the team say.

“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” said the expedition’s leader, Richard Pettigrew, before he set sail this month. “Confirming the plane wreckage there would be the smoking-gun proof.”

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator. By that point, Earhart, 39, was already a celebrity and aviation pioneer, having broken several records including being the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight​.

Locating the wreck of the twin-engine plane would confirm a long-held – but unproven – hypothesis that Earhart and Noonan ditched at the atoll of Nikumaroro, part of the archipelago country of Kiribati and about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.

They were en route to Howland Island, about 400 miles north of Nikumaroro, when their plane ran low on fuel and disappeared.

After a six-day sea voyage from Tarawa, the capital of Kiribati, the research group is expected to arrive on the uninhabited atoll on Tuesday local time and will spend several days searching for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image.

The expedition says it has been lying there for several years, and is even visible in aerial photography dating back to 1938.

Pettigrew, who heads the Archaeological Legacy Institute, a nonprofit organisation, raised funds for the mission with Purdue University in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and which funded her ill-fated final flight on the modified plane she called her “flying laboratory”. The university runs an airport and opened an Amelia Earhart Terminal last year.

The expedition builds on an already large body of evidence pinpointing the atoll as the location where the aviators went down. Much of it was gathered during dozens of visits between 1989 and 2019 by teams from the US explorers group Tigher (The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery).

Tighar’s co-founder – and perhaps Earhart’s most well-known explorer – Ric Gillespie, said the Taraia Object was likely a dead pandanus tree, which is ​native to the area, that washed into the ​lagoon.

Gillespie, who is the author of One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy, said he and other teams had visited the exact site where the object was located in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors.

“There’s nothing there, or we would have found it,” he said in an interview this year. “If they suddenly discover that Amelia Earhart’s wreckage is there, I’ll be very surprised, but I’d be the first one to congratulate them. But I don’t think they are going to find anything.”

While Tighar agrees the Electra made an emergency landing on the atoll, they believe it was washed off a reef and now probably lies undiscovered and in pieces in deep water off the island’s western end.

Tighar’s version of the mystery was that Earhart, and possibly Noonan, were marooned on Nikumaroro but survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating small fish and turtles. This theory is based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and 1930s-era artefacts, such as a jar of what is believed to be cosmetics freckle cream.

The pair’s disappearance led to a large US government search, including a flyover of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The Purdue mission says the object may not have been found by previous expeditions as it could have been covered with sand.

Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:14:04 GMT

Boaz Weinstein’s hedge fund is waging an aggressive campaign against the FTSE 250’s Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust

Business live – latest updates

Here we go again: another episode in the Saba saga, the story of a New York hedge fund causing havoc in the UK investment trust sector by taking big stakes in funds and then demanding change, often in only vague terms.

The best that can be said about Saba Capital (and it’s not much) is that its belligerent boss, Boaz Weinstein, has disturbed the complacency that used to infect corners of the UK investment trust world, meaning companies that invest in other companies. It is now harder for a board to do nothing if the share price sits at a wide discount to the value of the underlying assets for long periods.

Too often, though, Saba’s assaults look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors. The attack on Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent usually known by its USA ticker, is all three.

Regular shareholders in USA have roundly told Saba to get lost twice in the past 18 months but they will have to do so again if they value what they own, which they should. The US raider, sitting on a near-30% stake, wants to install three of its nominees on the board via a vote at next week’s annual meeting.

On a long view, USA’s performance has been excellent: an annualised return of 16.7% since launch in 2018, beating the S&P 500 over the period and within the top 10% of all UK investment companies. The only reason an opening, of a sort, has appeared for Saba is because the 16.7%-a-year returns haven’t happened in a straight line. The pop in AI valuations in late-2022 means USA’s five-year statistics are less impressive.

But volatility is what investors accept when they buy into a strategy of backing high-growth US companies for the long-term. The portfolio is stuffed with stakes in big names in the AI world – Anthropic, Databricks, OpenAI, SpaceX and Stripe – that were acquired when the companies were smaller and sometimes still privately owned. A little bit of biodiversity in the UK investment landscape will be lost if USA falls under Saba’s control.

What would a Saba-dominated board do? It’s hard to say definitively because this is all Saba says: “If our nominees are elected, we would urge them to offer all USA shareholders a 100% cash exit at or near NAV [net asset value] – providing a long-overdue liquidity event.”

The absurdity of that proposal lies in the fact that the board of USA says it has already offered Saba what it supposedly wants – a chance to get out at a price nearly equivalent to the value of the assets. But the US hedge fund declined.

The suspicion is that Saba’s nominees could try to appoint Saba itself as manager, or wrap USA into a Saba-managed vehicle. And, note, Saba’s main funds in the US now trade on far wider discounts to asset value than USA’s relatively modest 3%.

Since Saba hasn’t spelled out much, all one can say is that its nominees cannot possibly be regarded as independent. One is a Saba employee; the other two are serial picks in Weinstein’s various campaigns.

Here is broker Investec’s assessment: “Saba offers no credible plan. Shareholders are being asked to give its nominees potential board control on the strength of a conditional, non-binding liquidity proposal, with no roadmap for the future manager, strategy or governance: vote first, then find out later what you’ve voted for.”

The choice, then, is between a known strategy that has been successful, with a few bumps, or a mystery ride under Saba’s tame directors. The analysis should not be hard: shareholders should stick with the existing board. Independence matters.

Here’s the tricky bit, however. Saba’s near-30% holding, plus 7.7% in the hands of assumed sympathiser Sessa Capital, means USA shareholders need to act. “Not voting is a vote for Saba,” says broker Panmure Liberum. “Support the board, or suffer the consequences,” warns Investec. Sound advice.

The annual meeting is on 23 October but, for anybody holding via an investment platform, the effective voting deadline can be as soon as this Wednesday. Those platforms – looking at Hargreaves Lansdown, AJ Bell and Interactive Investor – should be warning clients of deadlines right now. Preferably in red for danger.

NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 12:59:56 GMT

Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.

The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”

Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.

The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.

Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”

NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”

In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.

In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

Mort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellion

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 11:14:33 GMT

Paul Greengrass’s Peasants’ Revolt epic, The Uprising, is just the latest in a long line of movies depicting an unsuccessful attempt at remaking the nation

The British are perverse. We fetishise our failures, even if they are essentially tangential to a national narrative that should be about imperial conquest, slavery and being unremittingly unpleasant to foreigners. We tell and retell, for instance, the story of Captain Scott even though he died in Antarctica in 1912 after losing the race to reach the south pole first to the unacceptably Norwegian Roald Amundsen. Similarly, Christopher Nolan’s 2017 film Dunkirk typified the British tendency to snatch national glory from the jaws of defeat. And then there was the tragicomic disaster of the Charge of the Light Brigade during the 1853-56 Crimean war in which our boys raced to putatively glorious if stupid deaths. It’s as if, for us British, pointless sacrifice and embracing failure are what heroism means. And our cinema has colluded with this perversity.

But there is an exception to this national veneration of failure. Britain has been reluctant to embrace its revolutionary defeats. There is, for instance, no film dealing with the Chartist movement’s 19th-century struggle for universal suffrage. Even more strikingly yet, it is only now, in 2026, that a film has been made about the calamitous 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, even though it is a pivotal event in British history. Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising, starring Andrew Garfield as a – let’s just get this over with – revolting peasant, joins a mere handful of other movies, including Kevin Brownlow and Andrew Mollo’s 1975 Winstanley, Bill Douglas’s 1986 Comrades and Mike Leigh’s 2018 Peterloo, that dare depict how radical collective action was crushed by a ruthless state.

For Stephanie Barczewski, author of Heroic Failure and the British, our fetishisation of glorious disaster is a corollary of the 19th-century British private school ethos of stoic duty and crypto-S&M suffering culled from an ancient Roman exemplar. Revolutionary failure doesn’t fit this template; hence, one might suppose, its absence from our cinema.

The Uprising, however, for all its flaws and missteps, is a bold attempt to correct a national wrong by depicting a collective uprising devoid of heroism. Greengrass tries to make sense of how a mass movement of riff-raff from the rough ends of Kent and Essex arose, and how its momentum was compromised of factionalism and conflicting aims. It shows how, ultimately, the revolutionary leaders were duped by the boy king Richard II, leaving the rebels winding up to be either slaughtered en masse in London’s Smithfield or skulking defeated back to their homes to work harder to pay the poll tax whose unfairness they had risen up against in the first place.

It is an important – if belated, improbable and commercially dubious – addition to our national story.

In contrast, other countries have been more fortunate in their revolutionary heritage and as a result their national cinemas teem with examples of successful uprisings. From the advent of cinema, for instance, Americans have incessantly revelled in making movies about their war of independence – including silent features such as 1917’s The Spirit of 76 and DW Griffith’s America (1924), not to mention Bugs Bunny in Friz Freleng’s delightful period romp of a cartoon Bunker Hill Bunny (1950). The French have been making cinematic homages to their 1789 revolution going back the 1913 biopic Robespierre.

In Russia, Grigori Aleksandrov and Sergei Eisenstein’s October, in 1928, typified how the Bolshevik revolution’s success against the odds made Russian spirit what it is. Movies such as Neil Jordan’s Liam Neeson-fronted biopic Michael Collins (1996) and The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006), set during the Irish war of independence and starring Cillian Murphy, depicted the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage – even if the latter had an English director in the shape of Ken Loach.

But it isn’t just the deeply classist notion of what failures count as heroic that has made British cinema reluctant to embrace our failed revolutionary heritage. It is the result of how our culture has been reverse-colonised by Hollywood, with historical narratives only deemed filmable if they fit into American movie industry’s tropes. Whenever Hollywood deigns to make a movie about British history, it includes Downton-style upstairs-downstairs hokum, those crazy sexed-up murderous Tudors and, of course, that cod-historical franchise that never stops giving, Robin Hood.

Equally, it is axiomatic in Hollywood that political struggles are always about one thing – a very American notion of freedom, individual freedom from presumed oppression. That’s why Mel Gibson’s 1995 Braveheart was possible: even though William Wallace’s struggles against the English ended in failure with his execution at Smithfield (not far from where Wat Tyler was murdered by Richard II’s lackeys), the biopic involved the classic Hollywood trope of the little guy fighting for freedom. Any other political goal (tax reform, wealth redistribution, solidarity, fraternity) scarcely makes a dent in the Hollywood narrative juggernaut.

And that’s what makes Greengrass’s The Uprising problematic. Compromised by Hollywood values, it is conflicted about representing a failed political revolution as what it was – a collective struggle. It depicts the Peasants’ Revolt in the frame of one fictional man, Garfield’s Ploughman. Conceived by Greengrass as a representative everyman, Ploughman – with a disregard for historical truth that should make the film’s historical adviser Dan Jones wince – pops up Zelig-like to parlay with the king, catch the king’s mother’s eye, rally the rebels, scythe down the bad guys, as if he were a real-life historical figure. The collective struggle becomes individualised drama, betraying the positioning of the apostrophe – what happened in 1381 was the Peasants’ Revolt not the Peasant’s Revolt.

Worse yet, the film includes a very silly coda in which, a year after the defeat of the revolt, Ploughman and a rump of rebels have retreated to the English greenwood to form an outlaw band of unmerry men. The corollary of this coda is to make the Peasants’ Revolt a kind of origin story for the legend of Robin Hood, even though that is nonsense: the folkloric rebel operated – if at all – about 200 years earlier. The whole idea may seem ridiculous, but the US distributors for The Uprising, Focus Features, leaned into this barmy interpretation by changing the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood earlier this year, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”. Sensible Guardian readers will know of course that Robin Hood was a supporter of Richard I and foe of King John both of whom ruled England almost exactly two centuries earlier.

Such absurdities are a great shame since Greengrass’s – worthwhile – intention was to make a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that resonates topically for our age. A collapse in trust of our rulers, a seemingly endless cost of living crisis, widening inequality, political discourse dominated by lies and nonsense: 2026 is more like 1381 than we realise.

It’s worth pointing out that there has been one successful military revolution in British history, namely the English civil war. Cinema of course has been a failure at depicting it: there was Ken Hughes’s wildly inaccurate 1970 drama Cromwell starring Richard Harris and Alec Guinness and Mike Barker’s 2003 To Kill a King with Tim Roth and Dougray Scott. But our most enduring and successful revolution was scarcely cinematic: the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 in which the Catholic King James II was replaced by his Protestant daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William III of Orange was hailed by Bertrand Russell as “the most moderate and successful of all revolutions. Its aims were modest, but they were exactly achieved.” Yawn! Who wants to see that movie?

Perhaps the greatest film about British revolutionary failure was the aforementioned Winstanley, about a group of proto-communists called the Diggers who settled common land on St Georges’s Hill outside Weybridge, Surrey during the English civil war. They hoped to create a utopia devoid of private property and for a few weeks lived self-sufficiently until they were violently evicted by the local gentry. To clinch the point that the Diggers’ experiment was a failure, just go on to property website Rightmove. There you can find a “stunning and elegant” £25m mansion on Cavendish Road, St George’s Hill with “fairway views, seven individually themed bathrooms, two staff apartments, and a leisure complex” and 1.5 acres of carefully landscaped gardens. Not what their leader Gerrard Winstanley wanted at all. He wrote: “Was the Earth made to preserve a few covetous, proud men to live at ease, and for them to bag and barn up the treasures of the Earth from others, that these may beg or starve in a fruitful land; or was it made to preserve all her children?” Our radical history, so often absent from our national cinema, has been built over in a field in Surrey for real estate scarcely any of us can afford. A very British coup if ever there was one.

Alexéi Rojas: ‘I’m passionate about sustainability – I told Arsenal: we need to fix this’

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:57:51 GMT

The 21-year-old goalkeeper wants to impress on football the need to change old habits for the sake of the planet

“I’m a bit of an outlier as a person, I like being unique in who I am and what I do,” says the former Arsenal goalkeeper Alexéi Rojas, who combines saving shots with saving the planet. “I would say that was one of the biggest pulls for me to become a goalkeeper. I like being different.”

There is plenty to make him stand out. By 15, Rojas was changing the way people thought at Arsenal, transforming attitudes at the academy’s Hale End training ground where he would cycle, rather than get a lift from his parents. Rojas’s interest in the climate crisis began thanks to his mother, who works in wind energy. He would visit her office to learn more about renewables and their potential.

“I spoke about sustainability in front of everyone [at the academy],” Rojas says. “The staff realised this is something I’m really passionate about. I jumped at the opportunity. I said: ‘We need to fix this.’

“First, there’s no recycling bins, we need to incorporate that. We use way too much plastic, which we can swap out for reusable things or compostable packaging; there’s a lot of energy wasted at the training ground where there’s lights on all the time that don’t need to be.”

This transformation led to more interest from teammates, who quickly switched to reusable bottles, a small indication of what can happen when someone makes a stand.

“It is really important that clubs are actively pushing what they’re doing in terms of being sustainable – that could be the way the kits are produced and where the materials are coming from, to sustainability campaigns,” Rojas says. His gloves incorporate recycled materials and the manufacturer donates towards the removal of plastic from the oceans.

At elite level, teams crisscross the globe for matches while major international tournaments attract fans from all over the world. The carbon impact is rarely considered.

“In our day-to-day, we may not see much of a [climate] impact right now but, as much as people love going to matches, love watching the World Cup, if we don’t protect the longevity of our game, we’re not going to be able to have these moments,” explains Rojas, who has spoken at the London School of Economics and the Net Zero Summit.

“You’re not going to be able to go with your mates and watch football because the game may not even be on because of the weather conditions. It’s making everybody associated with football understand the potential impacts in the future. And that way, by making it relatable, people can actually start to understand things.”

Rojas, who was born in the Essex town of Basildon and educated in England, has represented Colombia at youth level and experienced the rapidly changing climate around the world and at home. The brutal 2026 summer left grassroots pitches across the United Kingdom looking like deserts.

The beginning of the season was delayed in parts of the country as dry and bumpy surfaces were deemed unplayable after months of dry weather. “It’s ultimately going to affect the longevity of the game because elite players start off by playing for local teams in the park and, without suitable conditions, opportunities will be lost,” Rojas says.

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

The 21-year-old has travelled to Kenya for Charity Boots to deliver donated kit. “You’re solving two problems in one,” he explains. “You’re solving the sustainability problem because they are not just going to landfill or being burned. You’re also solving equality by helping disadvantaged people in different countries around the world have access to sports equipment, football boots, that they can then use to enjoy, have fun, and then maybe inspire.”

Rojas featured on the Arsenal bench twice, once in the Champions League and another in the Carabao Cup, under Mikel Arteta but never made a senior appearance for the club. He was part of the goalkeeper department when Arsenal won the Premier League last season, training every day with David Raya and Kepa Arrizabalaga, but left in the summer after eight years with the club to join Penafiel in the Portuguese second tier.

“To be part of a group of so many elite, world-class players is something that you dream of,” Rojas says, “especially when, five, six years back, a lot of these players I was living my day-to-day with, training with, were players that I was watching on TV and looking up to. Being part of a squad sitting in the Premier League, in the Carabao Cup, in the Champions League – things that you dream of as a kid.”

The childhood dreams have diversified for Rojas but the power of football is at their heart, on and off the field.

I don’t have children. So who will I leave my precious possessions to when I die?

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:00:50 GMT

The quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problem

A friend of mine recently discussed his will with me. He talked about the importance of looking after his daughter financially when he’s gone. As a child-free woman, I confidently told him my money will go to organisations that have meant something to me: Macmillan Cancer Support and animal charities. It bemuses me how people think the absence of children is a problem when it comes to inheritance money; it’s always been obvious to me that I’d give my money to causes that touch my heart. But then my friend served something of a curveball. He asked me who will have my deceased mother’s ring?

It made me think: where do the precious artefacts from our lives go when we are no longer here? Whenever I’m away from home I look forward to being reunited with these things: the quirky vase that sits in the window of my study, and the owl candlestick, a birthday gift from my potter friend. These items carry parts of me – what will become of them? If you have children, the answer to this question is not presented to you as a puzzle; like a constellation of stars, the answer is perfectly aligned. If you don’t have children, the question can lead to existential angst.

This problem has caused both consternation and fascination among my child-free friends. It is a conversation topic that is something of a black hole.

I have a 12-year-old goddaughter – if I passed my mother’s ring to her (she was one when my mother died and so doesn’t remember her), can I trust her to cherish it? If she was my own daughter, would it be different, would I still feel this angst? My friends and I have wrestled with this question.

I’ve seen enough episodes of Antiques Roadshow to know that the world is full of people who cherish items that once belonged to relatives they have never met. If the ring went to my goddaughter, I’d be the last custodian who really knew what it meant to my mother. But a new relationship would be anchored with it: the one that I have with my goddaughter. Understanding this has made me realise that sentimentality can and does still get passed down.

I realise my concerns about the passing on of my mother’s ring stems from trying to hold on to what is tangibly left of her. Inadvertently, I have been willing time to stop. The philosopher Heraclitus said: “No man steps in the same river twice. For it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man.” Life moves forward and the lives of the first custodians of the things we hold dear, who have long passed, will become backstories.

When I’m gone, I will no longer be the custodian of the ring – and its meaning will alter with its new owner. This is how life works; in the exchange of hands. One day I will have to let go of what can no longer belong to me. Acknowledging this has brought me some clarity and comfort.

However, an unexpected conundrum has also popped up in my circle of child-free friends. My friend has two nieces and a nephew. The nieces don’t make an effort to be in her life and she plans to leave what she has to her nephew. She has been told this would cause strife among the siblings and her plan is “inconsiderate”. How much should we consider the feelings of others when it comes to writing our wills?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The contents of our wills are not just the last performance of our lives – but the lasting performance. Child-free people may be at liberty to choose the recipients of our possessions without being bound by expectation and tradition, but we’re more open to rigorous criticism because of that freedom. It’s not as formulaic as leaving it to the kids.

The artist David Hockney died without having had children, but will leave a bigger legacy to the world than most. I’m a writer; perhaps my words will touch 10 or a thousand people, certainly more than the number of children I could have had. I will be a benefactor to many, rather than a few, through my words and the money I will leave to charity.

In the end, we all leave some form of a legacy whether we have children or not; traces of ourselves that whisper of our past existence. I’m not interested in any grandiose legacy when I’m gone, but I cannot deny, there’s something beautiful about leaving a token of ourselves in a world that we’ve left behind.

Kiran Sidhu is a freelance journalist and writer. She is the author of I Can Hear the Cuckoo. She also wrote the Bafta award-winning documentary Heart Valley.

The Deshaun Watson revival derailed, much to the joy of those with a functional memory

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 07:00:49 GMT

After three straight game-winning drives, Cleveland’s quarterback was sacked eight times in a dismal defeat that punctured the hype surrounding him

I guess the New York Jets didn’t get the memo. This was supposed to be a Deshaun Watson lovefest. A day where, much to the chagrin of those of us with a moral compass and a functional memory, football fans worldwide could declare Watson was “so back” and that the Browns were in some blinkered, alternate universe, a Super Bowl contender. No such luck, as the Browns looked like the Browns – reminding an otherwise jubilant city of Cleveland that they are trapped in the sports equivalent of the Backrooms.

Limping along for 155 passing yards and one touchdown, Watson fell to Earth harder than David Bowie in a Nicolas Roeg film (yes, I just watched the Dennis Miller Monday Night Football documentary on HBO). He completed fewer than 50% of his passes and ended the day with a 69.6 passer rating. I should also probably mention he got sacked eight times. Yes, eight times. EIGHT TIMES. He only completed seven more passes than he received punishing hits behind the line of scrimmage. It was a performance NBC NFL writer Patrick Daugherty called “unspeakably bad.” Actually, I think the performance was very much speakable, as I’ve demonstrated here. Stick around for another 400 words.

The thing that has defined Watson’s run as a potentially viable NFL quarterback has been his ability to march down the field and win a game in the dying embers of the contest. After three game-winning drives to start the season, it seemed like the Browns were poised to pull out another improbable victory from deep where the sun don’t shine, but no. Not today.

On fourth and 11 – with less than a minute left in the fourth quarter, down by five – Watson dropped back, only for his pocket to evaporate faster than a spilled Dasani in the middle of the Mojave Desert. Ejected violently from the pocket, Watson begins to scramble. On fourth and 11, by the way. He’s unceremoniously tackled near the line of scrimmage, putting the game on ice.

Starting off Sunday, these seemed like two teams going in the opposite direction, but the reality on the field was more like the Spider-Man pointing meme. Offensive ineptitude, with both the Jets and Browns recording fewer than 300 yards of total offense, giving away two fumbles, and failing to convert touchdowns twice in the red zone. The New York Post might have called this game “tense” and “gritty”, but I’m sure many viewers could think of more apropos adjectives to describe what they witnessed – a game that hinged on a botched snap sailing through the hands of Browns punter Corey Bojorquez. That wayward punt turned into a game-winning touchdown for Jets RB Braelon Allen.

This loss, dropping Cleveland to 3-2 on the year, felt like a necessary corrective to the hyperbole and early extension talks around Watson’s early successes. American sports fans love a comeback story, but this one is mired in issues that are far more important than football. It certainly makes everyone’s life easier when he plays like this.

Cam Little, K, Jacksonville Jaguars. Sure, there’s probably more splashy statistical performances from today. You could make a strong case for Drake Maye, whose 374 yards and four touchdowns gave the Patriots a resounding win over the Raiders. But I’m not going to do that, because we ride for placekickers when I’m around. In a bleak, dystopian ending that felt more like the final five minutes of Digger than a football game, the Eagles went up 17-16 with a mere eight seconds left in the contest. Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni, misplacing his copy of Football for Dummies, decided to have his kicker boot the ball in play rather than ice it with a touchback. A 53-yard return by Ameer Abdullah perfectly set up a gargantuan field goal to win the game for the Jags.

“I didn’t make the right decision, and I lost us that game, and that’s what I said to our guys,” Sirianni told the media after Christmas came early in London for Jacksonville. Now, a 57-yard field goal with nearly no time left on the clock isn’t exactly a gimme. One could maybe forgive Sirianni for thinking the chances of a field goal from distance to steal the game was unlikely. Except, the Jaguars’ kicker is Little – the man who holds the record for the longest made field goal in NFL history. A record he set almost a full year ago. The Eagles gave Little a dagger. He should be commended for knowing how to use it.

The Texans won their first game of the year, demolishing an equally troubled, still-winless Titans team 26-3. CJ Stroud dropped 261 yards, a passing touchdown, and a running touchdown on Tennessee, cementing a bounce-back moment that has the NFL buzzing about just how much money he’ll command on the free-agent market. More importantly, today’s result is coupled with news of Houston getting Stroud reinforcements. WR Marvin Harrison is on the way to the Texans from the Cardinals and Houston coach DeMeco Ryans was more than happy to officially drop the bomb in a brief post-game presser:

This article includes content hosted on platform. x. com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Brevity really is the soul of wit.

Before their drubbing by the Patriots, the Raiders had scored at least 26 points in all four of their games this season. Here, they didn’t score more than a touchdown until the fourth quarter, managing a meager 17 points on the road at Gillette Stadium. Las Vegas had a chance to keep pace with the AFC West leading Chiefs during KC’s bye week, but Kirk Cousins was sacked three times and couldn’t convert scoring opportunities into touchdowns. Cousins was replaced by rookie Fernando Mendoza in garbage time, showing how thoroughly the Raiders were handled. They certainly didn’t benefit from giving up 165 rushing yards, spread across multiple New England players (including 25 yards on the ground for Maye). The Pats grabbed 8.1 yards per play, as efficient and deadly as it gets.

After a World Cup in North America, I hope everyone here has gotten used to the concept of a tie. The Giants and Commanders certainly have. In an example of hopeless, foggy-eyed game management, Washington blew a chance to win the game in overtime. A Cam Skattebo turnover handed the Commanders the ball with enough time for Jayden Daniels to march down to the New York 24-yard line. A luxurious 12 seconds remained on the clock. More than enough time to plunk in a field goal to win it. Except, the Commanders wandered around the line of scrimmage for exactly 12 seconds and never did snap the ball, let alone spike it to stop the clock to set up for a kick. Commanders coach Dan Quinn, like Sirianni in the Eagles-Jags game, took the blame for the mistake. For once, I’d like to see a coach just completely throw his players under the bus. “Hey man, I’m not playing. Don’t look at me.” Just for variety.

Put the phone down. No need to call the authorities on your friends who are Steelers fans. After a game with visible tension between Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy on Thursday Night Football on 1 October, the ship was righted in Steel City, USA. Rodgers looked tidy and comfortable, connecting in the end zone with Pat Freiermuth twice to defeat the Colts 34-22.

The Vikings are still undefeated, dropping the Saints to 1-4 on the year. The game was not as close as the 23-13 score, with Minnesota dominating every major team category. New Orleans finished with a paltry 142 total yards. Only 55 of those came on the ground. The Saints only recorded one offensive touchdown, with the other coming on a fumble recovery. The story was far different for the Vikes. Minnesota RB Aaron Jones gobbled up 113 yards and one touchdown in front of moribund Saints fans in the Superdome. Kyler Murray benefitted greatly from Justin Jefferson’s return to action, throwing for 229 yards and a touchdown. Can anyone beat this Vikings team? They’ve got a bye in week six, then the 2-3 Colts, back at US Bank Stadium. That doesn’t seem promising for Indy.

The winless Dolphins almost pulled off a last-second miracle against the Bengals, getting within a touchdown with less than a minute left in the game. But kicker Riley Patterson missed the extra point before an onside kick attempt to recover possession was unsuccessful. Cincinnati took the win 31-24 off a splashy four-touchdown day for Joe Burrow. Can anyone lose to this Dolphins team? They’ve got a bye in week six, then the 2-3 Jets, on the road at MetLife Stadium. That doesn’t seem promising for viewers.

The NFL’s oldest rivalry continued, with the Packers tossing the Bears in a meat freezer and locking the door. Green Bay danced away with the win in the teams’ 214th ever matchup (including playoffs), 31-7. Caleb Williams, perhaps the most hated man in Wisconsin after his ruthless comeback win against Green Bay in last year’s playoffs, remained out. In his stead, Tyson Bagent looked worse than anyone could have imagined, 12-of-21 for 87 yards and two interceptions before being benched for Case Keenum. At most, Bears coach Ben Johnson would say that Williams is “on track” to return, but with no definitive date set. NFL reporter Ian Rappaport did suggest that there’s a chance he can play in week six against the Atlanta Falcons. Perhaps the Chicago faithful should place a call to Pope Leo to speed this thing along.

As a Rams fan still smarting from our disastrous Australian drubbing, the last thing I want to talk about is the 49ers looking like the class of the entire NFL. But San Francisco’s trip to Lumen Field to face Seattle might have been the most consequential matchup of week five. The NFC West has three legitimate Super Bowl contenders (and the Cardinals), and two of them faced off here on Sunday. Seattle and San Francisco traded punches all day, but the game came down to rare, crucial mistakes, as matchups between good teams often do.

Sam Darnold threw two pivotal interceptions, RB George Holani fumbled right before halftime, leading to a touchdown that put the 49ers up by eight. Seattle exploded for a touchdown and two field goals in the third, tilting the scales back in their direction. But a seven-yard TD pass from Brock Purdy to Brandin Cooks flipped the script yet again. A successful two-point conversion gave the Niners a three-point lead. Seattle kicker Jason Myers tied it up with a little under seven minutes to play, but the Seahawks couldn’t get a stop to force overtime. A 44-yard Eddy Pineiro field goal gave the 49ers a slim advantage. Darnold linked with WR Cooper Kupp, who just nearly converted a fourth-and 10 at the 50, which would have given Seattle one last crack at the ballgame. But a controversial spot of the ball left Kupp short and handed San Francisco their fifth win of 2026. And they did it without ace receiver Deebo Samuel, who left the game in the third quarter with a hamstring injury. Niners fans hold their breath. And I put another pin in the voodoo doll.

The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 06:00:49 GMT

The latest attack by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia may prove to be more calamitous for the region than the world imagines

On Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking and deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response.

Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge.

The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just over a year ago, when Iran fired missiles at an airbase in Qatar that hosts American troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. But even then there was a degree of warning and coordination that signalled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later in 2025, with no similar warning or choreography, Israel struck Doha, targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation – that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US.

Then came Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran, which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants – an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace.

The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks have disrupted the integration of these countries into the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securing Formula One, golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk.

The result is a fractious unravelling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shia homelands, took over the capital city, Sana’a. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe. The war deescalated in 2022 with a de facto but unformalised division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran.

But the 2026 war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory in order to gain control of the now crucial Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea. Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed government bombing its own airport in Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.

These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the west. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit. A senior Houthi official said that Saturday’s attack took place “so that the world understands” that Yemeni civilian infrastructure has been, and is being, targeted by the Saudis, gesturing towards that sense that Riyadh treats Yemeni lives as cheap.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

From another perspective, what we are witnessing in the region is another consequence of Hamas’s 7 October attacks on Israel, and what followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The final piece that was stabilising the region’s tense equilibriums fell away when Trump decided that the safety and security of the US’s Gulf allies was secondary to his Iran “excursion”, as he called it. The limits of relying on the US security umbrella became clear both to allies and enemies.

Last month, the Trump administration refused to extend military assistance to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis, after a meeting of US officials with the Houthis, who assured them that they would not attack US ships in the Red Sea, only Saudi vessels. What is upon Saudi Arabia now is a long, intractable war with a resourceful and impassioned antagonist, one willing to sustain a high degree of pain in ways that Riyadh can’t match without orienting itself entirely towards war. If the 2015 campaign is anything to go by, it will claim thousands of lives with only a remote possibility of a decisive outcome.

And so Saudi, and the entire Gulf, are pulled further into the relentless storm. Trump cannot bring the Iran war to an end, Gaza remains an open wound, Israel continues to strike and occupy parts of Lebanon. The Houthi resurgence represents a new reality in a region that is bewildered and losing lives and capital, stuck between old alliances that no longer work and new hostilities that are too calamitous to confront.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Ministers preparing to slash heat pump subsidies to fund defence spending

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:47 GMT

Exclusive: Some of £2bn savings needed from energy budget expected to come from boiler upgrade scheme, sources say

Ministers are preparing to slash the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as they look for ways to fund higher defence spending, sources have told the Guardian.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has been tasked with finding more than £2bn in savings from her budget to help pay for defence investment under a plan drawn up by the previous government.

Sources say a portion of those savings will come from cutting the boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) for England and Wales, which provides grants of up to £9,000 to help households switch to cleaner heating methods. The programme will not be abolished altogether but sources say hundreds of millions of pounds will be cut from its £2.7bn budget.

The scheme has helped tens of thousands of households install an electric heat pump in place of an old gas boiler, but Treasury officials have long considered it a subsidy used mainly by middle-class households.

Critics say cutting the scheme would damage the nascent British heat pump industry and further undermine the government’s commitment to tackling the climate crisis. Ministers are also expected to give the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield as soon as this week.

Madeleine Gabriel, a director at the charity Nesta, said: “Bills are soaring again because of high gas prices. Our reliance on gas is the reason we are in an energy crisis, so cutting funding for heat pumps makes no sense.

“It’s a kick in the teeth for the businesses and tradespeople who’ve put in time and money to build the industry.”

Greg Jackson, the chief executive of Octopus Energy, said: “The boiler upgrade scheme is doing exactly what it was meant to do. It’s kicking off an industry to drive down the costs of heat pumps – they can now cost the same to install as a gas boiler after the grant.”

He added: “Just as EVs are becoming the new normal, heat pumps are too. In the last 18 months, more than 500,000 have asked us for a quote.

“The market is taking off. Cutting the engine now would be brutally damaging. Heat pumps are undoubtedly our energy future – slashing the cost of living and insulating us against fossil fuel costs and global dictators.”

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Savings for the defence investment plan (Dip) are a small part of [the department’s] overall budget, which saw a significant uplift at spending review.

“We will set out how we will fund essential investment in our national security this autumn.”

The overall cuts were agreed to by the former energy secretary, Ed Miliband, as the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, looked for ways to fund a £15bn rise in defence spending over four years. Miliband agreed that the energy department would cut its capital budget by £2bn to help pay for the Dip.

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Energy officials say the cuts pale in comparison with the overall growth in the energy department’s capital budget, which is one of the fastest growing in Whitehall.

The chancellor, John Healey, resigned as defence secretary in June under Starmer, arguing that the defence uplift was not enough. He now has to find an additional £4.7bn in savings over a four-year period beyond what departments have already agreed.

Bloomberg reported this month that as part of the cuts to the energy department, ministers were planning to reduce spending on carbon capture and storage (CCS) and green hydrogen schemes.

The government had been planning to spend £21.7bn on CCS from now until 2050 as ministers look to make the UK a leader in the still-developing technology.

CCS supporters say it is the best way to cut carbon emissions while still protecting Britain’s North Sea oil industry.

But its critics say the technology is being promoted by fossil fuel companies who are not being honest about how much it will end up costing the country.

Asked recently about the future of the CCS programme, Martin McCluskey, an energy minister, told Politico: “I’m not betraying any confidences when I say that we are having to make some difficult decisions because of what happened as a result of the defence investment plan.”

The Guardian has learned that heat pump subsidies are one of the other significant schemes due to be raided to fund the increase in defence spending.

The scheme, which offers £7,500 as a basic grant towards an electric heat pump, has subsidised nearly 80,000 heat pumps since it began in 2022. Some properties that are off the grid can claim as much as £9,000 to upgrade.

However, given those subsidies cover only just over half the cost of the median heat pump, much of that money has gone to better-off households.

The scheme’s supporters say that more than 40% of the money has gone to households with an annual income of below £52,000.

But more important, they add, is the fact the subsidies have helped to build a fast-growing domestic heat pump industry, which is expanding by more than 25% a year.

Other countries have a far more developed industry. France sold four times the number of heat pumps the UK did last year.

However, the technology also has vocal critics. Dale Vince, the energy entrepreneur and Labour donor, published a report recently that said: “Cleaner heat does not yet mean cheaper heat.

“Electrifying heat without fixing electricity pricing risks shifting higher costs on to households rather than delivering savings.”

I will have more police officers of colour in the UK capital – and the culture wars won’t stop me doing it

The Guardian Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:46 GMT

In our major recruitment drive, the focus must be on underrepresented communities. It is not favouritism, it is fairness – and it’s essential

Mark Rowley is commissioner of the Metropolitan police

Met chief says ‘toxicity’ around DEI will not stop him recruiting more Black and Asian officers

Effective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent that stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.

Last Monday, we launched a major recruitment campaign. We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity.

London is the world’s greatest and most diverse and globally connected city. Nine million people live here. Hundreds of languages are spoken. The scale and complexity of policing London today is unlike anything Sir Robert Peel imagined when founding the Metropolitan police. Yet, in 1829, he recognised that policing success in a democracy relies on public approval, respect and cooperation as much as on “impartial service to the law”.

We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us, or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences.

An inclusive workforce is not a public relations exercise. It makes us better at protecting victims, catching criminals and preventing crime.

We cannot provide an equally good response to all victims if our understanding of some Londoners is weaker than others. That is obvious when it comes to issues such as language barriers or supporting deaf people, but it is just as important when culture, experience or background may make a victim less willing to talk about sexual abuse, domestic violence or other traumatic crimes.

When victims speak to officers and staff who understand them, and therefore feel fairly and impartially treated, we solve more crime and prevent more harm. When victims feel understood, they are more likely to come forward. When communities trust the police, they are more likely to report crime, share intelligence and support investigations. That trust underpins our effectiveness and goes to the very heart of policing by consent.

We cannot police London effectively without the trust and confidence of the communities we serve. By listening to people’s lived experiences and working in partnership with communities, we can build stronger relationships and greater legitimacy. This is particularly important when using police powers, including stop and search, where fairness, empathy and accountability are essential to maintaining public confidence and keeping London safe.

We need men and women who can carry out surveillance, work undercover and operate effectively across London. We need officers and staff who can build trust with victims of violence against women and girls, who can connect with London’s communities and who bring different experiences, perspectives and skills to complex policing challenges.

These are not ideological arguments. They are practical policing realities. And yet, despite progress, we are still not attracting talent equally. Some worry they will not fit in. Others are discouraged by family or friends. We have a responsibility to challenge those perceptions and remove those barriers. That is what our recruitment campaign is designed to do.

Last year we had the most representative intake of recruits in our history. More women joined. More Londoners from ethnic-minority backgrounds joined. That is welcome progress.

We want the talent from every corner of London to join our courageous and resilient teams and to close the gap with communities we have previously drawn least from.

Some will wrongly suggest that increasing representation means lowering standards. Nothing could be further from the truth. For generations, talented people from some communities have faced barriers that limited opportunities to join policing or build a career within it. Tackling those barriers is not favouritism. It is fairness. Our standards are unchanged and uncompromising. By reaching further into communities where we have historically been underrepresented, we are ensuring we attract the widest and strongest possible pool of talent, helping us build a Met that truly reflects and understands every corner of London.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

We want to be an inclusive organisation in which everyone has an equal chance to thrive. Fairness, not favour, should be at the heart of opportunity.

I also want to see more women and people from underrepresented backgrounds putting themselves forward for some of the most exciting roles in British policing.

That means firearms teams, the flying squad, counter-terrorism, specialist operations, public protection and major investigations.

Public debate about inclusion has become increasingly polarised in recent years. Too often there is an assumption that inclusion and impartiality or merit are competing objectives. They are not.

As commissioner I know the Met’s success, in protecting communities and helping London thrive, requires inclusivity as well as impartiality. We will not be blown off course by the culture wars. This is not an ideological choice. It is, as Peel’s founding vision for “policing by consent” described, an operational necessity.

Mark Rowley is commissioner of the Metropolitan police
