Lower East Side Parishioners Mourn Loss of ‘Spiritual Home’

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As the temporary closure of Most Holy Redeemer Church stretches on, congregants fear it will suffer the same fate as other shuttered houses of worship.

By Maya King

Since Most Holy Redeemer Catholic Church stopped holding weekly Mass over a year ago, some of its most devoted parishioners have continued to pray in front of its locked gates nearly every Sunday morning and Friday evening.

Between Hail Marys, the half a dozen faithful ask God to save both their souls and the 175-year-old church that many of them have belonged to for years and, in some cases, generations. Irene Sysak, who has attended services at the church for more than two decades and whose teenage nephew received his first communion there, called it “a second home.”

“Or really, the first home — our spiritual home,” she said.

But parishioners fear that home’s future could be dictated by economic forces reshaping neighborhoods around the city like the Lower East Side — forces that they fear could affect even institutions as enduring as the Roman Catholic church.

Most Holy Redeemer was closed last August, with little explanation from the Archdiocese of New York outside of a priest shortage and slight structural damage to its ceiling, parishioners and church leaders said. Its weekly Mass was cut to just two services each year to observe its feast day and consecration anniversary.

But in the past year, its members say the church has not opened for either of those two services, and its ceiling has not yet been fixed. Special programs like the church’s Spanish-language Mass and soup kitchen have ceased. And its doors — once open all day, every day to members and passers-by wishing to meditate and pray — have been largely closed. In fact, while the church tower’s bell still chimes every hour, the last time the church’s doors opened to the public was in January, for the funeral of a longtime member, according to several parishioners who attended the service.

Catholic churches, once a mainstay of neighborhoods like the Lower East Side, have become endangered: Many have closed to merge with other churches as part of a reorganization plan that the Archdiocese of New York put forth in 2014 to conserve resources. Others have been torn down and rebuilt as parking lots, college dormitories or, in one case, luxury condos attached to a Barnes & Noble.

This is why members and allies of Most Holy Redeemer have so feverishly fought its closure, fearful that their church home will soon become something else entirely. At the heart of their fight lie questions of identity in a changing New York neighborhood.

“If we just keep putting up all these luxury buildings, what do we have?” said Amy Sacks, who lives across the street from Most Holy Redeemer and has resided and worked in the Lower East Side for more than 20 years. “We have no integrity.”

Parishioners say they have repeatedly asked the archdiocese and parish leadership when repairs would be made so that services could restart but haven’t received satisfying answers. They have held protests, pursued local and national landmarks status and appealed to politicians. And one lawyer has filed a challenge with the Catholic church against the Archdiocese of New York, arguing the cessation of Mass violates canon law because the archdiocese has not issued a formal decree declaring the church or its parish closed.

Against the backdrop of a potential $800 million settlement between the Archdiocese of New York and victims of sexual abuse from its clergy and lay leaders, Most Holy Redeemer’s sudden closure and what parishioners view as the church leadership’s limited response stands to further damage an already strained relationship between the nation’s foremost Catholic archdiocese and its members.

“I think that the lack of an open line of communication is probably the most disturbing thing to the parishioners,” said Laura Sewell, the executive director of the East Village Community Coalition, which is helping lead the fight to reopen Most Holy Redeemer.

Joseph Zwilling, a spokesman for the archdiocese, said the church’s closure was unrelated to the archdiocese’s pending settlement. Construction on the church ceiling began last month and Mr. Zwilling said the Mass schedule will be determined after the repairs are completed. The frequency of Mass will depend on several factors, Mr. Zwilling added, including “the needs of the people, the availability of Mass elsewhere and the ability to provide priests to celebrate the Mass.”

And Mr. Zwilling disputed that the archdiocese was violating church law, saying that the status of the church itself has not changed and that it was closed only for safety reasons.

Representatives for the parish that includes Most Holy Redeemer did not respond to requests for comment.

The more than 150 parishioners who belong to Most Holy Redeemer said the church’s temporary closure has left them feeling spiritually homeless. They have now moved to smaller churches in the area, where they say space is tighter.

It has also underlined a disturbing trend in their neighborhood and many others in the city. Scores of houses of worship in Lower Manhattan have suspended regular services, closed or been demolished over the last two decades.

During an Aug. 31 rally at the church, held one year after its closure, local leaders and longtime parishioners spoke emphatically of their love for the church and its place in the community. In English and Spanish, over the roar of motorcycles and other passing traffic, they vowed to keep fighting to “save” the church as they noted how the changes in where they worship have hurt them.

“As much as people say, ‘You have your faith’ — yes, I do have my faith but I don’t have my home,” Gladys Cortez-Feliciano, who was born in the Lower East Side and is of Mexican heritage, told a crowd of more than 100 supporters at the rally. Her family once attended services at a nearby Catholic church that has now been made into a luxury building.

“I feel like I’ve been displaced,” she added.

Brody Hale, a lawyer and lifelong Catholic who has assisted dozens of churches that have closed, including Most Holy Redeemer, argued that the archdiocese benefits from parishioners’ ignorance of canon law.

“They take advantage of that lack of knowledge and use it against parishioners, to get away with things that they otherwise would have no ability to get away with,” he said of the New York Archdiocese.

In the weeks before the church closed its doors, sudden changes fueled anxiety in its congregants like the departure of its young, active priest who was moved to another parish in the Bronx. And in recent weeks, a break-in at the church has stirred tensions further.

The parishioners view Most Holy Redeemer as a symbol of the history and culture of its neighborhood. The church opened in 1851, built by German immigrants with the Redemptorist Order, which aimed to serve immigrants and the poor — some of its deceased founders remain buried in its crypt. When the church was first constructed, it was counted among the tallest towers in New York City.

“It’s certainly a touchstone,” said Andrew Berman, the executive director of Village Preservation, which is helping lead the effort to designate the church as a city landmark, thus shielding it from demolition. “It’s an element of continuity in a neighborhood that’s undergone an enormous amount of change.”

Today the church sits at the intersection of demographic shifts transforming both the Lower East Side and the Catholic church. Core members of Most Holy Redeemer skew older and have deep roots in the neighborhood; many of its most senior parishioners are Eastern European and Latino Catholics.

It is unclear whether the church will receive landmark designation, as landmarking efforts citywide have currently stalled. Mr. Berman said his coalition has been in touch with the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission, and he has reached out to Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office directly. Parishioners have rallied in front of the church and at St. Patrick’s Cathedral in Midtown.

Some members, like Phyllis Hinkson, saw those efforts as part of preserving a lifeline. Ms. Hinkson, 82, said she has attended the church since her family moved to the Lower East Side from Barbados in 1950. She, her siblings and her children were baptized, christened and received their first communions there. She worked in the church as an usher, lector and food pantry volunteer.

When the church closed, she was “at a loss.”

“Devastated. Devastated,” she said, adding, “It took a part of my life away.”

She pointed to an apartment building down the block and said she often looked out her window there to see and pray for the church. The apartment where she lives now — a rent-controlled building — has come under threat from real estate developers who have tried to buy it out, she said. To her, all of it is part of an alarming trend.

“The neighborhood has changed,” she said. “And the community has changed.”

Masha Hamilton contributed reporting.

Maya King is a Times reporter who writes about the intersection of politics, religion and ritual in New York City.

How to Buy and Eat Seafood Responsibly

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Our investigation into the farmed fish industry found human-rights violations and health concerns. Here’s what you can do.

By Ian Urbina

Ian Urbina is the founder and executive editor of The Outlaw Ocean Project.

Fish farming, known as aquaculture, was supposed to help solve overfishing by producing more seafood without taking as much from the sea. But it’s actually made the problem worse. Most farmed seafood is raised on fishmeal, a nutrient-rich powder that is made from cooking and pulverizing other wild-caught fish. Our multiyear investigation revealed that the fishmeal industry is not only exacerbating this environmental crisis but has also been linked to a host of other ills: forced labor, pollution, worker deaths and injuries, and harmful chemicals that end up in the seafood.

In light of our findings, readers may be asking themselves: Is it possible to shop for and eat seafood ethically?

Consumers who want to reduce their exposure to the harms associated with fishmeal can:

Bivalves such as mussels, oysters and clams grow by filtering nutrients from the water and require little or no manufactured feed. By contrast, farmed salmon, shrimp, sea bass and other fed species generally depend to some degree on fishmeal or fish oil.

Seafood imported year-round from far away often passes through longer, more complicated supply chains, obscuring labor abuse, illegal fishing, pollution and other hidden costs. Local does not automatically mean sustainable, but shorter supply chains are generally easier to scrutinize. In the United States, the Local Catch Network helps consumers find seafood caught and processed nearby without overseas intermediaries.

The aquarium has a Seafood Watch program to help diners compare seafood based on species, origin and production method. Its recommendations focus on environmental sustainability, however, and generally do not incorporate labor or human-rights concerns.

Consumers can only make informed choices if companies make those choices possible. Seafood companies have access to shipping records, contracts and other trade data that consumers, journalists and watchdog groups often do not, as well as the leverage to demand credible audits and greater transparency from suppliers. A growing number of nonprofit organizations are trying to shed light on the problem. SeaChoice’s Seafood Progress and Oxfam International’s Supermarket Scorecard track companies’ adherence to human-rights and environmental sourcing commitments. But retailers sometimes exclude large portions of the seafood they sell from those sourcing policies altogether.

Certification programs are supposed to provide another layer of reassurance. Best Aquaculture Practices, the Aquaculture Stewardship Council, MarinTrust and Friend of the Sea are among the most prominent programs tied to farmed seafood. But critics warn that certification can create a false sense of security. Audits may not reach far enough up the supply chain, and true surprise inspections are uncommon.

The Outlaw Ocean Project created Bait to Plate to help consumers, journalists, companies, regulators and researchers see where seafood comes from and how it moves through the supply chain. Bait to Plate tracks seafood across tens of thousands of ships, fishmeal plants, fish farms, processors and grocers, documenting cases involving forced labor, unpaid wages, crew abandonment, illegal fishing, shark finning, chemical dumping, avoidable deaths and other forms of misconduct. The Ocean Actions Index compiles proposals about steps that individuals, companies and governments could take to address the problems documented in the reporting.

Consumers alone cannot police a global industry. Companies have to make their supply chains more transparent, retailers have to demand better information from suppliers, and governments have to enforce laws against illegal fishing, forced labor and other abuses. The burden should not fall on a consumer to investigate a product that companies themselves cannot — or will not — trace.

There is no obvious silver bullet for making fish feed more sustainable. Researchers have experimented with insects, algae, microbes, soy and other alternatives to fishmeal, but each brings trade-offs involving cost, scale, nutrition, land use or food security. These substitutes may reduce reliance on wild fish, but none offers a consequence-free way to maintain the same level of production. That is one reason some researchers argue that the solution cannot be technological alone; it also requires rethinking what — and how much — we eat.

For some, responsible consumption has meant eating less seafood and meat altogether. Producing animals for food often requires catching or growing other food to feed them, adding another step between ecosystems and the dinner plate. Sustainability will require eating less animal protein, wasting less, demanding more transparency and accepting that seafood produced responsibly may sometimes cost more. Until the environmental and human costs of cheap seafood are reflected in its price, those costs will continue to be paid elsewhere.

NATO Details Plan to Shield Ukraine’s European Allies from Russia

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

With the Russians intensifying sabotage, arson and cyberattacks against European nations supporting Ukraine, NATO divulged a blueprint, in case of war, to deter the Kremlin.

By Marc Santora and Steven Erlanger

Marc Santora reported from Warsaw, Poland. Steven Erlanger reported from Berlin.

With Russia intensifying efforts to destabilize European nations that support Ukraine, NATO’s top military commander on Monday detailed a blueprint to deter Moscow in the event of outright war, a concept he summarized as “block, blunt and break.”

The commander, Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich of the U. S. Air Force, said the alliance does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable,” despite Russian sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and disinformation aimed at rattling European resolve and severing weapons supply lines to Ukraine.

But in that environment, the general said he had made a deliberate decision to publicly disclose the core of NATO’s classified war plan — known as its “theory of victory” — to bolster confidence across 32 allied countries.

“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this,” General Grynkewich said on Monday at the Warsaw Security Forum. “We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”

Yet even as the American four-star commander stressed that NATO’s ultimate defense rests on unity, stark geopolitical contradictions echoed through the conference hall. President Trump’s decision to unilaterally ease sanctions on the Kremlin in order to purchase Russian diesel fuel highlighted a jarring disconnect between NATO’s military planning and European support for Ukraine, and the White House’s transactional diplomacy and hostility toward Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump appeared to blame Ukraine — not for the first time — for the war, and said it should “get a new president.”

By injecting hard cash directly into the Kremlin’s coffers, the administration risked undercutting years of allied economic pressure, muddying the Western coalition’s deterrence messaging and testing the very solidarity General Grynkewich was in Warsaw to project.

Even if the amounts of diesel purchases are small, the symbolism of division is large. Ukraine and Europe argue that only economic and military pressure will persuade President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to end the war he started. Mr. Trump and his envoys apparently favor enticing Mr. Putin with “deals,” instead.

The tension was evident earlier in the day when Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland warned that the defense of Ukraine and the security of NATO are inextricably tied.

“Anyone who, for any reason — treason, stupidity, or money — wants to weaken Ukraine in its defense against Russian aggression is clearly acting against their own nation, the security of their own state, and its sovereignty,” Mr. Tusk said.

Pressed afterward on whether European allies could count on Washington to defend them, General Grynkewich dismissed suggestions that the United States would waver, citing the thousands of American forces along NATO’s eastern flank, including in Poland. He also pointed to recent summit communiqués that reaffirmed the bedrock collective-defense guarantee of Article 5.

European fears of an emboldened Russia have been increasing. Michal Koudelka, the director of the Czech Security Information Service, the country’s external spy service, warned his Parliament on Monday that Russia could escalate “in a matter of months rather than years to a significantly riskier and more serious operation,” which could include, down the road, limited military action against a NATO state.

General Grynkewich said the new NATO doctrine draws directly on modern battlefield lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East.

Specifically, he said, the blueprint pairs precision weapons with what he described as “affordable mass” — large numbers of autonomous systems, drones, and electronic warfare assets designed to sustain a protracted war of attrition.

The “block, blunt, and break” strategy he outlined is designed to stop an invasion in its tracks without trying to conquer the enemy’s homeland.

First, he said, allied forces immediately “block” an attack at the border to prevent enemy from seizing territory, a change in strategy since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Next, they “blunt” the offensive by hitting advancing troops from the air, sea, and land to strip their momentum. Finally, if the attack continues, they “break” the enemy by targeting the supplies, communication links, and command networks that keep their frontline forces fighting, weakening the aggressor to the point of collapse.

General Grynkewich stressed that NATO is not interested in taking an adversary’s land. By limiting the objective strictly to the tactical and operational neutralization of the adversary, NATO intends to deny the enemy any pretext for escalation, he said, placing the moral and strategic burden of expanding the war squarely on the aggressor.

“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt, should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”

Kremlin officials have routinely dismissed the alarms being raised across Europe.

“We have no intention to fight Europe, to engage in warfare with Europe; that is utter nonsense,” Sergey V. Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, said during a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly in September. “But Europe is preparing for war with us,” he said. “This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy.”

Adam Goldman contributed reporting from London.

Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

Steven Erlanger is the chief diplomatic correspondent in Europe and is based in Berlin. He has reported from over 120 countries, including Thailand, France, Israel, Germany and the former Soviet Union.

A Trump Loyalist, a Turkish Investor and a Battle for Wealth and Influence

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

A Turkish businessman once allied with the Maduro regime has tied the knot with President Trump’s former personal lawyer, Alina Habba, at the same time he is seeking to retain a big contract in Venezuela.

By Anatoly Kurmanaev and Tyler Pager

Anatoly Kurmanaev reported from Madrid, and Tyler Pager from Washington.

When President Trump’s former personal lawyer, Alina Habba, married a Turkish businessman last month, the lavish ceremony cemented their status as a MAGA power couple.

Ms. Habba, 42, a longtime Trump loyalist, and Turhan Mildon, a 29-year-old investor, hosted some of Washington’s most powerful people, including Attorney General Todd Blanche, the F. B. I. director, Kash Patel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel.

It was a striking official entry into Trumpworld for Mr. Mildon, who nearly a year ago faced the loss of his extensive business interests in Venezuela because of his ties to the inner circle of Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan leader who was captured by U. S. commandos in January.

It also put a new focus on the intermingling of personal relationships and foreign policy in the Trump era, in this case highlighting a battle for wealth and influence involving well-connected people in both Caracas and Washington seeking to use access to Mr. Trump to their benefit.

Before the United States captured Mr. Maduro, aides to Mr. Trump and some U. S. intelligence officials expressed concern about Mr. Mildon’s work with the Maduro government, according to multiple people briefed on the matter. Mr. Mildon had spent months trying to build ties between Alex Saab, one of Mr. Maduro’s closest confidants in Venezuela, and Republicans in Mr. Trump’s orbit. The Trump administration had considered placing sanctions on Mr. Mildon, two people involved in the discussions at the time said.

Once Mr. Maduro was out of the picture, things for Mr. Mildon got even worse.

Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, ordered an audit of the state-owned cement plants that Mr. Mildon was operating. In June, she issued an order revoking his contract altogether, citing a failure to meet investment targets, according to a copy of the document seen by The New York Times.

At that point, his patrons could no longer protect him. Mr. Maduro was not only out of power, but sitting in an American jail. Mr. Saab, Mr. Mildon’s most powerful ally in Venezuela, was arrested and extradited to the United States.

But there was a bright spot: Mr. Mildon had met Ms. Habba, one of Mr. Trump’s most prominent legal defenders. They started dating this year, soon after Mr. Maduro’s downfall. By this past summer, the couple’s burgeoning romance had begun to draw attention. Specifically, it caught the eye of Ms. Rodríguez, according to two people close to her. Mr. Mildon was in a serious relationship with a woman who had high-level access to Mr. Trump — the one person keeping Ms. Rodríguez in power.

Since taking office, Ms. Rodríguez has been trying to balance the interests of the competing MAGA factions, and gauging their relative influence over Mr. Trump. After learning of Mr. Mildon’s powerful allies, she decided to pause her order terminating his cement contracts, allowing him to continue to profit from them, according to people familiar with her thinking.

A spokesman for Mr. Mildon said the government had never carried out the audit and that his company was only notified of the contract’s termination on Oct. 8, the day The Times began inquiring about the status of his operation in Venezuela.

The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said his client believed the letter was a mistake and that he was working to address the issue. The spokesman also took issue with the suggestion that the United States had considered sanctioning Mr. Mildon, calling it a “totally false and malicious rumor.”

An administration official also disputed whether the government had considered sanctions against Mr. Mildon.

The Venezuelan government did not respond to a request for comment.

White House officials say that Ms. Habba, who now goes by Mrs. Mildon, has not discussed her husband’s business dealings with Mr. Trump or any other White House officials.

“I have never, under any circumstances got involved with this White House or administration on behalf of my husband, nor would he ever ask me to,” she said in a statement.

The U. S. sanctions proceedings against Mr. Mildon were shelved after the regime change in Caracas, overtaken by bigger targets inside the government, according to a person familiar with the matter.

In the meantime, Mr. Mildon’s relationship with Ms. Habba grew closer. In September, they were married, in a ballroom in New York’s Waldorf Astoria hotel.

This article is based on interviews with more than two dozen people with knowledge of the events, most of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the details of the relationship and Mr. Mildon’s business interests.

Mr. Mildon explained his business strategy in an interview published earlier this month with Forbes Turkey. “In my grandfather’s time, know-how, (knowledge) was very important,” Mr. Mildon told the magazine. “Now, know-who (who you know) is important.”

Mr. Mildon grew up in a provincial Turkish town near the strait of the Dardanelles, where his family ran a network of local businesses, including auto-repair shops and gas stations.

His big break coincided with his first marriage, in 2021, to a daughter of a construction magnate close to Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Shortly after the wedding, Mr. Mildon met the president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Félix Tshisekedi, at an event in Istanbul and jumped on an airplane to explore investment opportunities in the country, Mr. Mildon’s spokesman said. He quickly built close ties with the Congolese political elites and won contracts for prominent construction projects.

Mr. Mildon became an adviser to Mr. Tshisekedi in 2023 and obtained a Congolese diplomatic passport. People who have met him in Washington and Caracas said he had on multiple occasions introduced himself as a Congolese official.

Mr. Mildon’s spokesman denied that his client had ever introduced himself as a Congolese official. Congo’s foreign ministry declined to comment.

In late 2023, Mr. Mildon, who portrays himself as a billionaire, flew into the Venezuelan capital at the invitation of a Venezuelan friend.

As he had in Congo, Mr. Mildon quickly made powerful friends. He won the support of the local Turkish ambassador and met the daughter of a powerful admiral.

His most critical relationship was with Mr. Saab, the Maduro confidant who had recently returned to Caracas from an American jail and been appointed as industry minister.

The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said his client had had only professional, and occasional, interactions with Mr. Saab, who was the official responsible for dealing with foreign investors. Numerous people close to the Venezuelan government, however, said the two became personally close.

In March 2025, Mr. Saab gave Mr. Mildon a contract to operate the cement plants.

A few months later, the Venezuelan government awarded Mr. Mildon a shrimp production and export business in western Venezuela. The government had seized the business months earlier from its private founder, José Enrique Rincón, after accusing him of financing the political opposition. Mr. Rincón remains in jail.

The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said Mr. Saab had played no role in the shrimp business award and that Mr. Mildon had participated in a bidding process with four others to obtain the cement business. The spokesman said he did not know who the other bidders were.

Mr. Mildon’s account is disputed by numerous prominent Venezuelan businessmen and people close to the government, who said that Mr. Saab and other Venezuelan ministers handed out state-run assets to private investors without competitive bidding.

As his fortunes rose, Mr. Mildon’s first marriage crumbled.

In June 2025, he became engaged to María Eugenia Ceballos, a Venezuelan admiral’s daughter, Mr. Mildon’s spokesman said. Her father, Adm. Remigio Ceballos, served for years as the operational head of Venezuelan military and is under U. S. sanctions for participating in corruption and human rights abuses.

The Trump administration at the time was escalating economic and military pressure on Mr. Maduro, and Mr. Mildon became increasingly involved in back-channel diplomacy between Washington and Caracas. His efforts put him in a group of multinational businessmen who had sought preferential treatment by ferrying messages between the capitals last year. These intermediaries have included a Brazilian beef billionaire, an American asphalt tycoon and a Venezuelan oil magnate.

Mr. Mildon also began attending social events organized by Republican insiders.

He became a frequent guest at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, where he networked with the man in charge of the institution at the time, Richard Grenell. Mr. Grenell was also working as Mr. Trump’s special envoy to Venezuela, and trying to broker Mr. Maduro’s exit from power.

Mr. Grenell introduced Mr. Mildon to some of the MAGA crowd. Mr. Mildon’s spokesman said his client and Ms. Habba had first met at an event at the Kennedy Center in late 2025, and started dating in early 2026.

Ms. Habba’s ties to Mr. Trump go back years. She met Mr. Trump through his golf club in Bedminster, N. J., and joined his legal team after his first term, representing him in two civil trials. She joined the White House at the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, then served briefly as New Jersey’s interim U. S. attorney.

She has maintained a close relationship with the president to this day, and met with him in the Oval Office last week.

Even as he was meeting Ms. Habba, Mr. Mildon was navigating the shifting political landscape in Venezuela after Ms. Rodríguez had been put in power by the Americans. His spokesman said Mr. Mildon had always supported Ms. Rodríguez, who served as Mr. Maduro’s vice president until his arrest.

But several people who met Mr. Mildon in Washington last year, before Mr. Maduro’s capture by U. S. forces, said Mr. Mildon had praised Mr. Saab, her ruling party rival, presenting him as Venezuela’s pre-eminent power broker and the key to a peaceful resolution of the conflict with the United States.

As it turns out, Mr. Mildon had backed the wrong side.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio sidelined Mr. Grenell and persuaded Mr. Trump to adopt a more aggressive stance toward Mr. Maduro. Mr. Rubio settled on Ms. Rodríguez as Mr. Maduro’s successor, and set in motion plans for a military operation that would topple the Venezuelan president and install her in power.

Mr. Maduro dismissed the growing threats from the White House as a bluff, right until U. S. military aircraft attacked Caracas in the early hours of Jan. 3.

The arrest of Mr. Maduro, and then Mr. Saab, threatened Mr. Mildon’s businesses in Venezuela. The new government accused him of failing to raise output and lower prices. Contractors complained of unpaid invoices.

Mr. Mildon tried to build ties to Ms. Rodríguez. When Christopher Ruddy, the chief executive of Newsmax, a pro-Trump news channel, secured a meeting with her in February, Mr. Mildon tagged along. The spokesman for Mr. Mildon said he has spoken with Ms. Rodríguez several times since.

Mr. Mildon told Forbes Turkey that he produces 4.5 million tons of cement a year in Venezuela. Data seen by The Times shows that Venezuela’s entire annual cement output is about a third of that figure.

He visited one of the cement plants in June, promising to bring new investment and raise output. He wore a red shirt of the type that was ubiquitous among ruling party apparatchiks, but had largely been abandoned since Mr. Maduro was captured. He gave two thumbs-up, Trump style.

Mr. Mildon also claimed in the Forbes Turkey interview that his shrimp business employed 20,000 people and would reach revenues of $500 million in two years. Data seen by The Times, however, shows that in the first eight months of the year the plants sold on average just 5 percent of the shrimp, in terms of volume, that they had been shipping before the government takeover.

After the The Times presented Mr. Mildon with the data, his spokesman said Mr. Mildon had been misquoted in the Forbes Turkey article.

As Venezuela evolved, so did Mr. Mildon’s fortunes.

Mr. Maduro was gone. Mr. Mildon’s powerful political backers were fired or sidelined.

His relationship with Ms. Ceballos, the daughter of Mr. Maduro’s longtime military official, also ended. (Adm. Ceballos did not respond to a request for comment. Ms. Ceballos could not be reached.)

But Mr. Mildon’s marriage ceremony to Ms. Habba, which the wedding planners boasted had come together in under 60 days, was a high-profile social event, attracting dignitaries, oligarchs and senior politicians from around the world, who were in New York for the annual meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. Nelly, the Grammy Award-winning rapper, performed.

And Mr. Mildon’s cement businesses are still operating, his spokesman says.

He is working to stave off Ms. Rodríguez’s revocation of his contract. It is a development that he apparently did not expect.

“When no one else had the guts to come, one man did and invested millions,” he said in the Forbes Turkey interview, referring to himself and his business in Venezuela. “They’re not the sort of people who would turn their backs, now that things are better, on a man who trusted them and came here in good faith.”

Reporting was contributed by Justin Makangara from Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Julian E. Barnes and Glenn Thrush from Washington and Benjamin Weiser from New York. Sheelagh McNeill and Safak Timur contributed research.

Anatoly Kurmanaev covers Venezuela for The Times.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Homeland Security Agents Search Home of Rep. Ilhan Omar

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The search takes place within the 60-day window of the midterm elections, when the Justice Department has historically avoided such investigative steps related to political candidates.

By Devlin BarrettHamed AleazizErnesto Londoño and Alan Feuer

Federal agents executed a search warrant at the home of Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Monday, according to three people briefed on the matter, the kind of investigative step the Justice Department has long shied away from so close to an election.

The court-approved search of her Washington-area home comes after Department of Homeland Security officials said in recent months that they were investigating Ms. Omar, a Democrat, over her family’s immigration paperwork. More recently, some federal investigators have also sought to investigate other issues, such as Ms. Omar’s finances, campaign funds and interactions with a foreign citizen, as The New York Times previously reported.

The three people who described the execution of the search warrant spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss it.

The search warrant, executed 22 days before Election Day, lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge, according to a person familiar with the document.

In a statement posted on social media on Monday, Ms. Omar called the raid “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she wrote, adding: “I will not be silenced.”

President Trump has frequently attacked Ms. Omar, focusing on her Somali heritage. At a political rally on Saturday in Tennessee, he said: “She comes from Somalia, they don’t have a government, they don’t have police. All they have is crime and squalor.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

He added: “These people from Somalia, what they’ve done to Minnesota, should never be allowed and let’s see what happens.”

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that Homeland Security Investigations agents — a part of ICE — executed a judicially authorized search of a home in the Washington area, as part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The spokeswoman declined to comment further.

In September, Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, said his department was investigating issues surrounding Ms. Omar and her family’s immigration to the United States, and suggested the end result could be deportation.

Ms. Omar was born in Mogadishu in the early 1980s. Her family fled their hometown when she was around 8, as a civil war engulfed Somalia, according to a memoir she wrote. In the mid-1990s, after spending time at a refugee camp in Kenya, Ms. Omar and her relatives were admitted as refugees in the United States. They started a new life in Minnesota, which is home to the largest Somali diaspora in the United States.

Ms. Omar has long said that suggestions that she and her family committed immigration fraud were false and politically motivated.

“I will say it again so it’s as clear as possible: I’m not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams,” she wrote in a fund-raising email in September.

Monday’s search of her home, which was reported earlier by Fox News, takes place within the 60-day window before an election. Justice Department policy has long urged prosecutors not to take any overt, unnecessary investigative steps that could affect an election during that period — especially if such actions could be taken after the election without causing any harm to the investigation. The guiding principle of the 60-day rule is that prosecutors should exercise caution in regard to politically sensitive cases.

The rule is not absolute, and there are exceptions, such as instances where prosecutors believe evidence could be destroyed, ongoing crimes are being committed, or people are in danger. The rule is also largely an interpretation of Justice Department regulations, and as such has been the subject of significant debate about its exact parameters. For many years, however, Justice Department officials have concluded that a publicly observable search — such as of a politician’s home or business — is the kind of overt activity that should be avoided during the 60-day period.

In the last federal election, Mr. Trump cited the 60-day rule in his own criminal cases to accuse the department of acting improperly in 2024 as he campaigned for election. He and his lawyers, some of whom now run the Justice Department, argued that the special counsel, Jack Smith, broke the 60-day rule when he filed court papers in September 2024 describing the evidence supporting charges that Mr. Trump had conspired to obstruct the results of the 2020 election. In that instance, however, the key filing was made in response to a court order, which is not subject to the department policy.

In a statement on Monday, the House Democratic leadership — Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Pete Aguilar of California — condemned the search of Ms. Omar’s house as a “rogue abuse of power.”

“The Trump administration’s raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries,” they said.

Ms. Omar has represented a solidly blue district that includes Minneapolis since 2019, and she faced no serious competitors during the primary this year.

Her immigration history has been scrutinized since she first ran for a seat in the State Legislature in 2016 and made history as the state’s first Somali American lawmaker, according to people familiar with the inquiries.

The Justice Department under the Biden administration also opened an investigation into Ms. Omar in 2024 that examined her finances, campaign spending and interactions with a foreign citizen, as The Times previously reported.

Previous federal inquiries — including one seeking to establish whether Ms. Omar married a sibling to get him a green card — ended without any charges. Ms. Omar has called such claims “absurd and offensive.”

Late last year, Tom Homan, the White House border czar told Newsmax that earlier efforts to investigate Ms. Omar’s immigration matters were stymied by statute of limitations.

Investigators were reviewing her immigration files again, Mr. Homan said, adding that he had no doubt Ms. Omar had committed fraud.

In March, Vice President JD Vance reiterated that claim, which he said he had discussed with the White House senior aide Stephen Miller.

“We’re trying to look at what the remedies are,” Mr. Vance told a conservative podcaster. “That’s the thing that we’re trying to figure out is, what are the legal remedies now that we know that she has committed immigration fraud, how do you go after her, how do you investigate her … how do you build a case necessary to get some justice for the American people?”

In recent months, federal investigators opened an investigation into Ms. Omar’s immigration history, focusing in part on whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied or omitted information as he sought legal status in the United States before becoming a U. S. citizen.

Among the questions investigators have looked at is whether Ms. Omar derived citizenship from a father who may have been ineligible to obtain naturalized status, according to a person familiar with the case.

If there is conclusive evidence that Ms. Omar derived citizenship improperly, the Justice Department could pursue a criminal or civil denaturalization case against her. In cases in which prosecutors prevail and persuade a federal judge to order someone denaturalized, the immigrant may be placed in deportation proceedings.

Annie Karni contributed reporting.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Ernesto Londoño is a Times reporter based in Minnesota, covering news in the Midwest and drug use and counternarcotics policy. He welcomes tips and can be reached at elondono.81 on Signal.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Judge Orders Trump Administration to Answer for Tree Removals at D. C. Golf Course

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

During a four-hour hearing, a federal judge demanded answers from the Trump administration about who authorized the removal of hundreds of trees at the East Potomac Golf Links.

By Zach Montague

Reporting from Washington

A federal judge on Monday excoriated the Trump administration for ripping up hundreds of mature trees at a Washington golf course over the holiday weekend, even though she had directed officials to disclose any major changes before work was started.

In an explosive, four-hour emergency hearing, Judge Ana C. Reyes of the Federal District Court in Washington ordered a one-day halt to any more tree removal at East Potomac Golf Links, and said she would continue proceedings on Tuesday.

But first she directed Justice Department lawyers to track down a succession of progressively more senior officials involved in the decision, and ordered them to testify on the spot, as she demanded answers about who had authorized the trees to be cleared and whether the decision was linked to the White House. President Trump has eyed the municipal course in southeastern Washington for redevelopment into a luxury championship course similar to those on his personal properties.

“I am thoroughly unamused right now,” Judge Reyes said, appearing remotely from Istanbul, where she had been traveling. She raised her voice at several points to near shouting level.

“What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case,” she said, before listing all of the times she had directed the government to alert her to major alterations.

The Monday morning hearing was technically to address the tree removal, but Judge Reyes made clear that her larger concern was the possibility that the Trump administration had flouted her instructions. Since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, judges have repeatedly been forced to interrogate whether the government has complied with orders across a variety of cases.

Two Washington residents and a preservationist organization had sued in February over the president’s stated goal to redevelop the affordable municipal course into a championship-level one. In June, Mr. Trump was photographed touring the grounds and studying blueprints with Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Tom Fazio, a well-known architect who has designed other courses owned by the Trump Organization.

At a hearing in July, Judge Reyes, a Biden appointee, ordered the Trump administration to notify the court before making sudden alterations to the course. She said that she was worried about how quickly plans were taking shape, and that she did not want to find out work had begun too late to “stop the trains.”

On Friday evening, the Justice Department filed documents showing the administration intended to remove 529 trees as part of a larger restoration. By Saturday morning, machinery could be seen cutting down trees. The government acknowledged on Monday that more than 400 were removed in one fell swoop over the weekend.

In a filing on Sunday night, lawyers representing the D. C. Preservation League asked Judge Reyes to block further action, noting that the government had indicated that there were still “hundreds more” trees to be cut, prompting her to call for the emergency hearing.

She fumed at the hearing that she had given the Trump administration “the benefit of the doubt” at every turn to disclose its plans for the course, only to learn while traveling that the government had moved ahead.

When Marissa Piropato, a Justice Department lawyer, could not explain why the government had waited until Friday night to alert the court to action planned for the following day, Judge Reyes reacted furiously.

“Ignorance is not an excuse here,” she said.

She told Ms. Piropato at another point that “what I find most frustrating about this, counsel, is that this is all double speak.”

Judge Reyes said she needed to figure out the chain of events that led to the tree removal, to figure out “whether or not I’ve been lied to.”

One official, Kevin Griess, a National Park Service official overseeing public lands in Washington, testified that plans for the tree removal were finalized on Oct. 5, and that he received the go-ahead to proceed over the weekend from Frank Lands, a deputy director at the National Park Service.

At that point, Judge Reyes ordered that Mr. Lands be located to testify. Appearing remotely from his car in a parking lot, Mr. Lands explained that he formalized plans to renovate the course with Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee at the Interior Department. Mr. Lands said that he and Mr. Wischer had also discussed Mr. Trump’s ideas to remake the site into a premier competition course.

Judge Reyes then ordered Mr. Wischer, a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, to appear, but Ms. Piropato said the department was unable to reach him. At that point, Judge Reyes concluded the hearing for the day, ordering that Mr. Wischer be prepared to testify as early as Tuesday morning.

“We’re going to get him in here tomorrow,” she said.

In the meantime, Judge Reyes blocked the government from removing more trees until 2:00 p. m. on Tuesday, and she said she would consider whether to block to the government from doing any work at the course for two weeks. She added that she would “try and take this step by step.”

She ordered Mr. Griess, Mr. Lands and their staff members to preserve records about the decision, and warned of repercussions if the government did more work at the course on Monday, given her orders to stop.

“I promise you, if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings,” she said.

Judge Reyes said she felt betrayed by the Justice Department after she had repeatedly declined to formally block the Trump administration from conducting work at the site, despite repeated requests from the group that had sued.

“I wanted you all to be better than you have been,” she told Ms. Piropato.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

After Russian Diesel Deal, Trump Faces New Crisis Over Ukraine

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump’s surprise decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel fuel stunned Ukrainian and European officials, who were meeting with U. S. envoys at an exclusive golf club near Miami.

By Anton TroianovskiJeanna SmialekAndrew E. Kramer and Steven Erlanger

President Trump’s new diplomatic crisis over Ukraine first erupted at Steve Witkoff’s exclusive golf club outside Miami on Friday.

Senior Ukrainian and European officials had traveled to the club, Shell Bay, for talks with Mr. Trump’s peace envoys, Mr. Witkoff and Jared Kushner. They had planned to discuss updated proposals to end the war in Ukraine ahead of another trip to Russia by Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner.

But Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner soon made an announcement that stunned the visitors and much of the world when the news became public shortly thereafter. The United States, the Americans said, would suspend sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. The Americans added a firm request from Mr. Trump: that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries.

One of the Ukrainians asked what they would get in return.

The Americans responded that the United States was doing a lot for Ukraine already, according to three people familiar with the meeting, and should not have to make a trade for Ukraine to stop its refinery attacks. The Americans then mentioned U. S. intelligence assistance, considered vital to the Ukrainian war effort.

Some in the room heard that as a veiled threat, according to two of the people. A U. S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy, denied any suggestion of a threat to withhold such support. But the official also said that Mr. Trump had grown so angry with Ukraine that it was hard to say what he might do.

Now, the dispute has ballooned into the biggest crisis between Washington and Kyiv since the Oval Office blowup with Ukraine’s president last year. The future of U. S. support for Ukraine again appears to be hanging in the balance. The escalating back-and-forth showed how Mr. Trump’s efforts to bring down energy prices before next month’s midterm elections have threatened to destabilize the fragile Ukraine talks.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are now indicating that they have put their expected trip to Russia on hold until President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine mends fences with Mr. Trump, two people familiar with the talks said.

To the Ukrainians and their European supporters, the attacks on Russia’s fuel refineries are Kyiv’s most effective way to respond to Russia’s bombardment of Ukraine’s energy grid. Ukraine is prepared to stop attacking energy infrastructure, Mr. Zelensky has said, if Russia does the same.

Russia has refused such a deal. Nevertheless, to Mr. Trump, Ukraine’s attacks are an affront to a U. S. administration that has continued to provide intelligence and some military support to Ukraine despite the American president’s harsh words about Mr. Zelensky. Diesel prices in particular have become a sore spot for Mr. Trump, causing farmers’ costs to spike just as harvest season arrives and the midterms are weeks away.

“He better damn well stop,” Mr. Trump told reporters on Saturday, referring to Mr. Zelensky and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, and ignoring Russia’s strikes on the Ukrainian energy grid. “He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers.”

Export statistics indicate that the increase in diesel and energy prices stems largely from Mr. Trump’s war with Iran, though Ukraine’s attacks on Russia have also played a role.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump said on social media that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” with immediate effect. Neither side confirmed an agreement. A person familiar with his thinking said that Mr. Trump was referring to a cease-fire only on refineries in both countries — even though Ukraine’s refining capacity had been all but destroyed early in the war.

On Monday, European and Ukrainian leaders suggested that while they would be open to an energy cease-fire, they were skeptical that Russia would follow through on one. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, noted that Russia had attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure Sunday night “just hours after” the announcement.

“We are ready for an energy cease-fire: We are ready for any mutual format, anything that is not one-sided,” Mr. Sybiha told reporters while entering a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Luxembourg.

The meeting on Friday at Mr. Witkoff’s golf club lasted about six hours, two people familiar with it said. Much of the meeting involved brainstorming about what the future peace talks might require to work, and the focus was on the standard issues, according to several people. The issues included accession to the European Union for Ukraine, for instance, and the question of territorial control.

Mr. Witkoff stepped out at one point to join a call between Russia’s president, Vladimir V. Putin, and Mr. Trump, according to one of the people, who was in the room for the meeting. In addition to Ukraine’s three-person negotiating team, the national security advisers to the leaders of Britain, Germany and France, as well as top officials from the European Union and NATO, joined the meeting.

But Mr. Trump’s diesel deal with Mr. Putin quickly overshadowed the rest of the talks. Mr. Zelensky on Friday called Mr. Trump’s deal with Mr. Putin to allow imports of Russian diesel fuel in order to lower prices a “weak decision.” As the dispute intensified, Mr. Trump on Saturday said Ukraine needed “a new president.”

European leaders, including France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the head of the E. U.’s executive arm, Ursula von der Leyen, issued statements of support for Mr. Zelensky. Members of Congress criticized the diesel deal as helping fund Russia’s war machine.

“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” a bipartisan group of six senators, including the Republicans Susan Collins of Maine and John Curtis of Utah, said in a statement on Sunday. “The administration must immediately reverse course.”

Björn Seibert, a senior E. U. official who attended Friday’s meeting in Florida, gave ambassadors from across the European Union’s 27 nations a briefing on the meeting on Sunday, according to one European official who was there and three diplomats briefed on the matter.

Both the official and two of the diplomats said that the Europeans in Florida were taken by surprise by the Trump administration’s diesel announcement. The official said the ambassadors were stunned by the announcement.

One major takeaway from Florida, Mr. Seibert told ambassadors, was that the Americans were engaging more with the Russians than they publicly acknowledge, the official and one of the diplomats said. No further details on those engagements were given during Mr. Seibert’s briefing, which lasted about 20 minutes, according to the official.

The Trump administration has argued that energy deals with Mr. Putin, in addition to lowering energy prices, could help pave the way for a settlement in Ukraine by showing the Kremlin that reintegration into the world economy was possible for Russia if it compromised in the war.

Marc Santora contributed reporting.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

Andrew E. Kramer is the Kyiv bureau chief for The Times, who has been covering the war in Ukraine since 2014.

Steven Erlanger is the chief diplomatic correspondent in Europe and is based in Berlin. He has reported from over 120 countries, including Thailand, France, Israel, Germany and the former Soviet Union.

What a Year of Free Money Meant: Softer Diapers, Clean Laundry, a Visit to Six Flags

Artificial Intelligence

For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of universal basic income programs, which Elon Musk and other tech leaders have promoted as a solution to A. I.-fueled job losses.

For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of universal basic income programs, which Elon Musk and other tech leaders have promoted as a solution to A. I.-fueled job losses.

Credit...

By Eli Tan and Rachel Bujalski

Photographs by Rachel Bujalski

Eli Tan and Rachel Bujalski followed families on guaranteed income programs around the San Francisco Bay Area.

One morning in December 2024, Mikole Weeks, then 35, received a phone call with surprising news. She had been chosen for an experimental program called guaranteed basic income, and it came with cash: $1,330 a month for an entire year, with no strings attached for how it could be spent.

“It felt like another chance to turn my life around,” said Ms. Weeks, a single mother and a part-time house cleaner in Santa Cruz, Calif.

Only it did not turn out to be quite that simple.

For decades, people have debated the merits of guaranteed income programs, also called universal basic income, as an alternative or complement to traditional welfare. Driving the efforts is the idea that the most effective way to improve people’s lives is to give them cash and let them spend it how they want.

The concept resurged in popularity a decade ago, driven by fears of automation and rising wealth inequality. Proponents argued that permanent payments would raise the standard of living for those on the margins, and ultimately lift millions off welfare. Critics contended that giving people money unconditionally would deter them from working in the first place.

In the age of artificial intelligence, these programs have again become a hot topic. Tech titans including Elon Musk, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic have hailed basic income as a solution to A. I.-fueled job losses. In April, Mr. Musk posted that “universal HIGH INCOME” was the best way to deal with unemployment caused by the powerful technology. In June, Dr. Amodei suggested a tax on A. I. companies as one way to fund these payments.

Across Silicon Valley, experimental guaranteed income programs have quietly taken off. Google began funding six different initiatives in 2022 as part of a $50 million donation to nonprofits in the San Francisco Bay Area, saying basic income could be a novel way to prevent homelessness in one of the nation’s most expensive locations. Each program has hundreds of participants who receive around $1,000 a month, and academics study the results. State and federal tax laws limit the lengths of the programs and the payment amounts.

The studies have found that most basic income programs improve short-term employment and mental health while reducing food insecurity. But while data from these efforts has been closely tracked, less is known about the individual journeys of participants.

In October 2024, after The New York Times contacted two social services providers that received Google’s funding, the organizations offered reporters the chance to follow basic income recipients in real time. The Times ultimately shadowed three people, including Ms. Weeks, to better understand their guaranteed income experiences, from their first payments through last month. All of the program participants, including the ones The Times followed, were previously homeless and transitioning off a housing stipend that paid for a portion of their rent, and many received the payments on top of other social assistance like food stamps.

The Times’s findings mirrored the academic studies. For all three recipients, the instant benefits of basic income were clear: They had breathing room for groceries, rent and other expenses. But the success of the payments in another area — giving people more free time and opportunity in the long term — was mixed.

“It’s a lot to ask of someone to get their life together in 12 months, when a lot of these issues are structural or systemic,” said Jennifer Loving, who runs Destination: Home, a nonprofit that administers basic income programs in Silicon Valley. “And the world around them isn’t getting cheaper.”

Ms. Weeks was homeless in 2023, living in a tent with her boyfriend at the time while struggling with drug addiction. “I was waiting for something to save me or kill me,” she said.

Then it came — she became pregnant with her son, Sky.

Ms. Weeks saw the pregnancy as a sign to turn her life around, and she did. She got sober and secured a $2,100 monthly housing stipend through Abode, a social services provider, for an apartment in Santa Cruz, a beach town about 40 miles south of Google’s Silicon Valley headquarters. She started working part time as a house cleaner for $20 an hour.

In December 2024, when Abode told her that she had been chosen for the basic income program, Ms. Weeks almost broke into tears.

The first trip she made after receiving the initial payment was to Target, where she filled her cart with organic banana baby snacks ($2.69) for Sky, then 14 months old, and a push bike ($61.99) to take him around the neighborhood. She loaded up on diapers that were softer for his sensitive skin than the ones she normally got for free at a food bank.

Then she called her mother, Christine Schell, now 60, who lived with Ms. Weeks’s now-23-year-old sister, Joanna McCall, in Elizabethton, Tenn. “Mom, do you want to see your grandbaby?” she asked.

Ms. Schell and Ms. McCall, who were living on social assistance, had never been able to afford the cross-country flights. A month later, Ms. Weeks received a call from her mother and sister: Her grandfather had died, and his house, where they lived, was being foreclosed on. What if they moved to Santa Cruz?

With the guaranteed income payments and more babysitting for Sky, Ms. Weeks said, she thought she could make the arrangement work.

Ms. Schell sold her belongings and drove from Tennessee to California with Ms. McCall. “It was chaotic, the emotions of leaving and also starting something new,” she said. “But we knew we’d be together.”

By April 2025, they were all living together in Ms. Weeks’s two-bedroom apartment. She slept on an air mattress in Sky’s bedroom, while her mother slept in Ms. Weeks’s bedroom and her sister on the couch in the living room.

As Ms. Schell cooked dinner one night, Ms. Weeks wrote a list of things she wanted to accomplish in the next 10 months with the help of the money. At the top was going to community college to study communications, a degree that could help her become a social worker.

“It feels like I’ve been given a head start,” Ms. Weeks said to her mother. Her ultimate goal was to be financially independent so she could give Sky opportunities that she never had.

She used some of the basic income money to pay for swimming lessons and music classes for Sky; on the weekends, they visited museums or a nearby aquarium. What she felt most was relief, she said, no longer having to wait until her food stamps reloaded every month to go to the grocery store. She could also afford to treat herself occasionally, getting her hair and nails done without worrying about paying for the electricity bill.

Seeing Ms. Weeks go to college also inspired her younger sister, Ms. McCall, who decided to enroll alongside her.

“It made me want to pursue our dreams together,” Ms. McCall said.

In a recent study of 3,000 universal basic income participants by OpenResearch, an organization partly funded by Mr. Altman of OpenAI, money spent supporting friends and family increased 26 percent, the most of any category. That was more than the increases for food (6 percent) and child care (11 percent).

But as the program went on, supporting two extra relatives — who had some social assistance but were also living on Ms. Weeks’s payments — weighed heavily on her. Ms. Weeks’s parenting style often clashed with her mother’s, leading to fights about how to raise Sky. Balancing college classes with a part-time job and parenting was harder than she expected.

By September 2025, “it had become a lot of change happening at once,” Ms. Weeks said. She moved her bed into the living room for more space and found herself saving less of the money than she had planned.

With one month to go until the payments ended, Ms. Weeks briefly relapsed into drugs. In November, sitting on her bed next to Sky’s giraffe stuffed animal, she told her mother that she needed to drop out of community college to focus on her health.

“I’m doing all I can do,” she said, burying her head in her mother’s chest.

“Mothers aren’t perfect by any means,” Ms. Schell said. “You’re doing your best.”

The payments ended in December. Ms. Weeks managed to save $2,000 from the program and continued to houseclean. Five months later, Ms. McCall moved into her own apartment, and Ms. Weeks, Ms. Schell and Sky used their savings to move into a house twice as big as their old place in cheaper, nearby Watsonville, with a yard for Sky to run around.

Ms. Weeks began feeling more settled. In August, she got a job at a hotel restaurant in Santa Cruz, working 32 hours a week making $24 an hour plus tips, health care benefits for herself and Sky and membership in a union.

She also re-enrolled in community college, taking one course at a time online instead of in person. Her first class began last month.

Nicholas Marquez, 44, could barely walk up the stairs to his Santa Cruz apartment one morning in mid-December 2024, his body still exhausted from open-heart surgery a week earlier. His power was shut off because of an unpaid electric bill, and his refrigerator was empty until more food stamps would arrive on Jan. 1.

Then he got the news from Abode that he had been selected for the guaranteed income program. “It felt like I had won the lottery,” he said.

He immediately called his mother, Denise Wiscowiche, now 66, a caretaker in Santa Cruz who had become his caretaker, too. “Mom, I have good news,” he told her. “I’m going to need your help.”

The $1,330 a month from the program immediately went to basics, like paying off his $500 utility bill to get the power back on. Mr. Marquez and Ms. Wiscowiche also went to the grocery store to buy high-calorie protein shakes, the only thing he could eat after his dialysis appointments on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

His heart and kidneys had been declining for years, he said, “punished by a lifetime of bad decisions” and a drug addiction. Unable to work, he was living on social assistance of around $800 a month on top of a housing stipend.

At the end of each month, Mr. Marquez had to choose whether to pay for electricity, for laundry or for groceries. With the basic income payments, he could do all three. It was the first time he could pay to do laundry in six months.

“There are a lot of little things that you don’t realize you need until you can’t afford them,” he said.

When his second payment hit in February 2025, Mr. Marquez brainstormed things he wanted to buy next. A new television and a PlayStation 4, to entertain him on days spent on the couch after dialysis; curtains for the living room; a blender to make smoothies.

Ms. Wiscowiche wrote reminders about each item on paper plates taped up around the apartment, covering his refrigerator and calendar with smiley faces and delivery dates. What the payments gave Mr. Marquez most of all was a sense of independence, he said. He could afford to take a friend out for a meal on occasion. He did not have to ration toilet paper.

But the extra money could not reverse the damage to his heart and kidneys. In March 2025, Mr. Marquez’s health took a turn for the worse, and his mother moved into his apartment to care for him.

At the end of that month, she stood by his bedside, crouching against a wall filled with skateboards and fishing rods from his childhood and posters of his favorite heavy metal bands.

“Mom, if I can’t do this anymore, you have to let me go,” he told her.

“I’ll never let you go, Nick,” she said.

A few weeks later, after returning home from the grocery store, Ms. Wiscowiche found Mr. Marquez unconscious on the floor. He had gone into cardiac arrest and died later that day.

Ms. Wiscowiche moved out of the apartment that month. Her other son, Benjamin Marquez, was struggling with a fentanyl addiction somewhere on the streets of Northern California. She could not imagine losing both sons.

She eventually tracked Benjamin down. “He told me to come save him,” Ms. Wiscowiche said.

Mr. Marquez had saved $900 of the payments for an e-bike to ride along the ocean. In May 2025, Ms. Wiscowiche used the sum and the rest of her savings to put Benjamin into a $15,000 drug rehabilitation program. With no money left, she moved into a tent in her stepmother’s backyard in Greenfield, Calif., a rural town about an hour south of Santa Cruz.

Benjamin finished his rehab program last fall. In July, he enrolled in a forestry job training program. Ms. Wiscowiche, who lives on Social Security, said she was still looking for the next place to live.

In the spring of 2024, KaMesha Staples, now 40, was financially stuck. She was making $800 a week as a part-time drug addiction counselor in Vallejo, Calif., a working-class city 30 miles north of Oakland. But she was spending $1,000 a week on child care for her two daughters.

“It felt like we were at a standstill, like crabs in a bucket,” Ms. Staples said. So she decided to quit her job and rely on social assistance.

Every few months, a new obstacle seemed to keep her from financial independence. Sometimes her car broke down, costing hundreds of dollars to repair on top of the Uber and Lyft rides she needed as a replacement. She had moved to Vallejo from Oakland because of the cheaper cost of living, but now she had no reliable public transportation. Her older daughter, Vera, a fifth grader, would often have to walk two miles to school.

In June 2024, Compass Family Services, a social services provider that offers housing assistance, told Ms. Staples that she had been chosen for the basic income program. When she received the first $1,000 payment that month, she set a goal: Get a higher-paying job in education, a field she was passionate about. That September, with her daughters back in school and extra cushion from the payments, she enrolled in community college.

One year of payments was “just enough time not to get comfortable,” she said, and the urgency motivated her.

Ms. Staples’s situation — just on the edge of financial independence — is common among basic income recipients, said Erica Kisch, the chief executive of Compass Family Services. The hope is that the payments can be “the thing that pushes them out of poverty and into some kind of stability,” she said.

“One of the things that we’ve been learning is how one very small thing can actually become a giant thing that derails your entire family’s life very quickly,” Ms. Kisch said. “Being poor is actually really expensive.”

In October 2024, Ms. Staples joined her community college’s “job club,” which helped her make a new résumé and a LinkedIn profile and practice mock interviews. She applied for jobs to be a coordinator or teaching assistant at nearby schools. She also applied for Vera to attend nearby charter schools for middle school.

“The payments made it feel like my 10 problems turned to nine,” Ms. Staples said. “I had more time to think about the life I wanted to start living.”

For Vera’s 12th birthday, Ms. Staples took the family to Vallejo’s Six Flags amusement park, just two miles away, for the first time. They had so much fun that she bought her daughters season passes, a $70 expense that she would have never splurged on before.

As the months passed, however, Ms. Staples did not save as much of the basic income money as she had expected.

“I got used to spending what I had,” she said. “That was my biggest regret.”

She also miscalculated how long the program would last. When the last payment hit in May 2025, she had planned for one more.

The program’s end is what researchers often call “the cliff” and the first test of its long-term success. It hit Ms. Staples hard. She missed a car payment and needed help from her grandmother to pay it off. A week later, she was short on money again, so she started driving for DoorDash.

Just as things seemed to worsen, Ms. Staples got an offer in August 2025 to be an after-school coordinator making $30 an hour, $5 more than her last job. The same week, Vera was accepted to a charter school.

In the year since the program ended, things have not been easy, Ms. Staples said, but her life feels more stable. In August, her younger daughter, Xavea, enrolled in the same charter school as Vera, meaning a reprieve from child care costs.

On a recent afternoon, she drove to pick up Xavea’s school uniform, her daughter giddy in the back seat to try it on for the first time. Returning to their house, Ms. Staples sighed in relief.

“Less helpless is how I feel now,” she said.

My father worked in the social services world his entire career, so I grew up going on lots of home visits that felt like the ones I did for this story. What struck me, then and now, is how precarious living on the margins can be, where one unexpected expense can be the difference between stability and sleeping on the streets.

The experience also made me think, as A. I. leaders pitch basic-income as a solution to mass joblessness, is this the vision for the future we should aspire to? Basic-income is meant to help people move upward on the economic ladder. What the tech leaders are pitching feels like the opposite.

Eli Tan covers the technology industry for The Times from San Francisco.

Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The world’s richest person has quietly become by far the biggest known midterm donor, trying to save Republicans’ Senate majority with some of the largest donations in American political history.

By Theodore Schleifer

Theodore Schleifer has written about Silicon Valley politics for a decade.

Elon Musk has quietly funneled more than $276 million into Republican groups and his super PAC since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.

The staggering amount of money makes Mr. Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Mr. Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Thursday.

In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, he gave a total of $158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team. In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.

Mr. Musk has also built a major Republican turnout operation through a super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. He donated over $76 million this summer to the group, which in turn spent that much on building a sprawling canvassing program to try to turn out hard-to-reach Republican voters. The group is active in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races.

2025-2026

$366 mil.

2023-2024

$290 mil.

+$276 mil.

Prior to July 2026

$90 mil.

2025-2026

$366 mil.

+$276 mil.

Prior to July 2026
