Sources: Federal Election Commission filings (prior contributions), representatives for Mr. Musk (most recent contributions).

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Mr. Musk has already given far more money, about $366 million, to federal committees during the 2025-26 election cycle than he did during the 2024 election, when he laid out roughly $290 million to help return President Trump and Republicans to power. He has given even more in undisclosed donations during both elections, according to people briefed on the giving.

The latest torrent of spending has helped give the Republican Party a financial advantage in the midterms, as well-funded outside groups like Mr. Trump’s powerful super PAC flood the airwaves with advertising in the final weeks. No Democratic billionaire is spending nearly as much as Mr. Musk, and money remains a central worry for the party in an otherwise favorable political environment.

The donations also clear up the mystery of how much staying power Mr. Musk wants to have in American politics.

“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.

Mr. Musk, who oversees a vast business empire that has benefited from enormous federal contracts, is famously unpredictable and often jumps from one project to another. He has been far quieter about his political work since his dramatic blowup with Mr. Trump last year. After months of wielding vast influence inside the White House and overseeing Mr. Trump’s government cost-cutting project, he raged against the president’s major domestic policy bill and floated threats to start a third party.

But the two men have warmed back up, appearing together at three events in the last two weeks and praising each other.

Now Mr. Musk has donated more than a quarter-billion dollars to help Mr. Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The money signals his commitment to the right and sets him up as a potential player in the 2028 presidential election, when his super PAC says it intends to remain active — the first time it has confirmed such plans.

Beyond Mr. Musk’s donations to his super PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund, his representatives said that from July through September, he had given smaller but still substantial amounts to other conservative groups:

$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans

$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas

$10 million to the Republican Governors Association

$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” said Andrew Romeo, a spokesman for America PAC. “These robust investments have allowed the G. O. P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”

On voters’ doors across Texas, the campaign literature carries a stark warning: “Radical Democrat socialists are winning elections all across America. Could Texas be next?”

The hanging door cards are the work of Mr. Musk’s voter-turnout operation, which deployed nearly 3,000 paid canvassers last week around the country, according to America PAC officials.

The group has devoted most of its more than $76 million in midterm spending so far to this canvassing program, shelling out smaller amounts on advertising, mail, phone calls and text messages. Much of the messaging targets Democrats, sometimes in misleading or overheated ways.

This spring, Mr. Trump’s political advisers asked Mr. Musk to reprise America PAC’s 2024 field program, a person familiar with the conversation said. Despite the challenging environment for Republicans, some party strategists believe that a field program can make the difference in particularly tight races.

America PAC relies on a few voter-canvassing firms that compete aggressively with one another for work and for staffing, according to people briefed on the operation.

Turnover in the canvassing industry is high. One canvasser who worked for America PAC told The Times that he was paid between $1.50 and $3.00 for each door he knocked on across Texas in the heat. America PAC says it has knocked on about 6.5 million doors across the country so far.

Mr. Musk and his operation, people close to them say, have been particularly focused on the Texas Senate race. The group has unloaded over a third of its disclosed spending in that expensive race, more than in any other. It is uncommon to run an extensive field campaign in large states like Texas, where television ads are more often used to reach voters.

Mr. Musk, a resident of Austin, has extensive business interests and property holdings in Texas. Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, has investigated Mr. Musk’s opponents, like Media Matters, a liberal group.

Mr. Musk’s $10 million donation to Mr. Paxton’s super PAC came at a critical time, when the Republican candidate was being badly outspent.

And Mr. Musk’s $158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Mr. Paxton after months of reluctance.

That is because Mr. Musk’s donations preceded the decision in late August by the super PAC, led by allies of Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, to start what has become a $149 million pro-Paxton ad campaign.

As it did in 2024, Mr. Musk’s operation is focused not on persuading swing voters, but on registering and turning out voters with conservative beliefs — especially “low-propensity” ones who are less likely to cast a ballot.

This is a lot harder for Republicans in a midterm election, without Mr. Trump at the top of the ballot.

To do it, Mr. Musk’s super PAC is leaning hard into the culture wars, especially transgender issues. (Mr. Musk’s daughter, who is transgender, has spoken about their clashes over her identity, and he has suggested that this led to his increased political engagement.)

At voters’ doors in Texas, canvassers are told to target Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, over her record on transgender issues, according to parts of a script reviewed by The Times.

Similarly, the Musk operation is leaving literature on doors that claims that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, has a “radical trans agenda.” And America PAC’s top ad in the state, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, denounces Mr. Talarico over his past comments suggesting that “God is nonbinary.”

The Musk group is also targeting other Democratic Senate candidates over transgender issues, including Josh Turek, the party’s nominee in Iowa. Nationally, one of the super PAC’s most visible ads on Facebook features a man in makeup and reads: “He made his plan to vote. Did you? Don’t stay home while crazies elect radicals.” The group is running ads and sending mail on a broad range of topics, but socialism is a core theme. The Musk super PAC regularly attacks Democrats as socialist and ties them to figures like Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, according to 48 pieces of direct mail shared by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm.

Online, it is even running personalized messaging that invokes a voter’s first name. For example, in a video showing smiling Democrats: “Why are they smiling? Because Christopher hasn’t made a plan to vote yet.”

Much of this outreach points voters to an America PAC website where conservatives can learn about how to register to vote. The super PAC is pushing what it calls an “America Pass,” a digital card on Apple or Google wallets on voters’ phones that lists their registration information, along with election dates and deadlines in their home state.

While Mr. Musk is spending big again and using some tactics that are similar to those he deployed two years ago, this is not 2024 anymore.

He is in a different place politically. While he and Mr. Trump appear to be on good terms again — “our modern-day Thomas Edison,” the president called him on Thursday — Mr. Musk is taking a hands-off approach this election and does not appear as personally passionate.

He has not brought up the midterm elections or the Trump presidency much in private conversations with friends, according to people who have spoken to him in recent months. He is focused on his businesses, these people say, and he and his business lieutenants have taken a less active role in America PAC’s operations, entrusting major decisions to Chris Young, his top adviser.

And on X, a semi-reliable indicator of where the billionaire’s mind is, Mr. Musk has written just seven direct posts this year about candidates in competitive midterm races, according to a Times review, a far cry from his relentless calls throughout 2024 to elect Mr. Trump. Five of those posts focused on Mr. Talarico — and one appeared critical of Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican in Maine.

Gone, too, are Mr. Musk’s barnstorming campaign stops, like the ones he did in Pennsylvania in October 2024 or a Wisconsin judicial election in the spring of 2025. There are no more sweepstakes where he personally hands an oversize check of $1 million to some registered voters who sign a petition, a gambit that drew legal challenges.

Mr. Musk has not evidently grown infatuated with candidates this time around, as he did with Mr. Trump. The closest he came was a $10 million donation for a long-shot Republican running for the U. S. Senate in Kentucky — an investment that went poorly.

The $276 million figure is, of course, just what is publicly known. Mr. Musk has also made some seven-figure donations to support midterm candidates through groups that are not required to disclose their donors, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

Juliana Castro Varón contributed analysis.

An earlier version of this article referred incorrectly to Elon Musk’s practice of handing out oversize checks during a Wisconsin judicial race in 2025. He gave checks to some registered voters who signed a petition, not to people who registered voters.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

Trump Gives Putin a Hand in Russia’s Economic War With Ukraine

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump is moving to buy Russian diesel while also pressuring Ukraine to halt attacks on refineries, a lifeblood of Moscow’s war machine.

By Constant Méheut

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

With the front lines largely frozen, Russia and Ukraine have turned the war into a contest of economic endurance. Kyiv has gone after Russia’s oil refineries. Moscow has hit Ukraine’s ports and heavy industries.

On Friday, President Trump sided with Russia in this all-important battle.

The American leader announced a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel and stepped up pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries. The diesel agreement, if it goes ahead, could send some $4 billion of American money into the Russian economy, energy experts said. A halt to refinery strikes, if Ukraine accedes to one, could be much more valuable to the Kremlin.

Mr. Trump is enlisting Russian help in his effort to bring down sky-high diesel prices, caused mostly by the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran, before the midterm election early next month. Ukraine is expected to get nothing in exchange, even as the American president demands an end to Kyiv’s refinery attacks, its most potent tool for depriving the Russian war machine of income.

Moscow remains free to continue hitting Ukrainian ports, steel factories, warehouses, power plants and data centers, a campaign that is gradually pushing Ukraine’s economy toward a breaking point. Such attacks destroy nearly $10 billion in business assets each year, Ukraine’s economy minister has said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine has condemned Mr. Trump’s decision to buy Russian diesel, saying in a social media post on Friday that “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”

Mr. Trump, who lifted sanctions to allow Russia to sell the fuel to the United States, struck an economic deal with Mr. Putin even as Russian attacks have driven civilian casualties in Ukraine to what the United Nations called a “new horrifying level.”

More than 100 Ukrainian civilians were killed in the past week alone. Moscow is striking Ukraine with an ever growing arsenal of increasingly powerful and precise weapons, taking advantage of gaps in Ukrainian air defenses.

Mr. Zelensky said on Monday that Ukraine had refrained from attacks on Russian oil refineries overnight. But he has said that Ukraine will agree to an extended cease-fire only if Moscow stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. There are fears of a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine this winter if Russia succeeds in its goal of taking down the Ukrainian power and water systems.

The diesel deal is another sign of Mr. Trump’s willingness to tip the scales toward Russia, the aggressor in the conflict. This time, he is offering the Kremlin assistance in an economic battle that could help decide the fate of the war, with both armies largely bogged down at the front.

Ukraine’s campaign against Russian oil infrastructure began in 2024, with strikes on oil depots and refineries. The effort at first had little effect. But as Ukraine expanded its fleet of attack drones and learned how to target critical components that are hard to repair, the effects increased.

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, combined with those on other businesses, have cost Russia about 1 percent of its gross domestic product, President Vladimir V. Putin acknowledged this month.

Reported gasoline output is down by 20 percent compared with 2025 levels, and diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30 percent, the International Energy Agency said in a report last month. The Ukrainian attacks prompted Russia to impose restrictions on diesel exports that Moscow now says it will lift to sell fuel to the United States.

The energy agency added that Russia’s oil tax revenue from January to August was nearly 17 percent below the level of the same period in 2025.

Should Kyiv be forced to halt its refinery strikes, Russia’s advantage in the two countries’ contest to starve the other of money will only grow.

Nowhere is that imbalance clearer than in the near closure of Ukraine’s ports.

For months, Russia has attacked commercial ships sailing in and out of the ports in the southern region of Odesa, aiming to discourage them from calling there. The ports are a lifeline for Ukraine’s economy, accounting for 60 percent of the country’s total export volume. They are used to export grain from the country’s fertile farmland, a key source of revenue.

Because of the Russian attacks, traffic through the three Odesa ports was down nearly 95 percent in August and September, compared with the same period last year, according to port data obtained by The New York Times. In September, only 12 ships made it out of the ports, compared to 266 in the same month last year.

Ukraine has tried to redirect some of the traffic to its ports on the Danube River, which connects the country to Romania. Ships can travel down the river through Romania and back into the Black Sea, sailing off the coast of NATO countries toward Turkey. But the Danube ports can handle only about half of the cargo that normally moves through the Odesa ports.

And the Danube route is now under threat, too. Last week, drones struck three ships off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, sinking two and killing several crew members. All three vessels had carried Ukrainian grain in the past, according to Romanian authorities and port data.

Ukraine has accused Russia of carrying out the attacks, though Romania and Bulgaria have steered clear of assigning blame. Russia did not comment on the attacks.

The halt to Ukraine’s seaborne exports could have catastrophic consequences for the country’s economy, with effects across many sectors. Ukraine’s agriculture minister said this month that farmers were unable to export about 30 million tons of agricultural products, worth about $30 billion.

Russia has also suffered from Ukrainian strikes on its Black Sea ports, which have constrained its agricultural exports. But economists say the impact is not comparable because Russia has more export routes than Ukraine, including through the Baltic and Caspian Seas, which Ukrainian weapons cannot reach as easily.

In a sign of that imbalance, Russia became the world’s largest exporter of sunflower oil in the 2025-26 marketing year, overtaking Ukraine for the first time in two decades, according to estimates from the U. S. Department of Agriculture.

Russia appears to be following a methodical approach to dismantling Ukraine’s economic base, striking all kinds of assets that an economy needs to function, including export routes, factories and energy facilities.

The fate of Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel manufacturer, is a case in point.

Its factories, including two large steel plants in southeastern Ukraine, were already suffering from power outages caused by Russian strikes on the grid. Then came attacks on the ports, which blocked a key export route, and on the railways, which left its products stranded inside the country. Finally, strikes on the plants themselves forced them to shut down last month.

The collapse of Ukraine’s steel industry, which contributed more than 7 percent of Ukraine’s economic output last year, will have severe economic consequences, said Oleksandr Myronenko, Metinvest’s chief operating officer. The company is planning layoffs for administrative personnel, and towns that depend on steel plants will see their budgets shrink.

In September, for the first time in a century, not a single metric ton of steel was produced in Ukraine for one week.

Constant Méheut is a Times correspondent covering the war in Ukraine.

Meta Unveils New Series of Advanced A. I. Models

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, are meant to compete with cutting-edge A. I. models from rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI.

By Eli Tan

Eli Tan reports on Meta and Silicon Valley.

Meta on Monday unveiled a new series of advanced flagship artificial intelligence models, as it tries to catch up to rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI in the A. I. race.

The two new models, called Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, scored nearly as well as Anthropic’s most advanced models on tests that measure reasoning, writing and coding, according to data provided by Meta.

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, revamped his company’s A. I. division last year after setbacks in developing the technology. He has since made progress with new A. I. models and other A. I. products for the company’s 3.5 billion users across Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. Muse, Meta’s A. I. agent app that can operate software and apps on behalf of users, climbed to the top of the App Store in the weeks after it was released last month.

Muse Wonder arrives amid growing concerns over advanced A. I. models and agents, some of which have gone rogue, hacking into companies and meddling with government websites. Mr. Zuckerberg has tried to market Meta’s technology, which is built in a similar way to Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models, with a different message than its rivals, saying that A. I. is meant to be useful and empowering, not dangerous.

Meta began developing Muse Wonder after hiring Alexandr Wang, a founder of the A. I. start-up Scale AI, to be its chief A. I. officer in June 2025. Muse Wonder is the second series of A. I. models released under Mr. Wang’s A. I. division, and is the first that Meta has said is meant to compete with other cutting-edge “frontier” A. I. models, which typically require the most computing power to run.

Muse Wonder will soon power parts of Muse, the company said. Muse Wonder Full is the more powerful model, and will be available only for users who subscribe to Meta’s premium A. I. coding tool, Muse Code.

The new models, which were internally referred to as Watermelon, are also significantly better at coding than Meta’s previous models. The A. I. coding market is dominated by Anthropic and OpenAI, though Meta has been trying to grow its business selling A. I. services to other companies.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Muse Wonder faced some setbacks during development. In July, Meta paused a stage of A. I. development called “pre-training,” which delayed the release of the models until this month, The New York Times previously reported.

In a livestream on Instagram over the weekend, Mr. Zuckerberg teased the new A. I. models while barbecuing meats. Also on the menu, Mr. Zuckerberg said: “A big watermelon.”

Eli Tan covers the technology industry for The Times from San Francisco.

One Grieving Mother, Two Mariners Tickets and a Season of New Friends

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Rhenda Strub invited strangers to accompany her to Seattle Mariners games this season to help overcome the loneliness of grieving for her son’s death.

By Tim Arango

Reporting from Seattle

On the last Sunday afternoon of September, Rhenda Strub was bundled up against the autumn chill for one final day at the ballpark, eating Cracker Jack and sweet and spicy pickles.

Another baseball season was ending as it often does in Seattle: abruptly and too soon. There would be no postseason for the Mariners, the only franchise never to have appeared in a World Series.

A. Bartlett Giamatti, a literary scholar who served as commissioner of Major League Baseball for five months until he died suddenly in 1989, famously wrote that baseball is “designed to break your heart,” because it “leaves you to face the fall all alone.”

Yet this season, Ms. Strub, 71, found that the opposite was also true: Baseball can help heal a broken heart.

After she lost her 27-year-old son, Wyatt, to muscular dystrophy three years ago, she retreated to his room and spent countless hours alone quilting and watching baseball games on television. The constancy of baseball helped to structure her days, but the loneliness only added to her grief.

So at the beginning of this season, Ms. Strub bought two season tickets to the Mariners in Section 120, on the first base side, thinking she would regularly go with her loved ones to T-Mobile Park. But her husband doesn’t like crowds, and the rest of her family has busy lives.

So she wrote a post on Facebook — with some trepidation, she said, because the “internet can be a cruel place” — asking strangers if they wanted to attend games with her.

“This season ticket adventure is part of me finding my way back out — getting out of the house, being around people, and doing something that brings a little joy again,” she wrote. “Baseball helps me heal.”

The post went viral in April, inspiring stories in local newspapers and on the radio.

Her family worried about her meeting up with strangers. Random people also messaged her with their concerns, offering safety tips.

But her inbox was also flooded with messages from people describing their own stories of loss. A child who died. The passing of mothers, fathers and partners. Failed marriages.

And a shared love of baseball.

“I had so many people contact me with remarkably similar stories,” she said. “They have had some sort of life event that left them feeling unbalanced to deeply grieving. And they didn’t really have someone to go to the game with but loved going to the game.”

“Baseball has a calming effect on them,” she added, “and they want someone to share it with.”

Ms. Strub is a lifelong baseball fan, having grown up just outside Kansas City, first rooting for the Athletics before they moved to California, and then for the Royals when M. L. B. expansion brought the franchise to her hometown. She loved George Brett, the Royals’ star third baseman, and Lou Piniella, who played five seasons for the team.

She and her husband began raising their four children in South Dakota, but moved to Olympia, Wash., 24 years ago in search of better jobs. She had a career as an engineering consultant and retired in 2016. She then began to devote much of her time to taking care of Wyatt, whose health problems worsened steadily until he died in 2023.

By the end of this baseball season, Ms. Strub had attended games with about 30 strangers and found that the people she connected with needed her as much as she needed them. She built an online community, bringing together the people she had met in a private Facebook group, calling the project “Strangers to Friends.”

If she couldn’t attend a game — she had to miss a few when her husband, Mike, had brain surgery — she handed off her tickets to strangers who had reached out to her but didn’t know each other.

She said she was “gobsmacked” by the reaction to her post.

“I have made so many friends this summer,” she said. “I have friends that will be my friends for the rest of my life.”

Over the summer, Jack Barrie, a young documentary filmmaker from Los Angeles, reached out to her. Mr. Barrie, who grew up in Seattle and roots for the Mariners, said he felt Ms. Strub’s story of grieving in public “needs to be shared.” The two began meeting and filming a short documentary, “You Sit Here,” a reference to the words on a silhouette next to her in her original Facebook post.

Already, people are booking games with her for next season.

“I just needed something to snap me out of the fog of grief I was in,” Ms. Strub said. “I don’t ever expect to be over his death. I don’t expect to ever recover. But I have been able to find joy again.”

Others found joy through her.

One woman who has a disabled child came from Australia to meet Ms. Strub at the ballpark. Steve Hayburn, a probation officer from Ketchikan, Alaska, flew to Seattle in September after the death of his father and the dissolution of a long relationship.

“When I saw her story, I knew I had to connect with her,” Mr. Hayburn, 55, said. “She kind of reminded me of my mom.”

They met up at the stadium for the second to last game of the season, on a Saturday night. Ms. Strub walked in with her cane, her hat on sideways, a pink chain around her neck holding her cellphone. “She kind of reminded me of a gangster, the way she was walking,” he said.

They watched the Mariners play the Los Angeles Angels and shared a tub of popcorn. “It was like I was spending time with my mom all over again,” he said.

Mr. Hayburn, who grew up in Ohio and rooted for the Cincinnati Reds, added, “It helped me deal with my trauma I’ve been through this year.”

Another new friend, Sheila Cook, lost her wife, Michelle, a few years ago, also to muscular dystrophy. Ms. Cook was shattered by the loss and felt angry and confused about why doctors told her Michelle was ineligible for a heart transplant.

Then she met Ms. Strub, who explained the disease in a way that finally made sense to her. (Ms. Strub also has three grandsons who have been diagnosed with the disease, having passed it down through her daughters with a mutation on one of her X chromosomes, she said.)

“We were just weeping and crying all the way to the ballpark,” said Ms. Cook, 74, who has a dog named after Ken Griffey Jr. “It was a wonderful gift. I truly believe it was a gift from God, that Rhenda was a gift from God.”

In the middle of the summer, the Mariners honored Ms. Strub as their season ticket holder of the year. For one night, she moved up from her regular seat to watch the game with friends in a luxury suite.

She was also asked to throw out the first pitch at that game. It was a nerve-racking proposition because she had never learned to throw properly.

It turned out that one of her new friends, Liz Brown, was a retired schoolteacher who had once taught gym class. So before Ms. Strub took the field at T-Mobile Park, Ms. Brown met her near her home in Olympia and taught her how to throw a baseball.

At the ballpark on the final day of the season, Ms. Strub stood to cheer for one of her favorite players, the pitcher Logan Gilbert, who was being removed from the game in the fifth inning.

Then she continued talking about her son, Wyatt, who had enjoyed going to a ballgame with family even though baseball wasn’t really his thing. He loved online games and singing and acting, and as a teenager, he had appeared in several musicals, including “South Pacific,” “The Sound of Music,” and “Peter Pan.”

“He always played the strong voice character,” she said.

All day at the game, the Mariners played tributes on the video board for Rick Rizzs, the longtime radio voice of the team who was retiring after 41 seasons. Fans offered testimonials about how they, like Ms. Strub, turned to baseball in their grieving. Ms. Strub noted the “constant theme of healing” in the videos and “the peace they found with Rick through baseball.”

Ms. Strub thought more about Wyatt as the game continued.

He had refused to meet with the chaplain as he was dying in the hospital. Then, on his very last day, with hours left, he asked for him.

Wyatt was quiet for a time when the chaplain appeared at his bedside, according to Ms. Strub. Then he turned to the man and said, “You’re not here for me. You’re here for my mom. I need to know she’ll be OK.”

Ms. Strub nodded to her surroundings at the ballpark — the thousands of people around her, the expansive green lawn, the ballplayers.

“This is me trying to be OK for Wyatt,” she said. “I know he’s with me. I can feel him all the time. This is a peaceful place where I can connect with him and feel joy.”

Rhenda’s social media post asking if strangers wanted to attend Mariners games with her went viral at the start of the season, but rather than write about it then I had the idea to wait until September and attend the very last game of the season with her. I found she built a community of people who found solace in baseball during tough times, and that the people she met needed her as much as she needed them.

Tim Arango is a correspondent covering national news. He is based in Los Angeles.

Social Security funds are on track to run short by 2032, which would mean a reduction in benefits. Here’s how four hypothetical households rely on the program in retirement.

Credit... Illustrations by Peter Arkle

Supported by

By Tara Siegel Bernard

If Congress doesn’t act, more than 60 million Americans could see their Social Security income drop by nearly a quarter in six years.

That’s when Social Security’s retirement trust fund is expected to run dry, and incoming revenue would be enough to pay only 78 percent benefits, reducing every retiree’s paycheck by 22 percent.

The program, which President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed into law in 1935 during the Great Depression, is not in danger of completely running out of money. While lawmakers have long known they would need to move to close that gap — through tax increases, benefit cuts or some combination — they have been slow to act on this politically charged topic.

But the window to do that is closing.

Many of the lawmakers being elected in the coming midterms will probably be entrusted with drafting reform packages, and they will need to contemplate crucial questions: Who will absorb the costs of any changes to shore up the program, and what will the consequences be? Will people be less prepared for retirement as a result?

Procrastination has been costly, making these decisions now more difficult. Even some Republicans, who often resist any tax increases, have recently proposed raising the income ceiling on payroll taxes, the dedicated tax that finances the program, so that wealthier households contribute more.

“Any serious Social Security reform package should be scored on what it does to household retirement outcomes, not only on what it does to trust-fund balances,” said Jack VanDerhei, director of retirement research at Morningstar’s Center for Retirement & Policy Studies.

The details of any fix-it plan are crucial given the program’s extraordinary reach, potentially affecting tens of millions of working Americans, as well as future retirees and current ones — many of whom lean heavily on the program.

Just how heavily do they lean on it?

To address that question, we looked at four hypothetical households — two singles, two married couples — with different income levels and resources to illustrate the role that Social Security plays in their financial lives, a topic we’ll continue to closely track in the year ahead.

In each illustration, individuals are 64 years old and plan to retire and file for Social Security at 67, the age at which they qualify for a full retirement benefit. All analyses were run by Mr. VanDerhei of Morningstar.

Social Security is often a primary source of income for the lowest-income Americans, according to other analyses.

In this case, a single man who earned $34,000 a year, on average, over his working life is one of the roughly half of households across the country that have no money in retirement accounts to draw on.

In this case, a single worker earned about $75,000, on average, over her career. That puts her monthly Social Security benefit at $2,548, which accounts for the vast majority of her monthly income because she has just $20,000 in retirement savings (generating about $70 a month), like households with similar earnings.

About three-quarters of similarly situated households also own their own homes; the median household holds $137,000 in home equity.

With pensions fading and ever-rising costs — health care, housing, college — continuously pushed onto families, Social Security has served as a stabilizer during retirees’ most vulnerable years. Should the stock market plunge on the eve of your retirement, damaging savings at the most inopportune time, Social Security remains unaffected.

Even households with solid income and savings need to stow away and accumulate substantial sums to draw even a modest income — one that must last for potentially several decades.

That $1 million savings milestone? It will typically generate $40,000 a year (adjusted upward for inflation in future years).

Each worker here earned $75,000, on average, over the course of their careers, for a combined total of $150,000. Retirement savings of $171,700 provide $572 in monthly income. Most households like theirs also own homes, with the median household holding $251,800 in home equity. A little more than a quarter also hold stocks, bonds or mutual funds outside retirement accounts.

This couple collectively earned about $261,000 a year — one spouse earned at least the maximum amount subject to Social Security payroll taxes each year, which works out to an average of about $186,000 over this spouse’s career; the other worker earned $75,000 on average.

Their retirement savings of $435,000 could generate monthly income of $1,450. Most similar households own their homes; the median household holds $400,600 in home equity. About half hold stocks, bonds or mutual funds outside retirement accounts.

Many retirees report feeling reliant on Social Security.

But it’s more than just a feeling: Among beneficiaries 60 and older in the middle of a five-rung income ladder, where median household income was projected at about $90,900 in 2024, Social Security made up 38 percent of household income on average, according to the Social Security Administration’s MINT model, which uses administrative earnings and benefits records to make projections.

Those in the next-highest rung, with median household income of $152,300, leaned on Social Security for a quarter of their income, on average, while the group just below the middle relied on it for 56 percent.

Other studies have shown that roughly 42 percent of households rely on Social Security for at least half of their retirement income.

The program is more than just an inflation-adjusted insurance policy against running out of money in retirement — it also provides disability, survivor and family benefits. When so much of our financial lives rides on luck, timing and our collective human vulnerability, this social contract has persevered.

Assumptions and sources for illustrations

— Each example pairs a Social Security benefit calculated for a hypothetical worker born in 1962 who claims at 67 in 2029, with the retirement savings of real households near retirement with similar wages. The low and middle earners’ pay follows a career pattern based on actual workers’ earnings, rising with national wages; the higher earner earns at least the maximum amount subject to Social Security tax each year. Career-average earnings are stated in 2026 wage levels. Benefits are in 2026 dollars adjusted for inflation.

— The reduced check assumes the retirement trust fund is depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032, as projected in the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, after which about 78 percent of scheduled benefits would initially be payable. It is an illustrative proportional reduction, not a benefit estimate provided by the Social Security Administration.

— Retirement savings figures are medians from the Federal Reserve’s 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, adjusted for inflation, for comparable households headed by someone age 55 to 64 in 2022. They are not projections; balances could rise or fall with contributions, withdrawals and investment returns.

— Retirement savings include individual retirement accounts, like Roth I. R. A. s, and employer plans such as 401(k)s and 403(b)s. Income from savings assumes a 4 percent annual withdrawal. It excludes pensions, earnings, home equity and other assets like stocks, bonds, mutual funds and annuities held outside retirement accounts. All income figures are before taxes.

— All data and analysis are from Jack VanDerhei, director of retirement research at Morningstar’s Center for Retirement & Policy Studies.

Tara Siegel Bernard writes about personal finance for The Times, from saving for college to paying for retirement and everything in between.

Histories & happenings

Four decades after his death, a revealing trove of the author’s possessions is up for auction.

A late 1950s portrait of Truman Capote by James Whitney Fosburgh, one of nearly 400 lots on offer at an upcoming auction of the writer’s memorabilia from the collection of his friend and biographer, Gerald Clarke. Credit... Henry Leutwyler

Supported by

By Jenny Comita

Photographs by Henry Leutwyler

Produced by Michael Reynolds

In June 1972, at a movie screening in Manhattan, the writer Truman Capote tried to give the journalist Gerald Clarke the Cartier timepiece right off his wrist. When Clarke, who was profiling Capote for Esquire magazine at the time, refused to take it, Capote was furious; it was Clarke’s birthday, and Capote insisted he needed a present. Rather than cause a scene, Clarke walked away with the extravagant offering, only to send it back the next day, eliciting an irate phone call from Capote. Though Clarke never did accept the watch — “It was beautiful. I wish I had it now,” he says with a laugh — the attempted gift proved the first of many that Capote, who became a close friend, would bestow upon him over the next dozen years.

Henry Leutwyler

Items in the auction include three of Capote’s bow ties, this classic black one among them.

This Playboy Club lighter and cigarette holder belonged to Capote, though, says Clarke, “his place was more Studio 54.”

The writer’s Capote Club (no relation) cigars came from Spain’s Canary Islands.

A Must de Cartier Trinity pen that belonged to Capote, who often wrote manuscripts in longhand.

A vintage pewter ashtray from Washington, D. C.’s Watergate Hotel.

This copy of “To Kill a Mockingbird” was inscribed to Capote by its author, Harper Lee, who was his childhood next-door neighbor in Monroeville, Ala., and a longtime friend.

“Harper went out to Kansas with him to work on [his 1965 true-crime novel] ‘In Cold Blood,’” says Clarke. “They went on interviews together, and they didn’t use a tape recorder because they thought it would make people uncomfortable. Afterward, they’d each write down their memories of what people said and then compare notes.”

During Capote’s lifetime, Clarke, whose authorized 1988 biography of Capote served as the primary source material for Bennett Miller’s 2005 biopic starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, was the recipient of dog figurines (reflecting their shared love of canines), assorted literary memorabilia and the American artist James Whitney Fosburgh’s large oil painting of a young and handsome Capote, captured in the late 1950s, at a time before the writer was subsumed by social scandal and alcoholism. “Several years before his death, he called to offer it to me, and I didn’t pick it up for three weeks. I couldn’t quite figure out how to get it to my apartment,” Clarke recalls. “Finally, he said, ‘Well, are you going to take it or not?’ So I found a big Checker cab and went to get it. It’s my belief that he gave it to me because he didn’t want to be reminded of that younger version of himself, of all the things that didn’t work out.” The portrait hung in the foyer of Clarke’s Bridgehampton, N. Y., home for decades.

Henry Leutwyler

One of the most intimate items is a medical invoice from a doctor in Rome.

This Valentine’s Day card is signed from Capote and his bulldogs Charlie and Maggie to his partner Jack Dunphy and his cat Diotima. According to Clarke, Dunphy rescued the animal from drowning on the Greek island of Paros and brought it back to New York.

This Olivetti Underwood typewriter belonged to Dunphy, who was also an author.

Capote collected little animal toys, some of which are included in the sale.

This painted bronze frog statuette is actually an inkwell.

A paperweight given to Capote by the French novelist Colette on his first trip to Europe, when he was 23.

“She had a table full of paperweights and as they were talking his eyes never left them,” says Clarke. “He kept looking at one with a white flower, and Colette said, ‘That’s one of the best. Take it, please.’ And he said, ‘No, I couldn’t. It’s your favorite.’ She told him, ‘My dear, really there is no point in giving a gift unless one also treasures it oneself.’”

After being gifted the white rose paperweight by Colette, Capote “became addicted to paperweights and collected so many of them,” says Clarke. He even made some himself, including these, which preserve flowers in resin or acrylic.

A paperweight made of stones from the Clutter family farm outside Holcomb, Kansas, the site of the 1959 murders that were the subject of Capote’s “In Cold Blood.”

Capote and Dunphy “had a perfect living arrangement: two very small houses in Sagaponack [on Long Island] about 100 feet apart,” says Clarke. “Each had his own. Jack would make them dinner every night.”

Capote’s monogrammed T. Anthony duffel bag.

A contact sheet from a shoot by the photographer Richard Avedon, another friend and collaborator.

After Capote’s death in 1984 at the age of 59, his longtime partner, Jack Dunphy, an author and Broadway dancer, passed along many more mementos, including correspondence, photographs, decorative items and even his house keys. (Dunphy would die six years later at age 77.) Taken as a whole, the collection offers an intimate view into both Capote’s professional ambitions and his day-to-day domestic life, and now Clarke, who is, at 89, attempting to get his affairs in order, is selling most of it through the Bellport, N. Y.-based Cornell Auctions on Nov. 21.

Henry Leutwyler

Capote “loved hats and caps of all kinds,” says Clarke. “These were about to be thrown out, and I rescued them from the trash man.”

Capote’s Cartier ice bucket with tongs, monogrammed with a “C.” “Truman really drank only one thing: vodka and orange juice,” says Clarke.

Some of Capote’s small personal items including, clockwise from left, a Paul Buhré Swiss folding travel clock, a vest-pocket lighter, a cigarette holder, two rectangular pill boxes and, at center, a 14-karat gold perfume bottle.

Capote’s Louis Vuitton wallet, small trinket box and eyeglass case, which was from New York City’s Keenan & Buck.

“Truman died in Los Angeles in [his friend] Joanne Carson’s house, and she had him cremated and the ashes put in this box,” Clarke says of a receptacle that just happens to look like a book.

“Jack had the urn on his mantelpiece at his apartment on West 13th Street in Greenwich Village until he died 34 years ago. Jack’s brother and I later took it to a pond in Sagaponack, not far from where they lived, and scattered both of their ashes.”

Carson told Clarke that she kept “a spoonful” of the ashes, which were sold at auction in 2016, as part of Carson’s estate, for $43,750.

Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

It’s Oct. 12 — 22 days away from the midterms. Here’s the state of play.

By Reid J. Epstein

Reporting from Washington

The Republican Party’s hopes of saving its majorities in Congress increasingly appear to depend on a few possible outcomes: G. O. P. advantages in money and on the map pay off, the polls are wrong, or a major news development suddenly brightens the party’s prospects.

In the meantime, Republicans in competitive races are doing whatever they can to try to loosen their ties to President Trump’s agenda, which is dragging their party down with just over three weeks to go before the midterm elections.

There have been new ads stating opposition to Trump’s tariffs from candidates who supported them, calls to end the war in Iran from candidates who backed it and efforts to look bipartisan from candidates who pledged to be Trump’s top allies.

The debates last week made clear that Republicans are on the back foot. Questions about high prices, tariffs and the war dominated the sessions in battleground states. While G. O. P. advertising often aims to link Democrats to their party’s left-wing figures and stoke disputes about transgender athletes, cost-of-living issues are paramount to voters this year.

Trump’s rhetoric is not helping his party. Even as his own approval ratings have plummeted, he urges voters to pretend that he is on the ballot. He touts data centers that are even less popular than he is. And he has shown no inclination to back off from his positions on the war in Iran or tariffs.

But then there is the money.

Thanks to Trump’s super PACs and well-heeled political allies, Republicans still hold a commanding financial advantage. The billionaire Elon Musk has directed more than $276 million to Republicans since the start of July.

Republicans hope that will help them pull through on a House map they sought to redraw in their favor and Senate map that features plenty of races in red states. But the time to change minds and move votes is shrinking by the day.

The New York Times

Republicans have all but conceded the race in North Carolina to Democrat Roy Cooper, a popular former governor. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff has a commanding lead over Representative Mike Collins. And now Democrats are on offense in deep-red Kansas, with Senate Majority PAC, the party’s main super PAC, beginning $5 million worth of ads in the state.

According to polls, Democratic candidates are leading or running neck-and-neck in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — all places Trump won three times by substantial margins. He and Vice President JD Vance have aimed to energize the base with appearances in those states, but the polls suggest the Democrats are holding their own.

In the eyes of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, Democrats even have a chance to take back the majority partly because of his recruiting efforts. In an interview Friday, he claimed credit for getting Cooper, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio and former Representative Mary Peltola of Alaska into their races and helping Josh Turek win his primary in Iowa.

“I couldn’t accept the map as is because the map as is consigns us to a minority, all things being equal, just because of the way the states are structured,” Schumer said. “So we had to expand the map. I didn’t accept the original map. I worked to build a better one.”

Still, some Democrats worry about Senate races that ought to be easier for them. Contests remain tight in Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire.

The New York Times

Things do not look promising for House Republican hopes of retaining their majority.

The Cook Political Report on Friday shifted 18 districts toward Democrats. Two Iowa seats, held by Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, are now considered “lean Democratic.”

That is in addition to Republicans already punting on the Omaha-based district held by the retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska.

Representative Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the House majority whip, said the issue is that Republican voters may be too “satisfied” with Trump to vote in November.

“The midterms, you typically have the party that wins the White House is satisfied,” Emmer said Sunday on ABC’s “This Week.” “If our people will turn out — you may be satisfied, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t vote. You show up and vote, we’re going to be fine.”

Democrats need to flip just three seats to take a House majority. Many election forecasters now suggest they will do much better than that. During a discussion last week, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, repeatedly declined to predict how many seats his party would win.

He did, however, suggest that Democrats would be able to repeat their successes from 2018, the last midterm with Trump in the White House.

“Past performance is not evidence of future results,” he said. “But it provides at least a path for us to ascertain what is possible.”

Even for Musk, a quarter-billion dollars is a lot to spend on politics in just three months.

The billionaire has once again become the largest single donor to Republican causes. The roughly $276 million he directed to groups during July, August and September means his tab for the 2026 elections is now about $366 million.

Musk’s funds are split between $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Senate G. O. P. super PAC; over $76 million to America PAC, his own outlet that focuses on voter turnout; $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which supports House Republicans; and other donations. One of them reflects Musk’s interest in the Texas Senate race: He gave $10 million to a super PAC backing Ken Paxton, who polls show trails James Talarico, the Democratic candidate trying to become the first in his party to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988.

In five states with competitive Senate races, 615,100 ballots have already been cast.

After vanishing from the campaign trail for nine days, James Talarico, the Texas Democrat running for Senate, emerged at the Austin City Limits music festival Friday. He said he’d been home sick with the flu.

Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, had been making hay out of Talarico’s whereabouts. What is next in the Texas campaign is unclear: Talarico on Saturday challenged Paxton to debate, and Trump has suggested Paxton should debate, but Paxton has yet to agree to a debate.

76 percent.

That’s the percentage of Ohio voters who said Trump’s policies have increased cost of living in the state in a CNN/SSRS poll. The poll found Brown, the Democrat, up by 6 percentage points over Senator Jon Husted, the Republican. Trump and Vance have both visited the state recently in an attempt to boost support for Husted.

Trump’s latest idea to bring down gas prices — importing diesel fuel from Russia — got a chilly reception from some of his fellow Republicans, including a few in battleground races. Former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan and Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are both locked in tight Senate races, panned the idea. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said on Saturday that he would force a vote to block Russian oil purchases. The U. S. has forbidden importing Russian fuel since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine.

In Maine, the cost of home heating oil is surging along with prices of seemingly everything else, forcing voters to pay more to stay warm just as fall temperatures drop.

Republicans concede the costs — up 80 percent over a year ago to fill a standard heating oil tank — are a problem for Senator Susan Collins, who backed the Iran war that drove up oil prices before she called for it to end.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.” — Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia

Ossoff pulled no punches in his debate attacks on Representative Mike Collins, his Republican opponent in Georgia’s Senate race. He said Collins had “hired half the Third Reich,” a reference to Collins hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views.

Collins responded that he had “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.”

A TikTok Tarot Card Reader Accused Me of Murder. My Life Turned Upside Down.

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Rebecca Scofield

Dr. Scofield is the chair of the Department of History at the University of Idaho.

It was a bright blue Thanksgiving Day. I was standing in a park listening to my kids play when I opened a TikTok video of a woman I had never met. She showed my faculty profile picture and contact information, and said that I had orchestrated the murders of four students at the college where I work, the University of Idaho. She claimed I was covering up an inappropriate romantic relationship with one of the victims.

I didn’t know any of the students, who had been killed only 11 days before I saw the video. The accuser knew nothing about me, lived in Texas and used tarot card readings as the only basis for her claims.

Over the next several weeks, while I was grieving with the rest of my community, this TikTok influencer uploaded over a hundred videos declaring that I had committed a quadruple homicide. The videos got millions of views. I was overwhelmed with calls, messages, comments and emails, many of which were disturbing or threatening. And I could have been anyone.

You cannot stand in digital spaces. I was not hit by a bus or punched in the face. Yet I saw up close how the online world can come to feel more real than the physical one. Even after the actual murderer was arrested and convicted, the accusations against me continued. And even though these outrageous claims were made online by someone I had never met, they were amplified by unsuspecting viewers and algorithm-driven platforms, and the harm seeped into every aspect of my life. I came to realize that all of us are responsible for the online world we inhabit, and all of us must fight its tendency to propagate lies.

Of course, the people around me knew these claims were ridiculous. Yet the gap between my knowledge of the truth and the falsehoods people were willing to entertain created a kind of purgatory. I desperately wanted to spend time with my colleagues, students and friends as we grieved, but I became isolated. I stopped going to campus, moved my course online and ceased using social media. I stopped sleeping well, and instead, I walked the hallway outside my children’s rooms, utterly terrified that they would be harmed by the person hyperfixated on me, any of her believers or the person actually responsible for the murders.

With the increased media attention, my relationship to my house shifted. It was as if our walls had been removed and anyone could peer inside. Doors and windows had new and frightening meanings. I sensed that perhaps I was unraveling, disintegrating — that I was no longer a real person. If my face and name were not my own, who was I?

As a professor of history, I know that technologies that disseminate speech have always reshaped truth. The printing press allowed the words of revolutionary religious leaders like Martin Luther to splinter the power of the Catholic Church by convincing people they had a right to read the word of God. The radio helped fuel the rise of fascism across the U. S. and Europe.

Digital platforms rewrite our reality in a much more profound way. It takes a long time to uncover the truth through historical analysis, and even then, it’s often at best partial. Social media destroys that process. Even though many content creators hold themselves to high standards of research, they are not professionally beholden to official codes of conduct or review. Stories that should be handled with care and respect become entertainment. Perhaps that’s why — despite an arrest, guilty plea and conviction in the students’ murders — the years passed and the accusations against me persisted.

No one needed to search for the accusations against me — the words were simply fed to them by TikTok’s algorithm. Endless scroll, autoplay videos and predatory algorithms give viewers the same levels of dopamine as other addictive substances. And with every view, a creator gets closer to securing sponsors or getting paid by the platform.

Against these incentives to distort truth, we need a countermovement. One option is to opt out of digital spaces. After decades of unregulated experimentation, many people — particularly younger people — are choosing digital detoxes, landlines and MP3 players. We can choose to scroll past stories that cannot be verified and only follow creators who are transparent about their research.

We can try to hold platforms accountable for the harmful content they spread. A federal law, Section 230, protects online platforms from many defamation lawsuits, meaning that only individuals are liable for misinformation, even if a platform helped spread it. Proposals that would reform Section 230 range from adding exceptions for extreme cases to revoking immunity for social media companies altogether. If the companies making billions of dollars off these platforms won’t protect us, what other recourse do we have?

We can sue. Defamation law exists to remind people that the freedom to speak includes the duty to speak responsibly. Having successfully sued my accuser, I will not pretend this is an easy or simple path. But it is necessary as a warning to other bad actors.

We can also share our stories. To anyone who has been targeted with ugly or untruthful words on these platforms: Do not feel ashamed. You are not alone. There are more and more people among us every day. Do not bear this injustice in silence.

It takes commitment to defend the truth, but then again, it always has. In 1892, a white mob descended on the offices of the Black anti-lynching activist and suffragist Ida B. Wells to destroy her printing press, thinking that might silence her. They did not succeed. She instead published her most famous anti-lynching pamphlet the same year.

A little over a decade later, in 1903, Annie Oakley, the famed sharpshooter, fought 55 libel cases to defend her reputation when newspapers ran a false story that she was caught stealing to support a cocaine habit. She would spend years fighting one of the most powerful men in American media to clear her name. Ida B. Wells and Annie Oakley probably did not agree on many issues. But they believed in the power of their own voice and the right to set the record straight.

We are all responsible for the world we create. I had many goals for my life. Being publicly accused of heinous crimes I did not commit was not one of them. I still manage the ongoing consequences of those accusations every day. Years of sleeplessness and stress have resulted in physical and psychological issues that will shape the rest of my life.

But those who have been subjected to unchecked online harm need to speak, to scream and to rage. If we cannot publicly endure the pain and humiliation that comes with being split open for all to see and comment on, then we cannot fight back, and our children will inherit a world designed for misinformation. I want my children, my nieces and nephews and my students to live in a world of hope and truth.

So, before you, too, are accused of murder on the internet, question the content you are consuming or creating. Ask yourself if the platforms that profit from enabling the spread of unverified information should continue to remain insulated from accountability. And remember that what seems like harmless entertainment could shape not only individual lives, but the course of history.

Rebecca Scofield is a professor of history and chair of the Department of History at the University of Idaho.

‘What You See in America Is Exactly What You Saw in Poland and Hungary’

The New York Times October 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Round Table

By David BroderCaroline de GruyterMattia Ferraresi and Tim Schneider

Mr. Broder is the author of “Mussolini’s Grandchildren.” Ms. de Gruyter is a columnist for the Dutch newspaper NRC. Mr. Ferraresi is a writer for the Italian newspaper QN. Mr. Schneider is an editor in Times Opinion.

The far right has been rising in Europe for a long time — Edward Luttwak called fascism “the wave of the future” back in 1994 — but last month’s electoral breakthrough in Saxony-Anhalt by the Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, felt seismic. For the first time in Germany’s postwar history, a far-right party stands on the brink of power. The AfD joins a legion of others, not least Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, either in office or perilously close to it.

In a written online conversation, Tim Schneider, an editor in Times Opinion, hosted David Broder, author of “Mussolini’s Grandchildren”; Caroline de Gruyter, a columnist for the Dutch newspaper NRC; and Mattia Ferraresi, a writer for the Italian newspaper QN, to discuss Europe’s thriving far right, the roots of its success, its plans for power and, of course, what President Trump has to do with it all.

Tim Schneider: An easy one to start: How did we get here?

David Broder: The post-2008 period is often described as a temporary “populist moment.” But nativist parties obsessed with civilizational decline have since established themselves as major forces, even where electoral systems or national histories offered apparent defenses against them. The reasons are many: a drop-off in mainstream parties’ ability to guarantee social progress; the specter of immigrants undermining national identity; and fewer people voting. The financial crisis helped undo the old mainstream. Now, some of these parties are becoming the right-wing establishment and building effective coalitions.

Caroline de Gruyter: The world is changing fast. Governments can’t keep pace, are incompetent or, for various reasons, don’t meet voters’ demands. Far-right parties jump into the void. But they do not win elections by just criticizing governments and uttering extremist views: They need the media to pay attention and, crucially, they need parties from the political center to start copying them. It is only when other political parties start shifting to the right that the far right can attract a sufficient amount of voters.

Mattia Ferraresi: I guess the short answer, for me, is the crisis of liberalism in the post-Cold War era. Mainstream liberal politics, in both its left- and right-wing versions, failed to deliver on its promises, not only in terms of welfare and economic growth but also in the more complex realm of identity and meaning. The apparent triumph of that worldview paved the way for its own demise. What we’re seeing today, all over the world, are different — sometimes very different — expressions of the same disillusionment with liberalism and its policies.

Schneider: A common perception is that these parties appeal to a particular type of voter, often older workers in left-behind, deindustrializing areas. Is that true? Is there a core far-right constituency in Europe?

Ferraresi: There’s some truth to the far right’s appeal to the post-working class, I guess, but I would tie it to a lack of political and cultural identity. The AfD’s strength in eastern Germany is only partly linked to the region’s dire economy; at a deeper level, the party offers a framework for identity. Voters across Europe who are drawn to the far right are often united by a sense of meaninglessness that was once filled by other structures and parties (mainly Christian Democracy and Communism). James Carville’s line about the economy was an effective campaign message for Bill Clinton, but it was ultimately shallow and wrong. It’s the identity, stupid!

Broder: These parties draw moral force from claiming to represent people the left forgot. Even their more middle-class voters like to think they’re on the side of the underdog. The real picture is more mixed: The National Rally, for instance, grew earlier in the areas you mention, but now its support is rising faster among white-collar groups. Though lower-educated voters in deindustrialized rural eastern Germany were early backers of the AfD, the party has since captured much broader attention and support. In many countries, these parties harvested former social-democratic voters after 2008. Today, they are cannibalizing the mainstream center right.

De Gruyter: Most voters will go for centrist parties — we are middle-class countries, after all. The problem is that if mainstream parties leave the center and all that is on offer is the far right, part of the electorate will go for that, and some will simply stop voting. People vote for far-right extremist parties because that is what is on offer. I think it is a myth that voters are shifting to the right. Parties are shifting to the right!

Schneider: It’s interesting that we’ve not really mentioned immigration, which most people regard as these parties’ signature issue. What about the rest of their platform — what is their offer economically or culturally?

De Gruyter: What they usually offer is the opposite of what mainstream parties offer. And they flip-flop in order to catch votes. For example, Ms. Le Pen used to protect the working class, with a plan to bring down the retirement age and so on. But now, with France drifting toward huge deficits and financial markets taking note, she suddenly switches tactics and proposes big cuts to welfare. N’importe quoi, really.

Broder: Often these parties are called “welfare-chauvinist,” in that they seek to protect social services by barring new arrivals. I think this is simplistic. Most offer some renewed idea of meritocracy and even retool the Third Way promise to reward “hard-working families,” while also prioritizing the nuclear-family model. They may even speak of integrating some deserving immigrants. But broadly the story is that migrants are unfairly cutting in line or being pushed ahead by elites, at the expense of hard-working nationals.

Ferraresi: Anti-immigration policies are essentially about providing an identity, whether rooted in whiteness, language, Christianity or something else. That, I think, is why they are so effective at energizing voters — far more so than other culturally conservative causes, such as traditional family values or opposition to abortion. In a culturally conservative country like Italy, Ms. Meloni did not win the election, and go on to lead the longest-serving government in the history of the republic, by rallying against abortion or same-sex marriage.

Schneider: What does Ms. Meloni’s tenure tell us about the far right in office?

Ferraresi: I think it tells us that going mainstream is the only way to govern. Ms. Meloni’s story is that of a shrewd politician who understood right away that her only chance of political survival lay in being legitimized by the European elite. Her success was forged in Brussels, so much so that when she was forced to choose between Mr. Trump and the European Union, she picked the latter. I’m not sure there’s a broader lesson here for other far-right parties, but the strategy has certainly worked for her.

Broder: Ms. Meloni has inspired imitators to become pro-NATO, pro-business parties who aim to change the European Union from within. Yet it’s also no surprise that a new further-right party, National Future, is quickly rising in Italy and ideas like so-called remigration are spreading. This is in part a critique of Meloni-style mainstreaming — she hasn’t delivered on more fiery promises — but also shows how such governments open space for more radical proposals.

De Gruyter: Ms. Meloni’s tenure tells us that part of the far right mellows when in power — though not all! The AfD is different, as is the Freedom Party of Austria. Once in power, Ms. Meloni suddenly became pro-NATO, pro-E. U. and pro-Ukraine. The far right in many other countries, including France, has also made huge U-turns. They do not want to exit the European Union anymore but to change Europe from the inside. This is a completely different strategy than before.

Schneider: The general shift of these parties toward accommodation with the bloc makes me wonder: Is a far-right European Union a contradiction in terms?

Broder: Though Ms. Meloni’s party still sometimes paints Brussels as a liberal blob, once-radical ideas like outsourcing border control to non-European states are now the norm — and conservative and far-right forces have repeatedly formed majorities, including in dismantling the bloc’s earlier green push. Most of the parties we’re talking about trade in vague ideas like a “Europe of nations,” emphasizing both civilizational solidarity and the defense of national sovereignty. They have no shared federalist project, obviously, but faced with issues like high energy prices or rearmament, they can agree to some cross-border collaboration. And no one really wants to dynamite the euro.

Ferraresi: The reality is that on some issues, most notably immigration, the Overton window in the European Union has shifted significantly over the past decade. On other subjects, the pendulum has swung in the opposite direction: Positions on abortion or same-sex marriage that are now considered fringe were common among conservatives until relatively recently. We could find plenty of shifts in other areas. Remember when the Union was remarkably soft on Vladimir Putin’s Russia and eager to do business with it? That was not so long ago.

De Gruyter: Short answer: yes. Europe is about living together on a crowded continent. The only way far-right parties can succeed in European politics is by making compromises and seeking alliances. This is exactly what they are doing now in the European Parliament. Have you noticed that these parties all support protecting the single market against China and the United States? And condemn Mr. Trump for intending to snatch Greenland?

Schneider: We clearly need to talk about Mr. Trump. Let’s start with his administration’s support for these far-right parties, especially the AfD: How significant is that?

Ferraresi: It’s hard to prove or measure, but I think the AfD benefited very much from the Trumpian endorsement. Overall, it’s still a small party, but the Trump administration, and especially Marco Rubio’s State Department, was instrumental in creating a platform where parties like it could thrive. A pretty huge boost, all things considered.

Broder: The Trump administration and figures like Elon Musk undermine any attempt to wall off more radical parties like the AfD or Restore in Britain. So, they definitely give a platform to minoritarian forces. Yet it’s also true that the practical consequences of Mr. Trump’s conduct can be bad for these parties if they are in or near power. Mr. Trump’s Middle East policy, for example, has had direct effects on voters’ pockets.

De Gruyter: Well, it doesn’t always work: When the United States went all in for Viktor Orban in Hungary, he lost! Mr. Trump is incredibly unpopular in Europe, including with far-right voters. So, far-right parties are keeping their distance. Remember also when Ms. Le Pen was found guilty of embezzlement and Mr. Trump supported her? She hated it and refused to talk about it.

Schneider: If not always a successful booster, is the Trump administration — militantly anti-migrant, economically protectionist, culturally aggressive — a useful template for what far-right governments in Europe could look like?

Broder: Many battle lines are comparable to the United States, on identity and immigration, though some countries (like France) have a far more racialized political conflict than others (like Poland). Still, most European societies are less violent than the United States and I think ICE-style units aren’t quite on the agenda, even if Europe’s own border agency, Frontex, has also been implicated in the illegal pushback of migrants. Fundamentally, the European Union is not the same kind of power as the United States.

De Gruyter: What you see in America is exactly what you saw in Poland and Hungary during the reign of the far right. Most people did not vote for Law and Justice or Fidesz because they wanted to abolish democracy. They voted for them because of gasoline prices or other dissatisfactions with the performance of the previous government. When the parties started to attack democracy, voters turned away from them. That’s why, in the end, they lost.

Ferraresi: I don’t think a successful far-right governing party in Europe could realistically look like the Trump administration. One reason is the dense web of E. U. ties; another is that parliamentary systems are mostly designed to balance political forces, at the expense of executive power (and sometimes governability). Ms. Meloni, I think, is once again a case in point. I suspect any far-right party that wants to govern would have to follow a similar path.

Schneider: There are elections in Spain next month, in France and Italy next year, and in Britain and Germany before too long. By the end of these contests, far-right parties could be in power, jointly or alone, in all of them. So the last question is simple: How can they be stopped?

De Gruyter: By other parties. The far right needs other parties to get into government. So if center-right parties stay the course and make clear they will not work with the far right, many unhappy voters will not go for the far right — because that would make their vote pointless. It is only when center-right parties express willingness to cooperate with the far right that those parties can attract great numbers of votes. It’s quite simple, really.

Broder: Not just by warning against them but by mobilizing more people for something better. That may sound trite. But Pedro Sánchez did that last time in Spain: Back then, he ran on a record of cost-of-living measures, as well as criticizing the conservative and far-right alliance. Ultimately, angry nativist parties’ message takes root when mainstream parties fail to uphold a broadly accepted model of social progress and reward for hard work. Attending to that is the key antidote.

Ferraresi: In a democracy, far-right parties can only be stopped by other parties offering something more appealing to voters who are confused, scared and feel voiceless. Whether we like it or not, unregulated immigration is a source of concern for many in Europe, and mainstream parties need to face that and come up with competitive platforms. The far right thrives on the questions everyone else refuses to answer.

David Broder (@broderly) is the author, most recently, of “Mussolini’s Grandchildren: Fascism in Contemporary Italy.”
